item.title: The Fold — 2026-10-27
item.description: The Fold morning briefing for 27 October 2026: Brazil and Serbia prepare for new governments, Britain plans carers’ allowance reform, and AI companies face financial scrutiny.
item.content:encoded:
Tuesday 27 October 2026 · London

The Fold

Your morning briefing from the UK & the world

In this edition

  • Lula celebrates a fourth term as Brazilian parties recognise the result.
  • Serbia’s Student List prepares for talks to form a government.
  • Britain plans to replace the carers’ allowance earnings cliff edge.
  • Visa and Mastercard face an application for a £5 billion fees claim.
  • Anthropic publishes its stock-market listing documents.
  • Manchester United consider Michael Carrick’s future after another defeat.

News

Lula’s fourth term begins with a fight over Brazil’s direction

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva used his first celebrations after winning a fourth presidential term to promise that Brazil would remain a democracy. Tens of thousands of supporters gathered in central São Paulo early on Monday after a second-round comeback that overturned his defeat in the first round. Lula secured 64.2 million votes to Flávio Bolsonaro’s 59.8 million, a margin of 51.79% to 48.21%. No candidate who lost the first round had previously won the runoff since Brazil returned to democracy after its 1964–85 military dictatorship. (Guardian)

Recognition of the result widened during Monday, even as Bolsonaro continued to reject it. His Liberal party acknowledged the outcome almost a day after the vote, while seeking clarification of issues it had raised. Parties that backed Bolsonaro, including Republicanos and MDB, also congratulated Lula. That leaves an important distinction between the defeated candidate’s objections and the response of organisations whose representatives will take their seats and negotiate with the returning president. The presidents of Brazil’s electoral court, Chamber of Deputies and Senate were among those recognising the victory. (Guardian, Folha)

Donald Trump questioned the election’s credibility without providing evidence of wrongdoing in his remarks. Other governments moved quickly to recognise Lula, including rightwing leaders in Chile, Peru and Colombia as well as Mexico, Spain, the UK, China and the European Commission. The spread of those acknowledgements matters for Brazil’s diplomacy: governments with sharply different politics are preparing to deal with the elected president. During the campaign, the US had faced accusations of using economic and diplomatic pressure to influence the outcome. Lula’s win now requires both countries to manage a relationship that extends well beyond their leaders’ preferences. (Guardian)

At home, the next stage is assembling support for another administration in a country still closely divided. Lula gained more than 10 million votes between the two rounds, helped by mobilisation on the streets and online and lower abstention. Environmental policy is one immediate area of consequence. His former environment minister Marina Silva welcomed the result after warning that another Bolsonaro presidency would threaten Indigenous territories and the Amazon. The election has settled who will govern; decisions over ministers, congressional alliances and public spending will determine how much of the campaign programme becomes policy. Lula’s age also keeps succession firmly on the agenda: his fourth term would end when he is 85. (Guardian, Meio, Folha)

Serbia’s students prepare to turn a majority into a government

Serbia’s Student List began preparing for government talks after an election victory ended Aleksandar Vučić’s 14-year domination of the country’s politics. Projections based on all ballot samples put the movement on 53% of the vote and 141 of parliament’s 250 seats. Vučić’s Serbian Progressive party was projected to take 103 seats on 39%, with the remainder going to national minority lists. Vučić conceded on Sunday. By Monday, supporters were celebrating a result that had grown out of two years of protests following the Novi Sad railway station canopy collapse, which killed 16 people. (Guardian)

The movement now has to choose a prime minister and cabinet through a collective structure deliberately built without a single leader. Its candidates include academics, actors and farmers alongside students. Prominent figures include cardiologist Ilija Srdanović, former central bank governor Dejan Šoškić and chemistry professor Radomir Saičić. The list’s approach helped unite people around corruption and failing institutions. Running a government will require quicker decisions, named officeholders and a clear division of responsibility. Its parliamentary majority gives it room to act, while its lack of governing experience makes the transition a substantial undertaking. (Guardian)

Proposals include an independent police unit accountable to prosecutors, removing officers linked to organised crime, preventing party appointments to state companies and opening major infrastructure contracts to independent scrutiny. Implementing those changes means working through institutions staffed under the outgoing administration. Foreign policy questions, including Serbia’s relationships with Russia and the EU, were kept in the background during the campaign. Moscow expressed hope that cooperation would continue; Germany offered support for Serbia’s European path. The constitutional timetable now requires parliament to convene within 30 days of the official result, followed by a 90-day deadline to form a government. A separate presidential election is due before 27 December because Vučić stepped down to seek the premiership. (Guardian)

UK sanctions commanders over atrocities in Sudan

Britain imposed travel bans and asset freezes on 15 commanders from Sudan’s warring forces on the first anniversary of the fall of El Fasher. The measures target figures from both the Rapid Support Forces and the Sudanese Armed Forces suspected of involvement in sexual violence during the siege. Those named include RSF colonel Hussein Abu Jalak and Al-Nour Ahmed Adam, also known as Al-Qubba. The sanctions seek to restrict the commanders’ access to money and travel while adding to efforts to establish responsibility for abuses. (Guardian)

El Fasher’s capture followed an 18-month starvation siege. As many as 10,000 people are believed to have been killed over two days, and another 40,000 remain unaccounted for. Fewer than 70,000 people are thought to remain in a city whose prewar population exceeded a million. Survivors’ accounts describe detention, torture and unlawful killings. Across Sudan, the conflict has forced 14 million people from their homes and increasingly involves drone attacks on infrastructure. The latest RSF strikes on power stations caused widespread outages in the east. The UAE continues to deny allegations that it supports the RSF. The siege forced civilians to survive on animal feed, and the scale of the missing population continues to complicate the accounting of deaths. Sanctions are one instrument available to Britain, while humanitarian access and the protection of people still inside the city remain urgent practical problems. (Guardian)

Downing Street clarifies the limits of Burnham’s EU opening

Downing Street clarified that Andy Burnham was proposing a public discussion about Britain’s long-term relationship with the EU, without committing the government to restoring freedom of movement. The prime minister’s weekend comments had prompted questions about which Brexit restrictions he might be willing to revisit. On Monday he ruled out rejoining the EU during this parliament and said the government would respect Labour’s manifesto commitments. He also said Britain would not join the freedom of movement scheme without a referendum. (Guardian)

Burnham nevertheless left open the possibility of a future election fought on a pledge to rejoin, saying he would personally like to see Britain return to the EU in his lifetime. That separates his longer-term preference from the agreements ministers are currently seeking. He is due in Brussels for a UK–EU summit on 20 November, where the focus is on practical changes to the existing relationship. Downing Street has yet to establish how the public would decide on any more ambitious proposals. For businesses and people affected by cross-border rules, the immediate question is what the summit produces; a broader change would require a further political mandate and negotiations with the bloc. (Guardian)

Economy

Carers’ allowance is set to lose its earnings cliff edge

Unpaid carers are to be offered a tapered earnings system under plans for Wednesday’s budget, ending a rule that can wipe out a whole week’s benefit when wages exceed the limit by a penny. Chancellor John Healey plans to replace the cliff edge with a £1 reduction in allowance for each additional £1 earned above the threshold. The change addresses a longstanding trap for people fitting paid work around intensive caring responsibilities. The proposed £1-for-£1 withdrawal would allow additional wages to replace benefit gradually over the taper range. Carers would still need clear guidance on which earnings count and when the new rules take effect, particularly while the existing system remains in operation. Implementation will take time: the digital system needed to operate the taper is not expected before the end of the decade. (Guardian)

The current weekly earnings limit is £204 and the allowance is £86.45. Someone exceeding the limit by a penny every week for a year can therefore face a demand to repay £4,495.40, despite having earned only 52p above the permitted amount. Small pay rises, overtime and changes to the minimum wage have pushed carers over the threshold, sometimes without them realising. The Department for Work and Pensions had information about breaches but placed responsibility on claimants to report changes. Debts could accumulate for months or years before a repayment demand arrived. (Guardian)

An independent review led by disability rights expert Liz Sayce found that around 180,000 carers had accumulated £300 million in overpayment debts between 2019 and 2025. One case involved a minimum-wage increase that lifted earnings 15p a week above the limit without any change in hours. The carer eventually faced a £2,000 repayment demand after earning just £5 above the threshold. Campaigners welcomed the planned reform while expressing disappointment at the wait. For households managing at least 35 hours of caring each week, the eventual taper should remove the risk of a small extra shift leaving them substantially poorer. (Guardian)

Other measures outlined ahead of the budget include additional parental support for 150,000 people, including self-employed fathers and partners who previously missed out. Payments could be worth up to £194 a week. Healey also plans to make higher tax-free mileage rates permanent, at 55p a mile for the first 10,000 business miles and 35p thereafter. The Treasury estimates that around three million employees and self-employed people use their own vehicles for work. The budget’s wider limits remain significant: pressure on the public finances, including the effects of the Iran conflict, has reduced the chancellor’s room for larger spending commitments. (Guardian)

Visa and Mastercard face a proposed £5 billion fees claim

An application at the Competition Appeal Tribunal seeks permission for a group claim against Visa and Mastercard over the fees UK organisations pay when customers use cards. Law firms Harcus Parker and Hausfeld allege that the companies restricted competition and allowed excessive multilateral interchange fees. These are set by the card networks and passed on to businesses through their banks. The proposed case covers charges since October 2020, plus interest, and could be worth about £5 billion. That figure is an estimate of the claim’s potential value, with liability still to be determined. (Guardian)

If approved, the action would automatically include an estimated one million UK businesses, organisations and charities with revenue below £100 million unless they opt out. Larger businesses would have to join actively. Individual recoveries would depend on the organisation and its payment history, and a conclusion could take years. Bench Walk Advisors is funding the litigation, which is led by businessman Stephen Allen. Mastercard disputes the basis of the case and describes interchange as important to secure, efficient payments. Visa likewise defends the fees as a central part of the digital payments system. The tribunal must first decide whether the proposed collective action can proceed. (Guardian)

Electric-car incentives could reward batteries that support the grid

Ministers are considering credits for carmakers that install vehicle-to-grid technology as part of changes to the zero-emission vehicle mandate. Bidirectional charging allows a car to draw power when it is plentiful and return some to the grid when demand is high. A compatible vehicle can also supply a home. Used widely, parked cars could help balance a system with more wind and solar generation, reducing the need to start expensive gas-fired plants during periods of low renewable output. Similar services already operate on a limited scale in Britain and elsewhere in Europe. (Guardian)

The proposed incentive raises a separate question about the number of petrol cars manufacturers would be allowed to sell. Extra credits for fitting bidirectional equipment could help a company meet its obligations while selling fewer fully electric vehicles. New AutoMotive argues that rewards should depend on the technology actually being used, especially while compatible home chargers remain expensive and uncommon. Driver representatives also question changing sales requirements before the service has been tested at scale. The National Energy System Operator estimates that participating cars could provide 1.2 gigawatts of power on demand by 2030, potentially rising to 41 gigawatts by 2050. Those forecasts depend on adoption: installing the capability, connecting cars and persuading drivers to participate are all necessary steps. (Guardian)

Technology

Anthropic’s public filing opens its finances to scrutiny

Anthropic has publicly filed for a US stock-market listing, giving investors a detailed look at the costs and revenue behind Claude. The company plans to trade under ANT after submitting a confidential filing in June. Estimates from analysts and investors have placed its value above $1.5 trillion, making the offering a major test of confidence in the AI industry. A final valuation and successful listing remain ahead. The prospectus makes it possible to examine the business against audited figures alongside the ambitious claims surrounding the technology. (Guardian)

Revenue rose from $41 million in 2023 to $386 million in 2024 and $4.585 billion in 2025, then reached $16.286 billion in the first half of 2026. The same six-month period produced a disclosed net loss of $80 billion. Anthropic had raised $141.1 billion by the end of June and disclosed $6.2 billion in debt. Its focus on business customers has brought rapid growth, but the top five customers account for a quarter of revenue. Losing a large account could therefore have a material effect even while the total customer base expands. Spending on computing capacity is another major demand on its finances. (Guardian)

More than 90 pages of risk disclosures cover commercial, political and safety concerns. The company acknowledges that safeguards against misuse can fail or be circumvented, including where systems could assist cyberattacks or dangerous weapons development. It also faces a dispute with the Trump administration after being designated a supply-chain risk, preventing military agencies from contracting with it; Anthropic is challenging the designation. Those issues now sit alongside conventional investor questions about customer concentration, debt and losses. The offering will test how buyers price a fast-growing company whose infrastructure commitments and exposure to government decisions remain substantial. (Guardian)

Microsoft offers buyouts as divisions reshape their workforces

Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, with divisions including Xbox, Windows and Copilot participating. Employees in some areas, including cybersecurity, data centres and marketing, are excluded. The company describes the offer as a supported route for eligible staff considering leaving and a way for participating organisations to adjust to changing needs. The number eligible is not a count of confirmed departures: take-up will determine the eventual reduction. (Guardian)

The programme follows an April offer of voluntary retirement to around 7% of Microsoft’s US workforce. Its global workforce totals about 223,000. Other large technology employers have also reduced staffing while increasing AI investment, although evidence that the changes are delivering productivity gains remains mixed. A recent National Bureau of Economic Research working paper covering 9,000 senior executives found that 90% had yet to see greater productivity from AI at their companies. Microsoft’s next decisions will show how far it intends to shift resources among established products, AI development and the infrastructure needed to run those services. (Guardian)

Apple updates software and acknowledges folding-screen cracks

Apple released iOS and iPadOS 27.2, adding support for the USB-C Apple Pencil on the iPhone Duo alongside further Siri improvements. It also announced a revised iPad mini with an 8.5-inch OLED display and a landscape Center Stage camera. The launches expand the uses of Apple’s smaller portable devices, with handwriting support reaching its folding phone and the mini receiving a larger screen. (MacStories, MacStories)

Separately, Apple acknowledged an inner-display problem affecting a small number of iPhone Duo units after users described cracks along the hinge. Affected owners can contact AppleCare for a replacement. The company’s statement does not establish how widespread the fault is or identify its cause, so the reports should be treated as an emerging hardware issue. The response gives owners a route to support while leaving questions about the pattern and frequency of failures unresolved. (9to5Mac)

Sports

Carrick waits as United consider their next move

Manchester United’s football leadership discussed Michael Carrick’s position on Monday after a 3–0 home defeat by Bournemouth left the club 16th in the Premier League, one point above the relegation zone. United have gone eight games without a win and have only two victories all season. Carrick attended Carrington to watch an under-21 match while director of football Jason Wilcox and chief executive Omar Berrada considered his future. No dismissal had been confirmed in the Monday account of those discussions. (Guardian)

Eddie Howe is Wilcox’s preferred replacement if United make a change, with contact understood to have taken place. Unai Emery and Julian Nagelsmann are also admired, although recruiting Emery from Aston Villa would involve substantial compensation. The uncertainty follows a 4–1 Champions League defeat at Como and Carrick’s decision to leave Bruno Fernandes on the bench against Bournemouth. Elsewhere, Arsenal’s 2–0 win over Everton brought Mikel Arteta a second booking of the season, leaving him one further caution from a touchline suspension. Aston Villa beat Manchester City 2–1, with goalkeeper Zion Suzuki helping protect the result. These developments leave United facing an immediate management decision while rivals assess a weekend that shifted pressure across several benches. (Guardian)

The Fold

A daily briefing for Londoners who want the full picture in one place.

Inspired by Brazil’s Meio · Tuesday, 27 October 2026 · leonardoresston.github.io/thefold

item.title: The Fold — 2026-10-26
item.description: The Fold morning briefing for 26 October 2026: Serbia’s election result, Storm Boelo, Britain’s European debate, and the week’s business, technology and football news.
item.content:encoded:
Monday 26 October 2026 · London

The Fold

Your morning briefing from the UK & the world

In this edition

  • Serbia’s student movement wins a parliamentary majority in preliminary results.
  • Storm Boelo kills two people and leaves thousands without power.
  • Burnham opens a debate on restoring free movement with the EU.
  • Audi plans a $4bn SUV factory in Georgia.
  • Early iPhone Duo screen failures prompt scrutiny of its hinge.
  • Manchester United consider Carrick’s future after a 3–0 home defeat.

News

Serbia’s student movement wins at the ballot box

Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat in Serbia’s parliamentary election on Sunday, opening the way for a student-led movement to take power after two years of protests. Preliminary projections gave the Student List an outright majority in the 250-seat parliament. Vučić acknowledged that his Serbian Progressive party had lost, putting the students on course to end his 12-year dominance of the country’s politics. Celebrations spread through Belgrade and other cities as supporters gathered in the streets, waving, embracing and sounding car horns. (Guardian)

The figures remained provisional. A representative sample from CeSID and Ipsos projected 138 seats for the Student List and 104 for Vučić’s party, with minority parties likely to share the remainder. By 7pm, estimated turnout had reached 67.6%, the highest since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992. Some voters waited for as long as two hours. That mobilisation followed a final campaign rally in Belgrade attended by an estimated 150,000 people, an indication of how far the movement had travelled beyond university campuses. (Guardian)

Its origins lie in the collapse of a concrete canopy at Novi Sad railway station in November 2024, which killed 16 people. Anger over evidence of poor construction and corruption grew into a national challenge to the government. Vučić resigned the presidency last month and gambled on a snap election. The students assembled a full slate of parliamentary candidates, including academics, athletes and farmers, and campaigned in rural areas long considered strongholds of the ruling party. (Guardian)

The immediate task is to turn that coalition into a government capable of delivering its promises of accountability and democratic renewal. The campaign took place against a ruling party with extensive influence over broadcasting and state institutions. Monitors raised concerns about surveillance, intimidation and irregularities, including suspected vote-buying on election day. Vučić’s concession substantially eased fears that he would reject defeat. Final results and the transfer of authority will now determine how quickly the new majority can begin its work. (Guardian)

Storm Boelo kills two and cuts power across Britain

Two men were killed by falling trees on Sunday as Storm Boelo brought damaging winds, electricity failures and transport disruption across Britain. A 60-year-old man died on a minor road at Mid Kelton in south-west Scotland. In London, a man in his 20s was killed when a tree fell on his car in Mill Hill at about 12.40pm. The deaths came during a weekend in which the strongest weather affected Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England, with dangerous conditions reaching well beyond the areas under amber warnings. (Guardian)

More than 160,000 properties were left without power. Around 53,000 Scottish homes remained disconnected at 5pm, according to network operators’ updates. Gusts reached 84mph in Argyll and Bute, 83mph in Eryri and 82mph on Tiree. Engineers were working to restore supplies, but high winds and difficult access limited where repairs could safely begin. Scotland’s resilience room met on Sunday afternoon, bringing ministers, emergency agencies and forecasters together to assess outages and the response. (Guardian)

Rail services faced speed restrictions and closures, with flooding and fallen trees affecting lines in Scotland. Flights were cancelled or diverted at Leeds Bradford airport. Network Rail also shared images of loose garden objects reaching the railway, including a trampoline beneath a train. The Met Office advised people in affected areas to secure outdoor items and stay indoors because of flying debris and dangerous waves. Boelo followed Storm Austen, which had brought strong winds to south-west England on Friday, leaving network operators and transport services dealing with successive periods of severe weather. Further difficult conditions were expected early in the week. (Guardian)

Burnham opens the argument over free movement

Andy Burnham has opened a debate over restoring free movement with the EU, with senior cabinet support and warnings from Labour MPs representing Brexit-voting areas. The prime minister signalled that keeping Britain outside free movement would cease to be an absolute condition in negotiations with Europe. He also suggested that a manifesto commitment could provide a mandate for rejoining the single market without another referendum, while full EU membership would require a new public vote. (Guardian)

Housing secretary Angela Rayner backed discussing the trade-offs and putting a proposal to voters at a general election. Foreign secretary Ed Miliband is among ministers favouring a closer European relationship. The political resistance is already visible: some MPs in the north and Midlands fear that reopening immigration arguments will expose their seats to Reform UK. Home secretary Shabana Mahmood has previously stressed the difficult choices involved in closer ties. The Conservatives and Reform attacked Burnham’s intervention, while Labour’s existing manifesto still rules out returning to the single market and free movement. (Guardian)

Businesses have a different immediate concern: the limits of the current arrangement for trade. The British Chambers of Commerce wants the Treasury to examine the economic effects of alternative UK-EU relationships, arguing that the reset agreed under Keir Starmer in May 2025 is approaching its practical limits. Paperwork and barriers to trading with European customers remain a source of frustration. Free movement would also restore reciprocal opportunities for British and EU citizens to work across borders, linking the immigration argument to the wider question of economic access. (Guardian)

Next month’s EU summit gives the discussion a near-term setting, although no change has been agreed. This week’s budget adds pressure to explain the growth consequences of Britain’s choices. Lower migration can reduce forecast tax receipts and narrow the chancellor’s room to meet fiscal rules. The Office for Budget Responsibility has previously estimated that Brexit’s trade and mobility barriers will leave long-run output about 4% lower. Burnham now has to turn an invitation to debate into a clear negotiating position and an electoral offer. (Guardian)

An extra £432m for the rough-sleeping pledge

The government plans to commit another £432m to tackling rough sleeping in this week’s budget, taking the announced funding close to £900m. Burnham wants everyone sleeping rough in England to have an offer of a safe route off the streets or wider support by Christmas. The additional money is intended to sustain that effort through the rest of the parliament, extending beyond the immediate winter deadline. An initial £442m from housing department budgets is due to be allocated before March 2027. (Guardian)

A Downing Street summit on Monday will bring together charities, businesses, housing providers and local leaders. Specialist outreach teams and additional accommodation are already operating in Coventry, with provision being expanded in places including Plymouth and Camden. The National Housing Federation is working with housing associations to identify at least 2,000 potential homes and bed spaces, including empty buildings that could be brought back into use. Those spaces will be central to translating a national funding announcement into somewhere people can actually stay. (Guardian)

Burnham’s Greater Manchester experience helps explain the emphasis on coordination. His A Bed Every Night programme expanded emergency accommodation, but reductions in rough sleeping were followed by renewed increases. He has argued that people travelled to the region because support elsewhere was weaker. The government’s current promise depends on councils and services across England moving together, and on support continuing after someone first leaves the street. Shelter welcomed the funding, while the Conservatives challenged its cost and Burnham’s record. With two months to the deadline, delivery will be judged through accommodation and sustained help for individuals. (Guardian)

France’s protest bill raises fears of collective liability

France’s senate will debate legislation this week that could make demonstrators liable for up to €10,000 of damage even when they did not personally cause it. The proposed law would apply to people continuing to demonstrate near vandals or within the same group, and would expand the use of drones over protests. Trade unions, civil liberties groups and leftwing politicians warn that the financial risk could deter peaceful participants from attending demonstrations at all. (Guardian)

The government is pushing the measure during a widening confrontation over schools, living costs and public services. High-school students have spent more than a month protesting over absent teachers, deteriorating buildings and the university applications system. Unions and yellow-vest activists have joined the demonstrations. Earlier this month, largely peaceful protests were accompanied by looting, fires and damage to public buildings, prompting tighter security measures and restrictions on gatherings. Prime minister Sébastien Lecornu argues that the new law is essential to respond to that destruction. (Guardian)

The bill was originally prepared after violence surrounding Paris Saint-Germain’s Champions League victory in May. It now sits within a broader set of restrictions, including bans on gatherings outside schools and demonstrations in city centres, as well as local curfews. Opponents fear these powers will create lasting constraints on public protest. Marine Le Pen, launching her presidential campaign in Orléans on Sunday, embraced the demand that vandals pay. Lecornu is due to meet student representatives on Monday, with pressure growing for a response on school funding and repairs alongside the security measures. (Guardian)

Machado returns to Venezuela

María Corina Machado returned to Venezuela on Sunday after almost a year abroad, appearing among supporters in Barquisimeto before travelling towards Caracas. Her ally Edmundo González, who remains in exile, confirmed her arrival and said he also intended to return. Images showed crowds greeting Machado at the Sanctuary of the Divine Shepherdess church and along the road as her convoy moved east. How she entered the country was not immediately clear. (Guardian)

Her arrival brings a leading opponent of interim president Delcy Rodríguez back into domestic politics. Machado left Venezuela last December to receive the Nobel peace prize, shortly before the US operation that seized Nicolás Maduro in January. Although her movement is widely believed to have won the 2024 presidential election, Maduro refused to relinquish power. Washington subsequently established a working relationship with Rodríguez, his former vice-president, leaving Machado outside the administration that followed his removal. (Guardian)

Machado has called for fresh presidential elections by July 2027. Whether the Trump administration supports that timetable remains unclear. US secretary of state Marco Rubio credited US-backed reconciliation talks with creating the conditions for her return, pointing to the release of political prisoners and the return of opposition figures. Venezuelan officials had previously suggested she could face arrest, but there was no visible intervention by security services as she travelled on Sunday. Her freedom to organise, and the government’s response to her renewed presence, will shape the next stage of the electoral dispute. (Guardian)

Audi commits $4bn to a US SUV factory

Audi plans to spend $4bn on its first US factory, shifting some production across the Atlantic as Volkswagen absorbs the cost of American tariffs. The plant in Macon, Georgia, is intended to produce 200,000 SUVs and create 4,500 jobs. It will build the Q7, Q8 and Q9, moving some output from Bratislava in Slovakia. Audi chief executive Gernot Döllner announced the investment alongside Donald Trump at a campaign rally on Saturday night, shortly before the US midterm elections. (Guardian)

The decision reflects the strain that 15% tariffs on EU imports are placing on European manufacturers. Volkswagen has estimated that the duties cost it up to €5bn a year before allowing for lost sales. The group has also been shifting some production of cheaper models from Mexico to the US. Building near American buyers gives Audi a way to reduce its exposure to import charges, although a new factory is a long-term investment whose benefits will depend on demand and the trading environment over many years. (Guardian)

The announcement comes as Volkswagen cuts jobs and closes factories at home. It has cited competition from Chinese carmakers, tariffs and the expense of investing in electric vehicles for other markets. Audi sees continued American demand for large petrol SUVs and is developing the Q9 with that market in mind. The investment gives Trump a prominent manufacturing announcement, while adding to the difficult allocation choices facing a European car industry trying to fund new technology and maintain competitiveness across markets with increasingly different policies. (Guardian)

Technology

The iPhone Duo’s hinge comes under scrutiny

Early reports of broken iPhone Duo screens have put the folding handset’s hinge under scrutiny just days after launch. Some owners describe cracks running down the centre of the inner display, accompanied by a horizontal strip of pixels glowing white. A teardown by iFixit offers a possible mechanical explanation, while stopping short of establishing a confirmed cause. The company suspects that part of the complex hinge may sometimes fail to descend properly, concentrating pressure in a vulnerable area. (The Verge)

An accordion-style cable passes over the same point, close to the battery’s edge. That arrangement could help explain the audible crack described by some owners. The evidence so far does not establish how widespread the failures are, and the proposed explanation remains a theory. Apple had not immediately responded to a request for comment. Establishing whether the issue affects a small batch, particular conditions or a wider design will require more information than individual failure reports and a single teardown can provide. (The Verge)

The inspection also found practical improvements. iFixit gave the Duo a repairability score of five out of ten, its highest for a foldable. The outer nano-texture layer can be replaced relatively easily without changing the OLED panel underneath. That surface scatters reflections, helping disguise the crease, while unusual subpixel arrangements may also reduce its visibility. Dust entered the port, speaker grilles and hinge, but less penetrated the phone than in the competing foldables used for comparison. Repairing the inner display itself remains difficult and expensive. Those findings leave the first weekend of ownership with encouraging repair features and an unresolved durability question. (The Verge)

Elvis catalogue owners sue Anthropic

The owners of Elvis Presley’s music catalogue have sued Anthropic, alleging that it used 274 songs without permission to train its AI models. Authentic Brands Group, which controls rights connected to Presley’s music and likeness, is seeking $150,000 for each allegedly infringed track, a total of about $41m. The case was filed on Friday and detailed on Sunday. The songs named include Can’t Help Falling in Love, All Shook Up and A Little Less Conversation. (Guardian)

The complaint also alleges that Claude generated infringing versions of copyrighted material and that safeguards introduced to prevent such output were ineffective. These are allegations to be tested in court. The filing brings an artist’s estate directly into the growing litigation over how AI developers obtain and use creative work. Record labels and industry bodies have already pursued copyright claims against AI companies, while musicians have raised concerns about imitation and the use of their work without consent. (Guardian)

For catalogue owners, the dispute concerns control of a commercially valuable body of songs and the ability to set terms for its use. For developers, cases of this kind bear on the material available for training and the measures needed to prevent protected text from appearing in responses. The Presley claim combines those questions in one action, seeking damages for the alleged use of the catalogue while challenging the effectiveness of output restrictions. No finding of infringement follows from the filing itself. (Guardian)

Sports

United consider Carrick’s future after another defeat

Manchester United’s hierarchy held crisis talks over Michael Carrick’s future after a 3–0 home defeat by Bournemouth left the club 16th in the Premier League. Rayan, Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson scored for the visitors, handing United a sixth defeat in 12 matches across all competitions. They have won only once in the league this season, and their last victory in any competition came against Sabah in the Champions League on 10 September. (Guardian)

Eddie Howe is the preferred replacement of director of football Jason Wilcox if the club makes a change. Other admired candidates include Unai Emery and Julian Nagelsmann, although Aston Villa would demand substantial compensation for Emery. No dismissal had been announced on Sunday. Carrick insisted he was continuing as normal and acknowledged that results and performances had fallen short. United would need to inform the New York Stock Exchange before announcing a managerial dismissal, with the exchange closed over the weekend. (Guardian)

The selection of Bruno Fernandes became a focal point. Carrick left his captain out of the starting side after Fernandes criticised his tactics following the midweek defeat at Como, but maintained that the decision was taken for football reasons. Fernandes remained an unused substitute. Supporters applauded Carrick as he left the pitch before booing players who followed him down the tunnel. Harry Maguire, captain for the day, said the squad backed the coach and needed to improve its own performances. The club enters the week facing a decision over leadership amid a prolonged shortage of wins. (Guardian)

Liverpool end Brighton’s winning run

Liverpool earned their first home Premier League win of the season, beating Brighton 2–0 through a Pascal Gross own goal and an Alexander Isak finish. The result ended Brighton’s run of four successive league victories and clean sheets. Isak’s goal took him to six in six Premier League appearances, providing another sign of his growing effectiveness in a forward line that also includes Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola. (Guardian)

Wirtz helped force the breakthrough after Ronald Araújo won the ball and delivered a low cross. The move ended with Wirtz’s shot taking a decisive deflection off Gross. Barcola then capitalised on a poor clearance from Olivier Boscagli and supplied Isak, who guided the ball into the far corner. Brighton had earlier wasted a clear opportunity through Yasin Ayari, whose missed chance became more costly as Liverpool scored twice in quick succession. (Guardian)

Ayari also hit a post after an Alisson passing error, but Brighton struggled to turn their second-half possession into clear chances. Araújo, Jérémy Jacquet and Virgil van Dijk made important interventions, with support from players tracking back ahead of them. Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola praised the aggressive start and the ability to recover possession and attack quickly. The match went ahead despite Storm Boelo, with conditions inside Anfield relatively calm. For Liverpool, the combination of sharper attacking play and sustained defensive work delivered a home league result that had been missing from their season. (Guardian)

The Fold

A daily briefing for Londoners who want the full picture in one place.

item.title: The Fold — 2026-10-23
item.description: The Fold morning briefing for 23 October 2026: Britain’s emergency guidance, Ukraine’s satellite dispute, Brazil’s runoff and the global PHP security response.
item.content:encoded:
Friday 23 October 2026 · London

The Fold

Your morning briefing from the UK & the world

In this edition

  • Britain asks households to prepare for three days of disruption.
  • Ukraine seeks clarity over restored satellite communications.
  • Brazil steps back from restricting large WhatsApp channels before the runoff.
  • City regulators propose reducing enhanced checks on financial services staff.
  • Organisations race to patch critical flaws in PHP.
  • Arsenal’s Bruno Guimarães describes his move from Newcastle.

News

Britain asks households to prepare for three days of disruption

Households are being asked to prepare for three days without the everyday services they rely on, as ministers warn about severe weather, cyber-attacks and sabotage. The new Be Ready campaign covers food, drinking water, warmth and ways to receive information during an outage. Defence secretary Wes Streeting said families and businesses should think through how they would cope if supply chains or payment systems stopped working. He said the advice was intended to improve general readiness, with no particular imminent incident behind its release. (BBC)

The checklist starts with three litres of drinking water per person each day, with extra needed for cooking and washing, and food that can be eaten without refrigeration or cooking. A torch and spare batteries, warm clothes, blankets, a charged power bank and a battery-powered or wind-up FM radio are among the suggested supplies. Written phone numbers and radio frequencies give people a way to stay informed when a phone has run out of power. The guidance also covers copies of important documents and a mix of cash and cards. (GOV.UK)

People are encouraged to start with what is already in their cupboards and buy missing essentials gradually. The list needs to fit the household: regular medicines, baby supplies, equipment and food for pets may all matter. Ready-to-feed baby formula is suggested because boiling water could become difficult. Households can review their supplies every six months, replacing expired items and changing the kit as their needs change. The campaign acknowledges that people have different resources and will be able to take different steps. (GOV.UK)

Preparation also means agreeing who will check on someone who lives alone, choosing a meeting place if family members cannot contact each other, and sharing details with neighbours. Eligible households can register for extra support from their utility providers. Streeting linked the campaign to this summer’s fires and the prospect of winter flooding, while security minister Dan Jarvis said better household readiness would let emergency services concentrate on people who need the most help. The advice arrives as public bodies are dealing with a major software security alert. (GOV.UK, BBC)

Military aircraft join Britain’s wildfire response

RAF Chinook helicopters and A400M planes will be available to help civilian firefighters tackle wildfires across the UK, under plans announced ahead of Friday’s first national wildfire summit. Fire services will be able to request support for difficult terrain, including steep hillsides and remote moorland. There have been 1,350 wildfires in England and Wales this year, according to the National Fire Chiefs Council, following Britain’s hottest summer on record. MPs have warned that arrangements for aerial support and water supplies need improvement. (BBC)

The government also plans £45m for lighter protective equipment designed for prolonged work outdoors, and a £25m programme running from April 2027 to April 2029 to restore dried-out peatlands in England. Rewetting peat can help create natural firebreaks. Support for farmers to make land more resistant to fire and closer work with devolved governments are also planned. The summit will bring together fire chiefs, local leaders and technology specialists as ministers consider stronger restrictions on activities and products that can start fires during periods of high risk. (BBC)

Ukraine waits for clarity over satellite access as peace diplomacy resumes

Donald Trump said Elon Musk had restored Ukraine’s Starlink internet access after restrictions hampered its armed forces. Earlier on Thursday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the military service had still not returned to its full operating speed. Musk has denied responsibility for the slowdown, and the White House has denied ordering restrictions. Ukraine uses civilian Starlink alongside the more secure Starshield network for military communications, including drones. Changes to connectivity can therefore affect both attacks and defence against incoming weapons. (BBC)

Trump declined to confirm whether he had personally asked Musk to remove limits. The competing accounts leave important details unresolved: who imposed the restrictions, precisely which services were affected and how fully access has recovered. Zelenskyy said he was waiting for information from US secretary of state Marco Rubio. The dispute comes as Washington presses Kyiv to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries, with Trump arguing that the attacks have pushed energy costs higher. Ukraine and European allies have criticised his easing of some Russian sanctions. (BBC)

Britain meanwhile rejected US envoy Steve Witkoff’s praise of Vladimir Putin after their meeting in St Petersburg. Downing Street pointed to the deaths caused by Russia’s invasion and its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Russia agreed in principle to resume talks with Ukraine and the US, while missile and drone attacks continued. Trump suggested a settlement might be closer. The UK has continued to back Zelenskyy, whom Andy Burnham received at Downing Street last week. Further negotiations would take place with fighting still under way and substantial differences over the terms of any settlement. (Guardian)

Brazil steps back from a WhatsApp restriction before the runoff

Brazil’s electoral court president, Kassio Nunes Marques, said a proposal to suspend large WhatsApp channels around the presidential runoff was unlikely to proceed for this election. The draft would have affected channels with more than 200,000 followers during the 48 hours before voting and 24 hours afterwards. Channels used by both Lula’s and Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaigns would have fallen within its scope. The proposal could return for the 2028 municipal elections. (Meio)

A group of 110 legal specialists, researchers and civil society representatives opposed the measure, arguing that it would restrict political expression and change the conditions of the contest shortly before voting. The draft envisaged preventive suspension based on audience size, without requiring a proven breach. Existing rules already allow punishment of unlawful digital campaigning. The debate has exposed divisions over how electoral authorities should respond to powerful online channels during a close presidential race. (Meio)

The campaigns are also trading demands for the release of financial and telephone records before the Globo debate. Lula challenged Bolsonaro to disclose eight years of records concerning himself and relatives, offering reciprocal disclosure. Bolsonaro responded with additional conditions and argued that the proposal would miss possible activity involving third parties. Lula accepted the conditions and promised to file an authorisation with the electoral court. Those public commitments still need to be distinguished from the records themselves: the exchange has created a test of what each campaign will actually make available. (Meio)

A global assessment puts coral reefs at severe risk

Almost all the world’s shallow-water coral reefs face a high risk of ecosystem collapse by 2075 when projected warming is included in a new assessment coordinated by the International Union for Conservation of Nature. It examined 127 reef regions across more than 80 countries. About 24% are already classed as critically endangered; the share rises to 96% when future climate impacts are taken into account. The projection assumes an emissions pathway leading to roughly 2.7C of warming by the end of the century. (Guardian)

Collapse means a reef can no longer sustain itself after a near-total or complete loss of living reef-building corals. That would affect fisheries, coastal protection and tourism, alongside the many marine species that depend on reefs. The assessment does not fully capture the latest global mass bleaching event. Scientists stress that rapid emissions cuts and local conservation could still improve the outlook. Reducing pollution and overfishing can help reefs withstand pressure, while the scale of ocean warming remains central to their survival. (Guardian)

Economy

City regulators propose narrower accountability checks

The Bank of England and Financial Conduct Authority have proposed reducing the number of financial services staff covered by enhanced personal checks. Around 140,000 managers would be freed from the additional requirements, while the most senior executives would still need to demonstrate that they are fit and proper annually and before taking a new job. The changes concern rules introduced after the financial crisis, when public anger centred on how few senior bankers had been held personally accountable. (Guardian)

Reporting requirements for lower-level misconduct would also be eased. Firms would generally report serious misconduct, final warnings and dismissals, while initial misconduct involving senior executives would still need to be flagged. Regulators estimate that removing the requirements could save businesses about £2bn over ten years. They say standards of conduct and accountability would remain in place. The proposals continue a broader push to make UK finance more competitive, following earlier changes including removal of the cap on bankers’ bonuses. Their practical effect will depend on how firms identify and escalate problems under the narrower regime. (Guardian)

AI investment costs weigh on technology companies

Technology shares fell sharply on Thursday as investors questioned the cost of financing the AI expansion, even where companies delivered revenue growth. Building datacentres and buying advanced chips has become more expensive, while borrowing costs have raised questions about the returns those investments will produce. Meta fell after revenue exceeded expectations but profit disappointed, and it announced a new class of stock to help fund AI spending and other costs. Chip equipment maker Lam Research also dropped despite slightly better-than-expected results. (Guardian)

The selling spread across major technology markets in Asia and the US. Nvidia and heavily indebted cloud provider CoreWeave were among the companies under pressure. Most companies in the S&P 500 actually rose, showing how strongly the largest technology businesses can determine the index’s direction. Higher oil costs added to concerns as the Iran war continued to disrupt expectations for energy supply. The combination puts corporate spending plans under closer scrutiny: businesses face expensive expansion projects at the same time as customers and investors are becoming more demanding about their payoff. (Guardian)

Technology

The race to patch PHP reaches public services and small businesses

Organisations around the world are checking and updating their systems after critical flaws were found in PHP, the programming language behind a large share of the web. Britain’s technology minister told the Lords that 32 government services were unavailable and four were partially unavailable, largely because operators had taken precautionary steps while applying updates. The government said major public-facing critical services were unaffected. The National Cyber Security Centre had no indication of successful breaches at the time of its statement. An unavailable website alone does not establish that an attacker gained access. (BBC)

The disruption has nevertheless reached everyday tasks. A garage owner in Chepstow described having to record MOT work on paper because its online system was unavailable. Websites and services in several countries were temporarily withdrawn while their operators checked exposure. Cloudflare described a rapid increase in attempted exploitation after the disclosure. The scale of attempted attacks and the number of confirmed compromises are separate questions, and the full impact may take time to establish. (BBC)

The vulnerabilities sit in PHP’s core engine, so a website can be exposed even when its own application code has no corresponding flaw. Research company Wiz demonstrated remote execution of code and disclosure of sensitive memory, which can contain passwords or authentication tokens. Its tests used WordPress, Drupal and Joomla as examples. A patch was released on Wednesday after coordinated work involving researchers, PHP developers and infrastructure providers. Updating the underlying software is central to the response. (Wiz)

Researchers also described how AI helped them connect longstanding weaknesses into working exploits and test variations across different systems. That can help defenders uncover problems that have survived years of examination, while reducing the specialist effort needed to develop attacks. The immediate challenge is the web’s varied ownership: large platforms, small charities and independently hosted sites all rely on shared software but have very different resources for maintaining it. The repair work reaches far beyond the organisations whose names appear on the biggest websites. (Wiz)

Higher component costs hit PC demand

Global PC shipments fell 21% year on year in the third quarter, according to Counterpoint Research, ending a long period of growth. Higher prices for memory, storage and processors have fed through to finished computers, squeezing buyers with smaller budgets. Manufacturers are shifting towards configurations that can absorb those costs more easily, leaving fewer affordable choices. Some are bringing older components back into use to keep prices down. (The Verge)

The comparison is also affected by last year’s purchases ahead of the Windows 10 support deadline and inventory changes associated with tariffs. Those factors make the drop larger, although the pressure on affordability remains. Counterpoint expects another sharp decline in the final quarter and broadly flat shipments in 2027. A stable shipment total would therefore leave the industry operating at a lower level. The figures describe units shipped rather than a direct count of people replacing computers, but they show how component inflation can slow demand across the wider hardware market. (The Verge)

Arc sets a December closure date

The Browser Company will shut down Arc on 22 December, ending the browser’s remaining support as it concentrates on Dia. New account creation has already stopped. On 23 November, Browse for Me and other AI features are due to be disabled, along with login and tab synchronisation. The final phase includes deactivating user accounts and removing Arc Search from Google Play. Security updates will also end. (MacMagazine)

The timetable gives existing users two separate deadlines to consider, with account and synchronisation functions disappearing a month before the final shutdown. Arc had already stopped receiving active development, although security maintenance had continued. The company considered making it open source and decided against doing so because its software development kit remained valuable to the business. The Browser Company is now owned by Atlassian. The announcement closes a product that built a following around a distinctive approach to tabs and browsing, as its developer puts its resources into an AI-focused successor. (MacMagazine)

1Password builds a sign-in route for AI agents

1Password has announced a platform that lets AI agents request access to accounts while keeping the credentials themselves out of the agent’s hands. When an agent encounters a login form, it identifies itself to 1Password and asks to use a credential. If the user approves, the password manager fills the details directly into the destination website. The service builds on an earlier Claude integration and is intended to support several agent providers. (MacMagazine)

The feature is optional and included without an extra charge for personal and family subscribers, with a waiting list for interested users. Agent connectors must be enabled before they can request access to a vault. That makes approval and account access part of the same workflow as the task the agent is carrying out. The design addresses a practical obstacle for assistants that act on websites: signing in can otherwise require handing sensitive credentials to another system or repeatedly asking a person to take over. (MacMagazine)

Australian court orders changes to iPhone app distribution

Australia’s Federal Court has ordered Apple to allow competing app stores, alternative payment systems and direct downloads on iOS following its antitrust battle with Epic Games. Developers using alternative distribution must receive access to equivalent tools and terms, and Apple is barred from penalising them for that choice. The order also limits attempts to collect commissions on purchases made through outside payment services or websites. (MacMagazine)

Apple can retain security and privacy checks, including notarisation, and can remove or disable apps that pose security risks or breach legal requirements. It cannot use those checks to obstruct alternative installation. The rules are due to take effect on 1 March next year, with the possibility of a court-approved extension to 3 May. Apple plans to appeal, citing intellectual property and safety concerns. The implementation timetable and appeal mean the ruling sets out required changes whose final operation still has to be worked through. (MacMagazine)

Apple adds an assistant to Pages, Numbers and Keynote

Apple has updated its office apps with an Intelligent Assistant that responds to ordinary language while taking account of the document being edited. Pages can help draft and reorganise text; Numbers can interpret data and help with formulas and charts; Keynote can generate slides and presentation notes. The assistant is in beta, works only in English and requires a device compatible with Apple Intelligence. (MacMagazine)

The AI features and new premium content are for Apple Creator Studio subscribers. Other users receive general fixes and performance improvements. Keynote also gains beta support for importing and exporting KEYX, an open interchange format intended to make presentation content easier to use elsewhere. All three apps add support for the iPhone Duo’s larger unfolded screen. The subscription and language requirements will determine who can use the most prominent additions when updating. (MacMagazine)

Sports

Guimarães settles into Arsenal’s midfield

Bruno Guimarães has described the emotional difficulty of leaving Newcastle for Arsenal in a £75m summer transfer, while welcoming the demands of his new club. The Brazil midfielder has already scored important goals against Sunderland and Leeds and is developing a partnership with Declan Rice and Martin Ødegaard. Mikel Arteta is still working through the balance of a midfield whose players can occupy several roles. (Guardian)

In Wednesday’s 2-2 Champions League draw at Bayern Munich, Guimarães played deeper while Rice operated further forward. Manuel Neuer denied the Brazilian with a close-range save before Rice scored Arsenal’s late equaliser. Guimarães described a squad determined to win even away at Bayern, with Everton next at home on Saturday. His return to Newcastle is scheduled for 21 November. The move has brought an early contribution on the pitch as he works to build the relationships he valued at his former club. (Guardian)

Carrick faces pressure after Manchester United’s difficult start

Unai Emery and Julian Nagelsmann have emerged as leading possibilities if Manchester United decide to replace Michael Carrick. Carrick is expected to remain in charge for Sunday’s match against Bournemouth, with no change announced. United have won two of their first 11 games this season, and Wednesday’s 4-1 Champions League defeat at Como has intensified scrutiny of the coach. (Guardian)

Emery’s contract at Aston Villa runs until 2029, making compensation a potential obstacle. Nagelsmann is available after leaving Germany following their World Cup exit. Other possible candidates include Antonio Conte, Eddie Howe and Kieran McKenna, while Brighton’s Fabian Hürzeler is understood to be unwilling to leave at this stage. Bruno Fernandes is not expected to face disciplinary action for criticising Carrick’s tactics after the Como defeat. United must now prepare for a Premier League opponent arriving after a strong European result of its own. (Guardian)

The Fold

A daily briefing for Londoners who want the full picture in one place.

Inspired by Brazil’s Meio · Friday, 23 October 2026 · leonardoresston.github.io/thefold

item.title: The Fold — 2026-10-22
item.description: The Fold morning briefing for 22 October 2026: Jackdaw approval, Brazil’s close runoff, an emergency web security update and Arsenal’s draw in Munich.
item.content:encoded:
Thursday 22 October 2026 · London

The Fold

Your morning briefing from the UK & the world

In this edition

  • The government approves gas production at Jackdaw while Rosebank remains undecided.
  • Russian missiles strike Kyiv amid a renewed diplomatic push.
  • A Brazilian presidential poll puts Flávio Bolsonaro and Lula within the margin of error.
  • Website operators take services offline to patch critical PHP vulnerabilities.
  • EA closes BioWare and cancels the next Mass Effect game.
  • Arsenal draw 2–2 at Bayern Munich after losing Bukayo Saka to injury.

News

Jackdaw gets the go-ahead, with no promise of lower winter bills

The government has approved production from the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea, opening the way for supplies to reach homes and businesses before the end of October. Energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh acknowledged that the decision would not lower bills this winter. Ministers are presenting the project as a way to sustain domestic supply and employment while Britain moves towards renewable energy and nuclear power. Environmental groups argue that the additional emissions undermine that transition. The announcement leaves a much larger decision, on the Rosebank oilfield, unresolved. (BBC)

Jackdaw lies about 150 miles east of Aberdeen and is operated by Adura, the Shell and Equinor joint venture. Its gas will travel through the existing Shearwater platform to the St Fergus terminal in Aberdeenshire. The operator expects it to account for roughly 6% of UK gas production, equivalent to about 2% of total demand once imports are included. Ministers put its economic contribution at £2.9bn over an expected 11-year life and say it will support hundreds of jobs. The distinction between domestic production and total consumption helps explain why the project can matter to the offshore industry without producing a noticeable reduction in household costs. (BBC)

The consent follows a legal reversal. In January 2025, Scotland’s Court of Session ruled that earlier approvals for Jackdaw and Rosebank were unlawful because their environmental assessments had failed to account adequately for emissions from burning the fuels. Preparatory work was allowed to continue while new assessments were drawn up. Labour’s ban on new exploration licences remains in place: these projects involve licences already granted. Alongside Wednesday’s approval, the government announced an energy wealth fund with an initial £2bn to invest in renewables, nuclear and other low-carbon projects. The budget is due to clarify which oil and gas tax revenues will support it. (BBC, Guardian)

Rosebank could produce a sharper argument within Labour. Fahnbulleh is understood to be leaning towards refusing approval, although no final decision has been taken and prime minister Andy Burnham could intervene. The department describes accounts of her position as speculation and says each project will be assessed individually. Rosebank contains an estimated 300m–500m barrels of oil, much of which would be exported, and its projected emissions are substantially greater than Jackdaw’s. Several Labour MPs have signalled opposition. A decision is expected before the end of the year, giving ministers another test of how they apply Britain’s carbon budgets to projects on existing licences. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch welcomed Jackdaw’s approval but urged Burnham to lift the ban on new licences. Scottish first minister John Swinney welcomed greater certainty for the north-east and called for the wealth fund to prioritise offshore renewables there. Unions and Aberdeen business groups also welcomed the production decision, while Greenpeace and Oxfam opposed it. (Guardian)

Kyiv comes under attack as a new round of talks is floated

Russian missiles hit Kyiv on Wednesday night, injuring six people and striking several houses, according to mayor Vitaliy Klitschko. The attack followed a meeting between Vladimir Putin and US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg. Russia indicated that it was ready in principle to resume negotiations, with Putin’s aide Yuri Ushakov suggesting talks around 10 November in Abu Dhabi. There was no announced ceasefire. Earlier three-way negotiations had stalled, and Russia has intensified attacks while Ukraine faces shortages of the interceptors used to defend its cities. (BBC)

Volodymyr Zelensky said he would accept a freeze along the current front line as a minimum step towards stopping the killing. Security guarantees and a possible halt to attacks on energy infrastructure had featured in his discussions with Witkoff in Oslo a day earlier. The positions remain far apart: Moscow claims its forces hold the strategic initiative, while Ukraine and European allies dispute that description. Russia occupies about a fifth of Ukrainian territory. Washington’s renewed push also comes amid friction over sanctions and military intelligence. Zelensky said intelligence sharing was working again after Kyiv had accused the US of withholding warnings of ballistic missile launches. A proposed meeting date leaves the immediate question of civilian protection unanswered. Russia also released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American who had been imprisoned for allegedly fighting for Ukraine. Trump said his release involved no prisoner exchange. That brought a tangible result from the diplomatic contact, while the broader negotiations still lacked an agreed route to ending the fighting or protecting Ukraine from another attack after a settlement. (BBC)

Care-home families describe the lasting cost of isolation

Bereaved families have described renewed anger following the Covid inquiry’s findings on social care. The inquiry concluded that the sector had been treated as an afterthought, that discharging untested hospital patients into care homes helped the virus spread, and that blanket restrictions on contact caused severe emotional harm. Relatives who accepted separation as a necessary protection now have to reckon with the finding that residents endured profound isolation while infection still reached them. The consequences extended across years, with some families unable to resume meaningful contact before their loved ones died. (Guardian)

Their accounts describe the practical limits of the arrangements intended to replace visits. Some residents could speak to family only when staff found time to bring a telephone; others struggled with conversations through windows or glass partitions. Families described withdrawal from meals and activities, fear and a sense of abandonment. Care workers also faced the loss of residents they knew well, shortages of protective equipment and anxiety about carrying infection home. These experiences give substance to the inquiry’s institutional findings. Future preparedness has to account for the support residents receive from regular human contact, alongside the measures used to limit transmission. Families are still living with the time they lost. (Guardian)

Brazil’s runoff remains close as work and religion divide voters

Flávio Bolsonaro and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva remain within the margin of error in a Meio/Ideia presidential runoff poll released on Wednesday. Bolsonaro has 48% of voting intentions and Lula 46%, with a margin of error of 2.5 percentage points. Blank and invalid votes account for 3.4%, and 2.6% are undecided. Once those responses are excluded, the figures become 51.1% and 48.9%. The survey interviewed 1,500 voters by telephone between 15 and 19 October, with a stated confidence level of 95%. It offers a close snapshot rather than a secure prediction of the result. (Meio)

The survey also asked what improving one’s life meant. About 43% chose owning a business or working independently; 32% preferred formal employment with guaranteed rights. Among people who aspired to their own business, Bolsonaro led by roughly 62% to 34%. Among those favouring formal employment, Lula led by about 65% to 30%. Religious affiliation produced another strong division: evangelical respondents heavily favoured Bolsonaro, while Catholics favoured Lula overall. Those breakdowns describe patterns within the sample and do not establish why individual voters choose a candidate. They nevertheless show the different expectations the campaigns are addressing. With almost 84% saying their choice is settled, the remaining contest is taking place within an electorate where many people already have firm commitments. The poll found that the two groups defined by their ambitions had broadly similar income distributions. Among people already self-employed or running a business, Bolsonaro’s lead was smaller than among those who wanted to do so. Lula led in the North and Northeast, while Bolsonaro was ahead in the Centre-West, Southeast and South. These subgroup estimates carry additional uncertainty beyond the headline result. (Meio)

Booking.com faces an EU investigation into fraud safeguards

The European Commission has opened an investigation into whether Booking.com does enough to prevent fraudulent accommodation listings and payment scams. Officials are examining its risk assessments and safeguards under the Digital Services Act, as well as whether paid promotion of accommodation is clearly identified. Opening the case does not establish a breach. Booking.com says it is engaging constructively with the commission and working with authorities and industry partners to protect travellers, accommodation providers and personal information. (Guardian)

The inquiry covers two distinct ways a holiday booking can go wrong. A fraudulent listing can leave a traveller arriving at a property that was never available to rent. In a reservation hijack, criminals use compromised booking information to impersonate a legitimate accommodation provider and demand another payment, sometimes through the platform’s own messaging system. Consumer researchers have demonstrated how a fake listing could accept payment for a stay at 10 Downing Street. Regulators will assess whether the platform’s systems adequately address such risks. The case also tests how its advertising disclosures help travellers understand why a property appears prominently. A breach of the DSA can carry a fine of up to 6% of worldwide annual turnover, though the investigation’s outcome remains open. (Guardian)

Technology

An emergency PHP update takes parts of the web offline

Governments and website operators took services offline on Wednesday as they raced to address two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language used across web hosting and content-management systems. A fix was released in the afternoon after details leaked ahead of the planned disclosure. Finland suspended public government web services, a Dutch cybersecurity agency took its own site down, and the Wikimedia Foundation removed some systems as a precaution while patching them. The interruptions do not, by themselves, mean that the affected organisations were hacked. Some chose downtime to reduce their exposure while installing the update. (BBC, The Verge)

The flaws can allow an attacker to run code on a vulnerable server without an administrator’s login. That creates risks for databases, credentials and other information stored there. Researchers at Calif and Wiz used advanced AI systems in finding and developing the vulnerabilities, which had remained hidden for years. Cloudflare’s chief technology officer said early attacks were emerging. Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre and counterparts abroad urged organisations to apply the fixes and consider taking systems offline when an immediate remedy was unavailable. For operators, the task includes locating PHP inside hosting services and third-party products as well as obvious websites. Older, unsupported installations add another complication. The PHP Foundation released updates for supported versions, leaving organisations on PHP 8.1 or earlier needing to move to a newer release. The vulnerabilities concern software running on servers, so ordinary visitors cannot repair them by updating a browser. For a small business using managed hosting, the provider’s response is part of the recovery; larger organisations must also check products that quietly include PHP. The scale of exposure remains uncertain; widely circulated estimates about the share of the internet affected should be treated cautiously. (BBC, The Verge)

Meta plans non-voting shares to help finance its AI expansion

Meta plans a new class of non-voting shares to help finance AI investment, acquisitions and employee compensation, with trading expected to begin in 2027. The announcement accompanied third-quarter results and another enormous investment forecast: capital spending is now expected to reach $135bn–$145bn this year, raising the lower end of its previous range. Data centres, computing capacity and recruitment are absorbing funds as the company competes to build models and consumer services. The proposed shares would provide an additional financing tool without giving their holders voting rights. (The Verge)

The results also show the financial weight of Meta’s legal settlements. Its quarterly costs included $9.89bn associated with the nationwide child-safety agreement reached with US attorneys general. Revenue reached $64.60bn, up 26% from a year earlier. The company put operating income before the settlement charge at $22.89bn, a figure that needs to be read alongside the substantial expense actually incurred. Meta’s new Muse agent has attracted millions of downloads, but privacy problems have accompanied the launch, including the suspension of a conversation-sharing feature after researchers found chats publicly accessible. Its expansion therefore combines a large construction and financing programme with continuing pressure over how its products handle personal information and protect users. (The Verge, The Verge)

The data-centre buildout puts cleaner air under pressure

A study of proposed data-centre expansion in Texas warns that the electricity needed could reverse years of progress on air pollution. The Houston Advanced Research Center modelled several paths for demand and power supply. In a scenario where all planned projects connect to the grid and use its anticipated generation mix, power-sector fine-particle pollution would more than triple within five years. Nitrogen oxide emissions would rise 136%, while carbon dioxide emissions would climb 90% above 2025 levels. These are conditional projections, dependent on which projects are built and how they are powered. (The Verge)

That distinction matters because many proposed facilities remain speculative. Developers also have choices about generation. Pairing grid electricity with renewable power generated on site could substantially reduce pollution; building gas engines to bypass connection delays could make it worse. Texas already has a large concentration of operating and under-construction data-centre capacity, giving those decisions consequences for surrounding communities as well as the national AI industry. Soot and smog-forming emissions affect local air quality, adding a separate concern to the carbon footprint of electricity use. The report makes the choice of power supply central to the environmental outcome. A rush to bring computing capacity online can lock in that choice for years. (The Verge)

EA closes BioWare and cancels the next Mass Effect

Electronic Arts is shutting BioWare and ending development of the next Mass Effect, bringing an abrupt end to a studio closely associated with story-led role-playing games. The closure forms part of cuts affecting about 400 EA employees, including roughly 50 BioWare roles. EA’s staff memo describes a decision to concentrate investment on a smaller set of opportunities. The company will close BioWare’s Edmonton workspace. For players who had followed years of previews and hints, the next game’s promised return to the series’ universe has ended before release. (IGN)

The decision follows disappointing performances from Anthem and Dragon Age: The Veilguard, and arrives a few months after EA’s $55bn leveraged buyout. EA is continuing major sports franchises, Battlefield, Apex Legends and selected action-adventure projects, including the next Star Wars Jedi game and Marvel’s Iron Man. Its executives envisage fewer large projects running simultaneously. The restructuring illustrates how a publisher can keep investing heavily while narrowing the range of games it makes. Mass Effect’s planned television adaptation remains in development at Amazon MGM Studios, but that does not provide a replacement for the cancelled game or resolve the future of the gaming franchise. The immediate, confirmed consequences are the project’s cancellation and the loss of the studio and its jobs. (IGN)

Sports

Rice earns Arsenal a point in Munich as Saka goes off injured

Declan Rice scored in the 82nd minute to earn Arsenal a 2–2 draw at Bayern Munich, finishing low after a pass from substitute Viktor Gyökeres. Eberechi Eze had put Arsenal ahead following Martin Ødegaard’s through ball, with a video review overturning the initial offside decision.
