Harry Kane then helped turn the match: his pass set up Alphonso Davies for Bayern’s equaliser, and he converted a penalty after Jurriën Timber handled. Rice’s late intervention gave Arsenal a point at a ground where Bayern have been exceptionally difficult to beat in the competition’s opening phase. (Guardian)

The evening also brought concern over Bukayo Saka, who left the pitch after ten minutes with a quadriceps injury. Mikel Arteta described the early signs as worrying, with further assessment needed to establish its severity and the likely absence. Eze came on to the left and Noni Madueke moved to the right, giving Arsenal a workable response during the game. Saka has already dealt with several interruptions to his fitness, including an Achilles problem last season and a hamstring injury that required surgery in 2024. His recovery timetable will matter as Arsenal balance domestic fixtures with their European campaign. Both goalkeepers made important saves: Manuel Neuer denied Bruno Guimarães from a corner, while David Raya stopped a close-range Dayot Upamecano header. Arsenal threatened a winner late on, but the draw leaves attention divided between a strong away performance and the fitness of one of their most influential attackers. (Guardian, BBC)

Villa keep winning; Como deepen United’s troubles

Aston Villa beat Viking 3–1 to make it three wins from three in the Champions League. Ross Barkley headed the opener from Ibrahim Mbaye’s corner and Emiliano Buendía added a penalty before Henrik Heggheim’s own goal put Villa three ahead. Peter Christiansen’s volley gave Viking a consolation after a video review. Villa’s first-half control did most of the work, although the visitors became more dangerous after the interval. Unai Emery’s team have nine points and 12 consecutive European home victories; a trip to Barcelona will offer a demanding next examination. (Guardian)

Manchester United’s night was much worse. Como won 4–1, with Nico Paz scoring twice and Tasos Douvikas and Jacobo Ramón also on target before Joshua Zirkzee’s late reply. Michael Carrick apologised to travelling supporters, while captain Bruno Fernandes publicly questioned the decision to hold off pressing Como. Carrick defended aspects of the approach and criticised his side’s effort. United have only two wins from 11 matches in all competitions and sit 13th in the Premier League, with Bournemouth due at Old Trafford on Sunday. The result intensifies scrutiny of the manager and leaves a visible disagreement over tactics between the bench and the captain. (Guardian)

The Fold

A daily briefing for Londoners who want the full picture in one place.

Inspired by Brazil’s Meio · Thursday, 22 October 2026 · leonardoresston.github.io/thefold

item.title: The Fold — 2026-10-21
item.description: The Fold morning briefing for 21 October 2026: UK approves the Jackdaw North Sea gasfield as the Covid inquiry condemns care home failures, Italy sends 500 soldiers to Milan and RAF Typhoons defend Saudi airspace, Lula accelerates Bolsa Família payments before Brazil's runoff, Google Cloud's London outage hits banks and courts, Tesla and SpaceX explore a merger, and Liverpool rally to beat Villarreal in the Champions League.
item.content:encoded:
Wednesday 21 October 2026 · London

The Fold

Your morning briefing from the UK & the world

In this edition

  • Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh and Chancellor John Healey approve North Sea drilling at the Jackdaw gasfield as the UK Covid-19 inquiry delivers a scathing verdict on pandemic care home failures.
  • Italy deploys 500 soldiers to Milan after cost-of-living protests turn violent, while Britain sends RAF Typhoon jets to defend Saudi airspace against Houthi missile and drone strikes.
  • President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva brings forward increased Bolsa Família payments and files a banking-secrecy waiver ahead of Sunday’s Brazilian presidential runoff against Flávio Bolsonaro.
  • A power fault at a London Google Cloud data centre disrupts UK courts and banks including Revolut, Lloyds and HSBC, while Flutter Entertainment plans up to 1,400 job cuts and Ryanair warns of 20% higher air fares.
  • Tesla and SpaceX form special board committees to explore a corporate merger as SpaceX posts $14.6bn in quarterly revenue and UK regulators challenge Apple’s contactless payment rules.
  • Liverpool rally from two goals down to beat Villarreal 3–2 in the Champions League as Phil Foden scores a hat-trick for Manchester City and Arsenal travel to face Bayern Munich.

News

Burnham faces climate revolt over Jackdaw gasfield approval as Covid inquiry condemns care home failures

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh and Chancellor John Healey travel to Aberdeen on Wednesday to grant final development consent for the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea, ending more than a year of legal and environmental deliberations. Operated jointly by Shell and Norwegian energy group Equinor, Jackdaw is one of the largest undeveloped fields in the declining basin and will represent 6% of UK North Sea gas output once production begins. Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government has pitched the decision around energy security and jobs, even though Labour’s 2024 manifesto pledged no new oil and gas licences because further drilling would fail to lower household bills. Because Jackdaw was first approved under the Conservatives in 2022 before court challenges over downstream emissions stalled work, ministers argue it honours an existing licence while leaving the larger Rosebank oilfield undecided. Climate groups and Labour MPs condemned the approval, with Uplift director Tessa Khan noting Jackdaw will supply barely 2% of UK gas demand over 10 years while operating largely remotely. (Guardian, BBC)

The UK Covid-19 public inquiry meanwhile published its sixth report, delivering a damning 287-page verdict on adult social care during the pandemic. Inquiry chair Baroness Heather Hallett concluded that government failures allowed the virus to spread “like wildfire” across care homes, where more than 43,000 residents died between March 2020 and July 2022. Hallett dismissed former health secretary Matt Hancock’s claim to have thrown a “protective ring” around care homes as unsupported by evidence, finding the sector was treated as an afterthought while ministers prioritised freeing NHS hospital beds. Around 30,000 hospital patients were discharged into English care homes between mid-March and mid-April 2020 without routine testing or isolation advice. Care staff described improvising personal protective equipment from clinical bin bags, plastic festival ponchos and painters’ overalls, while blanket bans on family visits left tens of thousands of frail and dementia-stricken residents in prolonged isolation. (Guardian, BBC, BBC)

In Westminster, undercover footage recorded in July by investigative group Verbatim heaped pressure on Reform UK over £72m donated last week by crypto billionaires Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo. In the video, Cambridge professor James Orr—Nigel Farage’s head of policy until his suspension last month—warned that the government’s proposed £100,000 annual foreign-donor cap, retrospective to March 2026 and requiring a year of UK residency, could make donations from Thailand-based Harborne or Hong Kong-based Delo illegal, three months before each gave £36m. Labour suspended a second MP in a week after Perran Moon (Camborne and Redruth) referred himself over a £50,000 pandemic Bounce Back Loan taken by his former firm Autoswot before it ceased trading in late 2022. Elsewhere, former Ofsted chief Sir David Bell’s review found three in five Jewish students in England experienced prejudice and recommended 27 measures treating antisemitism as a distinct category of harm, while counter-terrorism police re-arrested a 24-year-old British man and a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national under the National Security Act over September’s incursion near RAF Fairford. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian, BBC, Guardian)

Italy deploys 500 soldiers to Milan after cost-of-living riots as RAF Typhoons defend Saudi airspace

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni ordered 500 soldiers into Milan on Tuesday and unveiled emergency security legislation after weekend protests over surging energy, fuel and food prices turned violent across northern Italy. Police in Milan used teargas and water cannon around Piazza del Duomo to disperse crowds that smashed bank windows and looted shops, detaining 271 youths and arresting 32 suspects, including 23 minors, alongside clashes in Turin, Bologna, Brescia and Bergamo. Meloni’s decree makes participating in a violent protest a specific offence and imposes civil fines on parents for looting by underage children, as luxury brands Chanel, Tiffany and Dior cleared display windows in Milan’s Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II ahead of Saturday marches. In France, where nearly 2,400 protesters were arrested last weekend, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez confirmed army troops will guard static buildings this Saturday to free police for riot control, while Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu met five union confederations and extended 11pm–6am curfews in central Paris and regional cities. (Guardian)

In the Middle East, Prime Minister Andy Burnham authorised his most significant military deployment since taking office, sending Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets to fly defensive patrols over Saudi Arabia against drones and missiles launched by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting stressed that British aircraft will protect Saudi cities, airports and oil facilities without conducting offensive strikes inside Yemen. The deployment follows a Houthi missile attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport that killed 13 people, bringing Saudi fatalities to 19 since cross-border strikes resumed in September. In Yemen’s Shabwa province, officials confirmed the death toll from Monday’s Houthi ballistic missile strike on the al-Alam training camp—used by UAE-backed Southern Giants Brigades forces allied with Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council—had risen from 53 to 73 soldiers. (Guardian)

In Oslo, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met US envoy Steve Witkoff, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb, with Jared Kushner joining by video. Zelenskyy confirmed Washington has resumed sharing satellite early-warning intelligence on incoming Russian ballistic missiles after a five-day pause that curtailed air-raid warnings, while pressing US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to lift Pentagon-backed curbs on SpaceX’s Starshield network ahead of Witkoff’s Wednesday talks with Vladimir Putin in Moscow. In the US, former New York mayor Michael Bloomberg injected $80m into Democratic midterm campaigns—including $24m via Everytown for Gun Safety and $16m to the House Majority PAC—against $400m committed by Donald Trump and $366m spent by Elon Musk for Republicans, while Trump and Vice President JD Vance handed conservative YouTuber Nick Shirley $10,000 to launch a $25m federal fraud tip bounty. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian, Verge)

Lula brings forward Bolsa Família payments and files banking waiver as Brazil’s runoff enters its final days

Five days before Brazil’s 25 October presidential runoff, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s government compressed October’s Bolsa Família disbursement schedule so all beneficiaries receive their payments—including September’s 15.04% increase—by Wednesday rather than 30 October. Senator Flávio Bolsonaro scrambled to delete 2014 social media posts in which, as a Rio state deputy, he called the number of Bolsa Família recipients a badge of national shame, while his economic coordinator unsettled centrist allies by floating a transition rule to move formal workers off the benefit. Seeking to neutralise opposition corruption claims before Friday’s final TV Globo debate, Lula filed a signed waiver with the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) lifting banking, tax and phone secrecy for himself, First Lady Janja da Silva and his son Fábio Luís (“Lulinha”), conditional on Bolsonaro releasing records for himself, his family and five companies—including a British Virgin Islands offshore firm—linked to lawyer Willer Tomaz. (Meio, Folha, Folha, Folha)

In Congress, Senate government leader Randolfe Rodrigues filed an ethics complaint accusing Bolsonaro of requesting R$134m from former Banco Master owner Daniel Vorcaro, while PT Chamber leader Pedro Uczai proposed a joint parliamentary inquiry (CPI) alongside Supreme Court probes into Willer Tomaz, former Rio governor Cláudio Castro and deputy Alexandre Ramagem; prosecutors also opened an inquiry into whether Federal Police chief Andrei Rodrigues leaked confidential INSS case data regarding Lula’s brother, Frei Chico. On the campaign trail, Bolsonaro held a closed session in Alphaville with 300 digital influencers coached by Pablo Marçal, won Paraná governor Ratinho Junior’s endorsement, and leaned on Assemblies of God pastors and São Paulo governor Tarcísio de Freitas—who has attended 12 Bolsonaro rallies against five official duties since 5 October—while Argentine President Javier Milei attacked Lula online. Lula rallied over 600 organised pop fan clubs in São Paulo, watched Bolsonaro’s Sunday debate stunt of writing “corrupto” on his palm become a nationwide meme, and secured Chamber Speaker Hugo Motta’s conditional backing for a weekend free-transit constitutional amendment provided parliamentary budget earmarks remain intact, as Meta’s Oversight Board criticised recurring election moderation failures. (Folha, Folha, Folha, Folha, Folha, Guardian, Guardian)

Google Cloud power fault disrupts UK banks and courts as Flutter cuts 1,400 jobs and Ryanair warns on fares

A power failure inside Google Cloud’s europe-west2-b London data centre zone on Tuesday morning caused cascading outages across British financial and public services. HM Courts and Tribunals Service lost its Cloud Video Platform across England and Wales, delaying remote bail and sentencing hearings for remanded prisoners, while the NHS app, Royal Mail tracking, and mobile apps at Lloyds, Halifax and HSBC suffered hours of disruption. Although Google restored most cloud services between 1pm and 3pm, fintech firm Revolut remained severely impaired into the evening: only six of its 27 platform functions worked normally at 5pm amid failed card payments, ATM withdrawals and transfers, prompting Financial Conduct Authority and Bank of England inquiries into financial reliance on cloud hyperscalers. (Guardian, Guardian)

Employers across banking, gambling and aviation also announced restructurings ahead of Chancellor John Healey’s 28 October budget. NatWest ordered 13,000 remote-first employees—previously required in an office twice a month—to attend at least two days a week from February 2027 across all 40,000 UK staff at NatWest, RBS, Ulster Bank and Coutts. Paddy Power and Sky Bet owner Flutter Entertainment announced plans to cut up to 1,400 roles—over 10% of its 8,960 UK and Ireland staff in Leeds, Dublin and Sunderland, plus hubs in Porto and Cluj-Napoca—blaming last year’s budget rises in remote gaming duty (21% to 40%) and online betting duty (15% to 25%) as Healey weighs higher slot-machine taxes. Meanwhile, Ryanair chief executive Michael O’Leary warned European air fares could climb up to 20% in 2027 as Middle East conflict doubles spot jet fuel above the $85-a-barrel level at which Ryanair hedged 15% of its 2027 fuel, while cutting 20 Brussels routes over Belgium’s boarding tax rise from €2 to €7. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

Technology

Tesla and SpaceX form committees to explore a merger as SpaceX revenue surges to $14.6bn

Elon Musk disclosed during SpaceX’s third-quarter earnings call—its second report since June’s initial public offering—that Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees of independent directors at shareholders’ request to evaluate a corporate merger, though Tesla’s bylaws require 50% of all outstanding shares to approve a related-party deal. SpaceX’s third-quarter revenue jumped 161% year-on-year to $14.6bn, led by its Super Intelligence (SI) division—formerly xAI—whose revenue climbed 830% to $7.6bn ($431m operating income) following its $60bn acquisition of AI coding platform Cursor, Grok enterprise sales and cloud contracts. Starlink generated $5.2bn in revenue and $2.4bn in operating profit across 13.6 million subscribers, while space launches brought in $1.8bn at a $7m operating loss amid heavy spending on orbital data centres and reusable rockets. (Verge, Verge)

Musk added that SpaceX will attempt next month to catch both the upper-stage Starship spacecraft and its Super Heavy booster using launch-tower mechanical arms in Texas for the first complete recovery of an orbital rocket after April’s Indian Ocean splashdown. Elsewhere in consumer technology, OpenAI introduced PIN-protected Locked Chats in ChatGPT across web, iOS and Android to keep sensitive chats out of search and memory; Google brought Gemini’s Personal Intelligence to Android Auto alongside Waze conversational reporting; Oura added Cardio Effort and automatic VO2 Max tracking for Oura Ring 3 and 4 users; and Snap hired actor Robert Downey Jr to promote its consumer Specs augmented-reality glasses. (Verge, Verge, Verge, Verge)

UK regulators challenge Apple over digital wallets as iPhone Duo orders are capped and Perplexity goes offline

Britain’s Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) opened a consultation until 17 November on conduct rules forcing Apple to lower fees and remove technical barriers on third-party access to the iPhone’s NFC contactless chip. CMA chief executive Sarah Cardell noted contactless payments represent 39% of UK transactions, up from 3% a decade ago, with 60% of British adults using mobile wallets. Meanwhile, Apple capped online purchases of its foldable iPhone Duo at two per customer in the UK, US, Japan, Spain and Brazil to curb scalping while moving some US and Japanese deliveries forward from December and January to 23 October and mid-November. Apple also committed up to $100m over three years to Pennsylvania titanium producer Perryman Company and expanded its partnership with Delaware’s Qnity Electronics for the iPhone 18 Pro’s variable-aperture camera among nearly 100 US-made components, while supply-chain filings showed Samsung plans six foldable models in 2027. (MacMagazine, 9to5Mac, 9to5Mac, MacMagazine, 9to5Mac, 9to5Mac)

On the desktop, Perplexity added a local-first mode to Perplexity Computer on Apple Silicon Macs (36GB unified memory recommended), allowing users to run open-weights Qwen 3.6 or PPLX Pro models 100% offline with local terminal, file and browser control. Apple seeded the visionOS 26.2 developer beta featuring WebP and AVIF support, multi-user enterprise tools and spatial audio previews alongside second release candidates for iOS 26.1 and macOS Tahoe 26.1, while Brazil’s Anatel opened a 60-day consultation on mandatory emergency cell broadcasts and certified a wave of tri-band Wi-Fi 7 routers. (MacStories, MacMagazine, 9to5Mac, MacMagazine)

Culture

Broadcaster axes linear TV channels in £500m cost drive as Liverpool plans a vast Beatles museum and Netflix viewing dips

Director general Matt Brittin and news director Rachel Jupp unveiled sweeping broadcast cuts on Tuesday as the corporation seeks to close a £500m funding gap, of which £200m has been found so far. Under the plan, linear television channels BBC Three and BBC Scotland will move online-only to iPlayer in spring 2027, Radio 4 Extra will close with its archive shifting to Sounds, and 100 news posts will be cut to save £5.5m, drawing union and political criticism in Scotland. In Liverpool, Apple Corps announced with Sir Paul McCartney, Ringo Starr and Prime Minister Andy Burnham that it will take ownership of The Beatles Story museum and relocate it in 2028 to the vacant 100,000 sq ft St John’s Market Hall—quadrupling its footprint—while turning the 450ft St Johns Beacon tower into a Yellow Submarine attraction and funding grassroots music via the new Apple Corps Liverpool Trust. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian, BBC)

In streaming and film, Netflix reported third-quarter revenue up 12% year-on-year to $12.9bn, outlined plans to expand its ad tier to 15 more countries in 2027, and named former Disney executive Peter Rice chief content officer from 26 October after cutting 1,000 jobs, though average monthly viewing per subscriber fell from 66 hours in early 2023 to 49 hours. Comedy creators Mathew Baynton, Simon Farnaby, Martha Howe-Douglas, Jim Howick, Laurence Rickard and Ben Willbond confirmed they are reuniting with Charlotte Ritchie and Kiell Smith-Bynoe for a feature film, Ghosts: The Possession of Button House. Meanwhile, Hollywood unions debated two indie films using generative AI: the western As Deep as the Grave, featuring an estate-approved digital recreation of a young Val Kilmer, and Misaligned, which casts synthetic AI actress Tilly Norwood. (Verge, Guardian, Guardian)

Ghent unveils carbon-absorbing brick museum extension as AI conquers the Times cryptic crossword and Rockstar films in Miami

London architects Carmody Groarke completed a €20m (£17m) mass-timber extension for Design Museum Gent in Belgium clad in 82,000 low-carbon white bricks made by compressing crushed local concrete, brick rubble and hydrated lime without firing, allowing the facade to absorb carbon dioxide as it cures. In publishing, Poet Laureate Simon Armitage released a four-beat alliterative verse translation of the 4,000-year-old Mesopotamian epic Gilgamesh with Faber. British puzzle culture also reached a milestone after Darmok, an AI solver created by University of Texas computer scientist Dr Sid Chatterjee, beat human champion Liam Hughes by three minutes at the Times cryptic crossword championship, solving all four finals puzzles cleanly. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

Ahead of next month’s launch of Grand Theft Auto VI, Rockstar Games closed downtown Miami streets with helicopters and camera cars to film custom Grotti and Emerus supercars bearing Vice City plates, while US federal label filings revealed a partnership with Florida’s Tripping Animals Brewing to sell real-life cans of in-game beers Pißwasser, Patriot Beer, Logger and No Mames Vice City. Elsewhere in gaming, Electronic Arts confirmed a new Fight Night boxing game is in development, and Aspyr Media set a 10 November launch for Shrek 2 Remastered with a trailer parodying GTA VI. (IGN, IGN, IGN, IGN)

Sports

Liverpool rally from two goals down to beat Villarreal 3–2 as Foden scores a hat-trick for Manchester City

Andoni Iraola’s Liverpool maintained their 100% Champions League record on Tuesday night by rallying from two goals down to beat Villarreal 3–2 at Anfield. Early errors by Virgil van Dijk and a high line allowed Georges Mikautadze and Sergi Cardona to put Iñigo Pérez’s visitors 2–0 up inside half an hour, before Alexis Mac Allister headed in a Kostas Tsimikas corner and 18-year-old winger Rio Ngumoha crossed for on-loan defender Ronald Araújo to level before half-time. Ngumoha then set up Mac Allister’s second goal after the break and substitute Florian Wirtz scored his first goal of the season before Tani Oluwaseyi’s stoppage-time volley. (Guardian, BBC)

At the Etihad Stadium, Phil Foden scored a hat-trick across right-wing and false-nine roles—following Saturday’s goal that ended a drought dating back to mid-December—as Enzo Maresca’s Manchester City rested Erling Haaland and beat AEK Athens 5–1 with additional goals from Elliot Anderson and Rayan Cherki. Elsewhere in Europe, holders Paris Saint-Germain defeated Barcelona 4–2 at a curfew-bound Parc des Princes through Désiré Doué and Vitinha, while Scotland midfielder Scott McTominay came off the bench on his return from September heart surgery to score twice in Massimiliano Allegri’s Napoli 4–3 win over Bodø/Glimt. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian, Guardian)

Arsenal travel to Bayern Munich for Champions League test as regulators take over Manchester City accounting inquiry

Arsenal face Bayern Munich at the Allianz Arena on Wednesday evening having won 10 of their 11 matches across all competitions this season, with goalkeeper David Raya and manager Mikel Arteta brushing off rival complaints about their physical set-piece routines and game management after Sunday’s 1–0 victory at Nottingham Forest. Speaking in Munich, Raya said the squad remained driven by the memory of last May’s Champions League final defeat on penalties against Paris Saint-Germain and relished measuring their progress against the German champions, whose head coach Vincent Kompany admitted a viral infection affecting his legs could keep him off the touchline while French winger Michael Olise serves a suspension. Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick, whose side sit 13th in the Premier League with a single league win ahead of Wednesday’s Champions League trip to Italian debutants Como, insisted he retains full board backing and dismissed predecessor Erik ten Hag’s serialised book claims that Old Trafford suffered from a toxic dressing-room culture after Cristiano Ronaldo refused to come on as a substitute against Tottenham in October 2022. (Guardian, Guardian, BBC)

Off the pitch, Britain’s corporate accounting watchdog confirmed it has stepped directly into the financial misconduct case surrounding Manchester City. Appearances before the Commons business and trade select committee revealed that on 30 September the Financial Reporting Council (FRC) assumed control of regulatory investigations from the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales into both the club’s historical financial statements and its long-standing auditing firm, BDO. The intervention follows an independent commission ruling earlier this year that Manchester City artificially inflated their declared revenue and financial position by more than £900m across nine seasons between 2009–10 and 2017–18 by disguising equity funding as commercial sponsorship—a verdict and sporting sanction that the Etihad hierarchy strongly deny and are currently appealing before an independent panel. (BBC)

The Fold

A daily briefing for Londoners who want the full picture in one place.

Inspired by Brazil’s Meio · Wednesday, 21 October 2026 · leonardoresston.github.io/thefold

item.title: The Fold — 2026-10-20
item.description: The Fold morning briefing for 20 October 2026: Andy Burnham demands radical public-control options for Thames Water, France imposes city curfews after riots, Brazil's presidential runoff reaches a dead heat, CoreWeave debt distress rattles the AI sector, and Arsenal prepare for Bayern Munich.
item.content:encoded:
Tuesday 20 October 2026 · London

The Fold

Your morning briefing from the UK & the world

In this edition

  • Andy Burnham orders Whitehall to draw up radical public-control plans for Thames Water while unveiling a statutory code for private car parks.
  • France introduces night-time curfews in Paris and several major cities after Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez admits police lost control of weekend riots.
  • Flávio Bolsonaro and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva enter a statistical tie in Brazil's presidential runoff after a combative televised debate.
  • Three Houthi ballistic missiles kill at least 53 recruits at a southern Yemeni training camp in the deadliest strike since the civil war resumed.
  • CoreWeave bonds fall into distressed territory as regulators examine Barclays' private credit exposure and Amazon backs a modular nuclear plant.
  • Arsenal prepare to face Harry Kane and Bayern Munich in the Champions League as Tottenham claim their first Premier League victory of the season.

News

Burnham orders radical public-control options for Thames Water and sets new rules for private car parks

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has instructed civil servants to tear up existing contingency plans for Thames Water and return with far bolder proposals to bring Britain's largest water supplier under public control. Shortly after taking office with a pledge to end four decades of neoliberal orthodoxy, Burnham rejected the cautious regulatory playbook he inherited in Downing Street, telling officials that decades of balance-sheet engineering and light-touch oversight had failed households and rivers alike. Thames Water, which serves 16 million customers across London and the Thames Valley, is currently asking creditors for an extra £2.4bn to stay afloat while carrying roughly £100m in unpaid regulatory fines for sewage pollution and leakage failures. (Guardian)

Among the options now under active examination in Whitehall is converting those unpaid penalties directly into a government equity stake, giving the public a foothold on the board without handing a bailout to existing institutional shareholders. Environment Secretary Angela Eagle is simultaneously preparing a water bill that will strip out a Thatcher-era statutory cap restricting how much of a privatised utility the state can own. By pairing debt-for-equity conversion with primary legislation, ministers want to avoid a prolonged legal battle with bondholders while establishing a template for utilities that fail basic public-service obligations. (Guardian)

That willingness to intervene in everyday household grievances also shaped the government's new statutory private parking code of practice, which will be laid before Parliament on Tuesday across England, Scotland and Wales. Under the rules, drivers entering a private car park will have a mandatory five-minute grace period to read the terms and decide whether to stay, plus a 10-minute window to return to their vehicle after a paid session expires. Charges for honest mistakes—such as typing a single wrong character into a registration keypad or forgetting to display a valid permit—will be capped at £20, a single independent appeals tribunal will oversee disputes, and debt-recovery firms will remain barred from adding up to £70 in extra collection fees. Consumer group Which? welcomed the protections against hair-trigger cameras after private operators issued a record 16.9 million tickets last year, a 17% jump, though the group criticised ministers for leaving the headline maximum fine at £100 rather than reviving an earlier proposal to halve it to £50. (Guardian, BBC)

While Downing Street sought to project domestic momentum—including plans led by former health secretary Alan Milburn to redirect welfare spending into guaranteed jobs and apprenticeships for under-25s—Reform UK spent Monday on the defensive. Undercover footage recorded by the investigative group Verbatim showed Dan Jukes, a senior aide to Nigel Farage, acknowledging that Farage had broken the party's official press line when he described a £5m personal gift from Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne as a reward for delivering Brexit. Reform's press office had insisted the transfer was strictly to fund Farage's personal security, and the contradiction deepened scrutiny at Westminster just as Reform MPs stayed off the broadcast round following an ITV investigation into racist and misogynistic remarks within the party's ranks. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

France imposes night curfews in Paris and regional cities after police admit losing control

France's Prime Minister, Sébastien Lecornu, authorised local and partial night-time curfews across the country on Monday after a weekend of anti-government marches degenerated into the worst urban disorder since the summer of 2023. Following an emergency cabinet meeting at the Élysée Palace, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez conceded that security forces had lost control in several cities after intelligence services severely misjudged the scale of Saturday's turnout. Domestic intelligence had briefed prefects to expect roughly 200,000 demonstrators nationwide; instead, more than 500,000 people took to the streets in protest against living costs, austerity budgets and political paralysis, overwhelming thin police cordons after nightfall. Nuñez offered his resignation to President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday evening, but the president refused to accept it. (Guardian, BBC)

In central Paris, the police prefecture introduced an immediate curfew from 11pm to 6am covering the Place de la République and the Les Halles shopping district, while four northern municipalities—including Lille—placed residents under stricter 8pm to 6am curfews. Prefects in Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon rolled out targeted evening bans on public gatherings and transit stoppages after municipal officials counted hundreds of ransacked premises. In Marseille alone, local business associations estimated that more than 600 shops had their shutters forced or windows smashed over two nights of unrest, while verified footage showed groups of masked looters stripping display tables inside Apple's flagship stores on Rue Sainte-Catherine in Bordeaux and in central Lille. Lecornu promised emergency legislation to make convicted rioters financially liable for damaged municipal property and commercial stock, while trade union confederations refused to suspend their campaign against public-spending cuts and called a fresh national day of strikes and demonstrations for 5 November. (BBC, BBC, MacMagazine, Guardian)

Brazil's presidential runoff reaches a statistical dead heat after a bruising televised debate

Brazil's presidential race has narrowed to a statistical tie less than two weeks before the 25 October runoff. A BTG/Nexus survey published on Monday put Senator Flávio Bolsonaro on 50.3% of valid votes and President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on 49.7%, shrinking the gap between the two candidates from 3.2 percentage points a week earlier to 0.6 points, well inside the two-point margin of error. Detailed precinct and polling breakdowns show that almost no voters are crossing the aisle—roughly 98% of those who backed either man in the 4 October first round remain locked into their choice. Instead, the contest is being decided by two contrasting pools: first-round supporters of third-party contenders Ronaldo Caiado and Augusto Cury are breaking heavily toward Bolsonaro, while Lula has clawed back ground by mobilising a portion of the 6.5 million voters who backed him in 2022 but stayed home three weeks ago. (Folha, Meio)

That tight arithmetic set the tone for a combative head-to-head debate on the Band network on Sunday evening, where policy discussion gave way to mutual accusations of family corruption and influence peddling. Bolsonaro repeatedly pressed Lula over ties between his son Fábio Luís, known as Lulinha, and lobbyist Roberta Luchsinger, as well as alleged favours involving Daniel Vorcaro, the former owner of Banco Master whose R$134m financial dealings are under federal investigation. Lula fired back by branding the senator a "malandro carioca", reviving questions over the Bolsonaro family's property purchases and accusing his challenger of hiding behind parliamentary privilege. Tensions spilled beyond the lecterns: Band production staff reprimanded First Lady Rosângela "Janja" da Silva after she spoke aloud from the studio audience during Bolsonaro's closing remarks, while allied federal deputy André Janones was admitted to the intensive care unit at São Paulo's Hospital Vila Nova Star with cardiac arrhythmia shortly after the broadcast. (Folha, Folha, Folha, Meio)

By Monday afternoon, the confrontation had shifted to the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) and the federal police. Campaigning in Porto Alegre, Lula announced he would formally ask the electoral court to lift banking secrecy for himself and all five of his children, challenging Bolsonaro to sign an identical waiver. Simultaneously, Lula's legal coalition filed a petition seeking the disqualification of Bolsonaro's ticket over alleged algorithmic manipulation on Instagram and Facebook, prompting TSE justice Marco Aurélio Bellizze to give Meta 24 hours to demonstrate that its recommendation systems treat both campaigns equally, while federal police searched the home of a former Superior Court of Justice clerk suspected of leaking draft decisions to lawyer Willer Tomaz, a close associate of the senator. (Folha, Folha, Folha, Folha)

Houthi missiles kill 53 in Yemen as Israel detains West Bank settlers and Kyiv warns over US missile alerts

At least 53 people were killed and more than 200 wounded on Monday when three Houthi ballistic missiles struck the al-Alam military training camp in Yemen's southern Shabwa province, marking the heaviest single loss of life since full-scale fighting resumed in mid-September. Medical officials and local commanders said the missiles hit as hundreds of newly arrived recruits were lined up on the parade ground in morning formation, overwhelming field clinics across the oil-producing province. The barrage came 24 hours after a Saudi airstrike killed nine people in Houthi-held territory, accelerating a tit-for-tat escalation that has unravelled years of fragile de-escalation talks along the Red Sea corridor. (Guardian)

Further north, Israeli police carried out a rare enforcement raid in the occupied West Bank, detaining 10 Israeli settlers after two consecutive days of high-profile attacks on foreign nationals near the Christian town of Taybeh. An Israeli magistrate's court extended the custody of six suspects following Friday's assault on veteran US photojournalist Heidi Levine, who was beaten with clubs while documenting the olive harvest and suffered four fractured vertebrae, a broken rib and a torn finger, and Saturday's attack on a delegation of European diplomats and a French mayor visiting the same hillside. In Ukraine, defence ministry adviser Serhii Beskrestnov warned that irregular and incomplete early-warning data from US satellites—compounded by lingering restrictions on Starlink terminal usage near the front—was leaving cities with only seconds to react to incoming Russian ballistic missiles after two overnight strikes hit Kyiv, while Ukrainian medics completed their first successful evacuation of a wounded soldier from a pinned-down trench using a heavy multi-rotor cargo drone. In Mombasa, meanwhile, a Kenyan court convicted self-proclaimed pastor Paul Mackenzie and 28 co-defendants on 191 counts of murder—190 of them children—over the Shakahola forest starvation deaths, where followers of his Good News International Church were ordered to fast to death in remote bushland settlements. (Guardian, BBC, BBC, BBC, Guardian)

UN biodiversity summit opens in Yerevan as UK energy grid, North Sea rigs and Thames wreck face strain

Delegates from nearly 200 countries gathered in Yerevan on Monday for the opening of the UN COP17 biodiversity summit, confronting stark evidence that governments are set to miss almost every one of the 23 nature-recovery targets agreed in Montreal four years ago. Roughly halfway to the 2030 deadline to protect 30% of the planet's land and seas, national progress filings show that the UK is on course to meet only three of the goals, with global conservation funding still tens of billions of dollars short of promised levels. The diplomatic stocktake coincided with a century-long European study confirming that wild bee populations have declined across every bioregion of the continent except the high Alps, driven by intensive agriculture, pesticide use and fragmented habitats. (Guardian, Guardian)

At home, Britain's energy and maritime infrastructure faced a trio of operational tests. An independent investigation by law firm Eversheds Sutherland into whistleblower allegations at the National Energy System Operator (Neso)—triggered after June's heatwave brought the country close to rolling blackouts—cleared senior managers of falsifying grid records, but uncovered high stress, weak governance and a culture inside the control room where engineers felt unable to challenge commercial assumptions. Separately, the Unite union warned that 48-hour strikes starting this week by hundreds of Wood Group and Apache offshore workers could disrupt British fuel supplies ahead of the 28 October budget, shutting down production across five North Sea platforms connected to the Forties Pipeline System, which carries 30% of UK crude oil. In the Thames estuary near Sheerness, maritime minister Keir Mather confirmed that specialist divers and engineers had completed a £9.5m operation to cut away all three decaying steel masts from the sunken Second World War cargo ship SS Richard Montgomery, relieving structural pressure on a hull that still holds 1,400 tonnes of unexploded munitions. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

Technology

CoreWeave bonds fall into distressed territory as regulators probe private credit and Amazon funds nuclear power

Financial tremors in the artificial intelligence build-out sharpened on Monday after corporate bonds issued by CoreWeave, one of the largest specialist cloud providers renting Nvidia graphics chips to AI labs, slipped into distressed territory. CoreWeave's debt traded at yields more than 1,000 basis points above US government benchmarks while its shares fell by more than 20%, reflecting bondholder unease over how quickly depreciating server clusters can pay down more than $35bn in high-interest loans. The company has been lobbying rating agencies for an investment-grade classification that would allow it to tap deeper pools of capital from pension funds and insurers, and the sell-off highlighted how heavily the AI infrastructure boom relies on leveraged private credit. (Verge)

That same credit market is drawing closer scrutiny in Threadneedle Street. The Bank of England's Prudential Regulation Authority opened a review into whether Barclays improperly accounted for £300m of total return swap derivatives linked to its £15bn private credit portfolio, knocking 3.5% off the bank's share price ahead of its third-quarter results on Thursday. While lenders and regulators wrestle with the balance-sheet risks of data-centre financing, utilities are struggling to supply the physical megawatts. A joint study by the Environmental Defense Fund and Atlas Public Policy found that construction of fossil-fuel power plants in the United States has reached a 10-year high as grid operators turn to natural gas turbines to meet immediate data-centre demand. Seeking a longer-term alternative, Amazon signed an agreement with reactor developer X-energy and utility American Electric Power to finance a 960-megawatt small modular nuclear plant on the site of the retired Breed coal station in Fairbanks, Indiana, deploying 12 high-temperature gas-cooled Xe-100 reactors to feed its midwestern cloud regions. (Guardian, Verge, Verge)

Apple sets 28 October 'Pro and tell' hardware event, details iPhone Duo battery and buys AI audio startup

Apple sent invitations on Monday for a special hardware showcase in Los Angeles on 28 October under the tagline "Pro and tell", scheduling its second major product event in less than two months. The presentation is expected to mark the biggest redesign of the MacBook Pro in five years, introducing a thinner chassis fitted with an OLED touchscreen and a pill-shaped Dynamic Island cutout at the top of the display, alongside M6-powered 14-inch MacBook Pro and iMac updates and an OLED iPad mini. Ahead of the event, Apple released the final release candidate builds of iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2 and macOS 27.2 Golden Gate to developers, while European Union energy-labelling filings disclosed the exact battery architecture inside the newly launched foldable iPhone Duo: a dual-cell pack combining 2,962mAh and 1,921mAh modules for a total capacity of 4,883mAh, sitting squarely between the eSIM-only iPhone 18 Pro (4,288mAh) and the iPhone 18 Pro Max (5,567mAh). (Verge, MacStories, MacMagazine, 9to5Mac)

Separate regulatory disclosures filed with the European Commission under the Digital Markets Act confirmed that Apple has acquired Samplab, a Zurich-based artificial intelligence audio startup whose software decomposes recorded music into individual instrumental stems and allows producers to edit notes inside audio files as easily as MIDI data. The deal—Apple's second AI audio move in a week following its acqui-hire of the team behind podcast generator Huxe—points to deeper machine-learning tools inside Logic Pro and Final Cut Pro. On the legal front, haptics patent holder Taction Technologies asked a federal judge in California to award ongoing royalties through 2035 on every iPhone 18 Pro and Apple Watch sold, seeking to build on a $5.7bn jury verdict over the Taptic Engine vibration mechanism. (9to5Mac, MacMagazine, 9to5Mac)

OpenAI bugging suspect linked to Saudi officials as AI models estimate cancer survival and beat Minecraft

Federal prosecutors in California opposed bail on Monday for Abdulrahman Alfozan, a former OpenAI infrastructure engineer arrested after security staff discovered a hidden audio recorder taped behind a television inside a San Francisco conference room where company executives held sensitive meetings with US government officials. In a detention filing, the Department of Justice alleged that searches of Alfozan's devices uncovered direct communications with members of the Saudi royal household and showed that a Saudi military official had paid for a one-way flight to Doha for his family days before his arrest. Elsewhere in applied artificial intelligence, clinicians at Mass General Brigham published a study in The Lancet Digital Health detailing FAHR-FaceAge and FAHR-FaceSurvival, deep-learning models trained on 40 million facial photographs that estimate a patient's biological age and survival odds across multiple cancers from a single smartphone selfie, outperforming standard clinical frailty scores. (BBC, Guardian)

Autonomous systems also crossed a threshold in virtual worlds as four Google Gemini 4 Argon agents working together inside Minecraft defeated the game's final boss, the Ender Dragon, in just over 27 hours of continuous play without human prompts. Connected through the Mineflayer programming interface, the agents divided up resource gathering, smelting, Nether exploration and combat, writing 2,783 JavaScript routines and recovering from 605 deaths along the way. In human-made games, former Rockstar North developers reflected ahead of the 19 November launch of Grand Theft Auto VI on how the studio's decentralised culture lets individual engineers slip unscripted simulation details into the open world without central sign-off, while players of the newly released Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 discovered an in-game memorial honouring series co-creator Vince Zampella, and Japan's Mars Moons Exploration spacecraft launched toward Phobos to return 10 grams of Martian moon dust after arriving in August 2027. (IGN, IGN, IGN, BBC)

Culture

Secret Elizabeth Holmes documentary breaks box-office records as Apu speaks again on The Simpsons

You Can See Everything, a three-hour documentary directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim and distributed by A24, took $15m across 855 North American cinemas over the weekend—the largest theatrical opening for a documentary since Michael Moore's Fahrenheit 9/11 in 2004. Kept under wraps until days before release and scheduled to open in UK cinemas on 20 November, the film centres on months of footage shot with convicted Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes and her family before she reported to federal prison in Texas, gradually turning into a hall-of-mirrors inquiry into reality television, performance and self-deception. On the small screen, The Simpsons ended an eight-year vocal silence for convenience-store proprietor Apu Nahasapeemapetilon on Sunday night, introducing Indian-born actor Sunil Malhotra as the character's new voice alongside Janina Gavankar as his wife Manjula in an episode written with South Asian consultants, six years after Hank Azaria stepped aside. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, BBC)

In broadcasting and music, Christiane Amanpour announced she will leave CNN in June after 43 years as the network's defining foreign correspondent and chief international anchor, while Brazilian musicians paid tribute to samba pianist and singer Benito Di Paula, whose syncopated 1970s hits such as Retalhos de Cetim and Charlie Brown brought piano-led samba to a mass audience. Across London's autumn museum season, Dulwich Picture Gallery opened Britain's first complete exhibition of all 46 woodblock prints from Hokusai's Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, Tate Modern unveiled Light and Magic, a global survey of turn-of-the-century pictorialist photography, and Senate House Library paired Charles Booth's colour-coded Victorian poverty maps with contemporary testimony from Londoners navigating temporary accommodation and private rents. (Guardian, Meio, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

Sports

Arsenal relish Bayern Munich test in the Champions League as Tottenham claim their first league win

Arsenal fly to Germany on Tuesday ahead of Wednesday night's Champions League meeting with Bayern Munich at the Allianz Arena, arriving with 10 victories from 11 matches across all competitions this season. Defender Ezri Konsa, who joined Mikel Arteta's side from Aston Villa for £51m in the summer, said the squad viewed the fixture as a measure of their European maturity as they prepare to mark England captain Harry Kane, who has scored 155 goals in 157 appearances since moving to Bavaria. Bayern warmed up for the tie by dismantling RB Leipzig 6–1 in the Bundesliga thanks to a hat-trick from former Liverpool forward Luis Díaz, though Vincent Kompany will be without French playmaker Michael Olise through suspension. Elsewhere in the competition, Manchester City prepare to host AEK Athens on Tuesday night short of attacking cover after forward Antoine Semenyo was ruled out for eight weeks with a knee ligament injury while Erling Haaland manages a bruised foot. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

In the Premier League, Tottenham Hotspur climbed off the foot of the table on Monday night by beating Frank Lampard's Coventry City 3–1 in north London to record their first league victory of the campaign under Roberto De Zerbi. Playmaker James Maddison marked his first start in 536 days following knee surgery by opening the scoring early on, before Omar Marmoush and veteran defender Ben Davies sealed the points to ease the immediate pressure on De Zerbi. Off the pitch, England women's head coach Sarina Wiegman signed a contract extension with the Football Association through the 2029 European Championship, the Portuguese Football Federation handed Cristiano Ronaldo a 30-day suspension and a €255 fine for walking out of the national squad's training camp after a dispute with manager Jorge Jesus, and UEFA general secretary Theodore Theodoridis gave FIFA until 2 November to answer more than 50 governance questions and release financial documents on Gianni Infantino's proposal to sell a 20% stake in World Cup commercial rights to private investors. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

The Fold

A daily briefing for Londoners who want the full picture in one place.

Inspired by Brazil’s Meio · Tuesday, 20 October 2026 · leonardoresston.github.io/thefold

item.title: The Fold — 2026-10-19
item.description: The Fold morning briefing for 19 October 2026: France’s weekend of unrest, the energy war in Ukraine, Brazil’s final campaign push, UK infrastructure pressures, AI security and Arsenal’s late victory.
item.content:encoded:
Monday 19 October 2026 · London

The Fold

Your morning briefing from the UK & the world

In this edition

  • Emmanuel Macron calls for calm after widespread unrest and roughly 2,400 arrests across France.
  • Ukraine regains US ballistic missile warnings as reciprocal strikes hit power infrastructure.
  • Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro rally supporters on the streets ahead of Sunday’s presidential runoff.
  • Microsoft pulls out of a planned Essex AI datacentre over long delays to grid power.
  • Computer analysis concludes that Shakespeare and Christopher Marlowe collaborated on Edward III.
  • Noni Madueke’s deflected late goal gives Arsenal a 1–0 victory at Nottingham Forest.

News

France counts the cost after a weekend of street fury

French cities spent Sunday clearing shattered glass and assessing burnt-out civic buildings after one of the most destructive weekends of civil disorder in recent decades. President Emmanuel Macron appealed for calm as smaller clashes and looting persisted in parts of Paris and Lyon. Across the country, police made roughly 2,400 arrests over the weekend, while the interior ministry counted around 1,000 injured officers on Saturday alone, seven of whom required hospital treatment for serious wounds. (BBC)

The demonstrations began as a broad movement over living costs, underfunded public services and fuel prices, after petrol reached a record €2.40 a litre late last month. What started among secondary school pupils in September grew rapidly once trade unions, university students and former yellow-vest protesters joined the marches. Between 550,000 and 800,000 people turned out across France on Saturday. Most marched peacefully, carrying union banners and calling for public investment in schools and relief from inflation, before black-clad groups and rioters clashed with police lines. (BBC, Guardian)

In Limoges, fire tore through the ornate 19th-century town hall on Saturday night, bringing down its clock tower and roof and leaving residents staring at the blackened shell on Sunday morning. Widespread looting also hit commercial streets in Paris, Marseille and Lille. Macron instructed local prefects and mayors to draw up security plans to protect shops and municipal buildings, while acknowledging that many demonstrators had marched over legitimate economic grievances. (BBC)

Policing tactics have become a second flashpoint. Riot officers used teargas, stun grenades, water cannon and batons to clear squares, and anger over an earlier incident in Lens, where a police grenade severely injured a 15-year-old pupil’s hand, helped draw younger crowds on to the streets. Macron promised full transparency over the conduct of the security forces. With the April presidential election six months away, Marine Le Pen has sought to link the government’s fiscal policies to the breakdown in order, while Jean-Luc Mélenchon and the left have focused on police violence and the social pressures driving the protests. (BBC, Guardian)

Ukraine regains US missile warnings as grid strikes escalate

Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on Sunday that the United States had restored intelligence sharing on Russian ballistic missile launches after a three-day pause that left Ukrainian cities without advance warning of incoming strikes. Even as that data resumed, Zelenskyy maintained his accusation that Washington had intentionally slowed Ukraine’s Starlink satellite internet connections through SpaceX to pressure Kyiv during diplomatic disagreements. US treasury secretary Scott Bessent denied any administration involvement, stating that Donald Trump and Marco Rubio had nothing to do with satellite speeds, while Zelenskyy noted that talks with American envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were continuing. (Guardian)

The dispute unfolded alongside heavy reciprocal attacks on power and industrial infrastructure following the collapse of Trump’s proposed energy ceasefire. Russian strikes killed a woman in Zaporizhzhia and wounded at least two others, including a six-year-old girl. Overnight, Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones against Russian oil depots, warehouses and datacentres. Fires broke out at an oil terminal and industrial sites in St Petersburg, where strikes also hit an Ozon logistics hub and a VK datacentre, while authorities in the surrounding Leningrad region reported 145 downed drones and power cuts affecting 20,000 residents. (Guardian)

Sunday’s barrages also sent an alert across Nato’s eastern border. Lithuania advised residents in central and northern areas to take shelter for roughly an hour and temporarily closed Kaunas airport after an unidentified object entered its airspace. Nato fighter jets scrambled to the area were unable to spot the object through thick cloud. Ukraine’s foreign ministry apologised for the possible diversion of its drones into Lithuanian skies, pointing to Russian electronic warfare as the likely cause and pledging to share flight data with Vilnius. (Guardian)

Footage counters Israeli doubts over West Bank diplomat assault

New video and eyewitness evidence from the Palestinian village of Taybeh has contradicted attempts by Benjamin Netanyahu’s office to cast doubt on Saturday’s settler attack against European diplomats and French visitors. After masked men armed with sticks assaulted the group during the olive harvest, knocking Bernard Baudoux, the mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, to the ground and smashing a reinforced window on a diplomatic vehicle, the Israeli prime minister’s office issued a statement questioning the sequence of events and warning of a campaign to smear Israel. Footage recorded moments before and during the confrontation shows the visitors retreating peacefully toward cars bearing diplomatic plates as masked settlers charged up the hill and targeted Baudoux while he wore his tricolour mayoral sash. (Guardian)

The assault came a day after American photojournalist Heidi Levine was hospitalised following an attack by Israeli militants at another West Bank olive harvest, an episode Netanyahu’s office had similarly described as disputed. On Sunday, more than a dozen former senior Israeli diplomats, including two former directors general of the foreign ministry and several former ambassadors, staged an unprecedented demonstration outside the ministry in Jerusalem. Holding banners addressed to Netanyahu and foreign minister Gideon Sa’ar, the retired officials demanded immediate state action to stop violent attacks against Palestinians and foreign representatives in the occupied territory. (Guardian)

Brazil’s rival camps fill the streets before the final week

One week before Brazil’s 25 October presidential runoff, supporters of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro staged competing street demonstrations across major cities. Along Rio de Janeiro’s Copacabana beachfront, a musical rally convened by Caetano Veloso and producer Paula Lavigne drew crowds across roughly a kilometre of the avenue, with performances by Djavan, João Bosco, Simone, Marina Sena and Fernanda Abreu. Earlier in the day, Chico Buarque joined a student march organised by the National Union of Students near the Candelária church in central Rio, while pro-Lula demonstrations also took place in Brasília, Salvador, Maceió and Curitiba. (Folha, Folha)

In São Paulo, Flávio Bolsonaro gathered supporters across eight blocks of Avenida Paulista alongside state governor Tarcísio de Freitas. Researchers from the University of São Paulo and Cebrap estimated the peak crowd at 71,900 people. Flávio kept his remarks brief to preserve his voice for Sunday night’s televised confrontation on Band, the first head-to-head debate between the two candidates of the campaign. He promised supporters that his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence for an attempted coup, would hand him the presidential sash if he defeats the Workers’ party next Sunday. (Folha, Folha)

Behind the street mobilisation lies a shifting electoral map. An analysis of first-round returns shows that Lula’s margin over the Bolsonaro ticket narrowed in 98% of municipalities across the north-east compared with 2022. While Lula still won 21.5 million votes across the nine north-eastern states, Flávio rose to 10.4 million, an 18.3% increase on his father’s total four years ago, driven by small and medium-sized interior towns linked to agribusiness and local mayors allied with centre-right parties. Separately, Brazil’s electoral court confirmed that 1,397 voting sections affecting 402,599 people have changed address because of storm damage or building works, prompting Lula’s coalition to ask for wider publicity and transport support. (Folha, Folha)

Flávio’s campaign also faced new legal questions after federal police asked the supreme court to open an inquiry into suspected money laundering involving lawyer Willer Tomaz, a target in the wider investigation into pension-deduction fraud at the National Social Security Institute. Police cited records showing that Flávio held master-user operational access to a bank account belonging to an offshore company, Alcazar Holding, in which Tomaz is a partner, until May 2025. Justice Alexandre de Moraes has been assigned the request; Flávio’s lawyers noted that no formal inquiry has been opened, and the senator maintains that his relationship with Tomaz is strictly personal. (Folha)

Whitehall presses for EU crime databases and winter NHS capacity

Home secretary Shabana Mahmood meets European home affairs commissioner Magnus Brunner on Monday for talks on border security, migration and counter-terrorism, as prime minister Andy Burnham seeks to reconnect Britain to European law-enforcement databases lost after Brexit. The discussions precede next month’s EU–UK summit and coincide with Frontex figures showing a 43% drop in small-boat crossings across the Channel. British officials are particularly eager to regain access to the Schengen Information System, which handles roughly 20 million daily checks on wanted fugitives, missing people and stolen vehicles, alongside the Eurodac biometric database used to track asylum claims and security alerts. Brunner will also hold talks with MI5 director general Ken McCallum during his London visit. (Guardian)

Domestically, health secretary Yvette Cooper announced £140m in capital funding for urgent care across England to prepare hospitals for a difficult winter. The money will fund 14 regional schemes, including expanded ambulance fleets, same-day emergency care and upgraded A&E departments, after summer heatwaves drove a record 7.3 million emergency attendances between June and August and early autumn flu admissions climbed sharply. The Royal College of Nursing welcomed the immediate relief while warning that extra rooms and vehicles cannot compensate for chronic nursing shortages ahead of the budget. (Guardian)

Hospitals are simultaneously navigating new NHS England guidance requiring single-sex wards, toilets and changing rooms to be allocated by biological sex following last year’s supreme court ruling on the Equality Act. An internal NHS England impact assessment concluded that while the policy supports privacy and legal clarity for many patients, transgender patients could face treatment delays, greater risk of being cared for in corridors if side rooms are unavailable, or distress that deters them from seeking care. In Westminster, an expected Liberal Democrat showdown failed to materialise after a meeting of the party’s 72 MPs ended without a challenge to Ed Davey, despite grumbling over his conference pledges on income tax cuts and the pension triple lock. (Guardian, Guardian)

Economy

Grid delays cost Essex a flagship Microsoft AI datacentre

Microsoft has withdrawn from an agreement to serve as the anchor customer for Nscale’s planned artificial intelligence datacentre in Loughton, Essex, dealing a blow to a project ministers promoted last year as the largest facility of its kind in Britain. Although the British developer has cleared the former scaffolding yard and hoped to open the site next year, electricity distributor UK Power Networks informed Nscale that sufficient grid capacity may remain unavailable until the early or mid-2030s. While Microsoft continues to partner with Nscale on a separate datacentre in Norway, the prospect of waiting years for power prompted the US company to walk away from the Essex deal. (Guardian, BBC)

Nscale insisted that it remains committed to developing the Loughton site and is exploring on-site power generation alongside alternative locations across the UK. The setback highlights a physical bottleneck confronting the government’s industrial strategy: attracting capital commitments from technology companies is far easier than securing high-voltage grid connections and building power infrastructure quickly enough to run energy-hungry computing clusters. (Guardian)

Home insulation weighed against North Sea oil in budget debate

Preserving the government’s £15bn warm homes plan would cut household energy bills by roughly £1bn a year, boost the economy by £1.6bn annually and support around 50,000 jobs across small installation firms, according to an analysis by the E3G thinktank. The programme, which funds home insulation and heat pumps with a focus on low-income households, is expected to draw in a further £15bn in private investment, yet faces potential reductions as ministers search for fiscal savings ahead of the budget. (Guardian)

E3G contrasted those domestic gains with the roughly 1,100 direct and indirect jobs projected for the proposed Rosebank oilfield west of Shetland, where oil would be sold on international markets rather than lowering British utility bills directly. Ministers are weighing consent for Rosebank and the Jackdaw gasfield, both of which held licences before Labour halted new exploration permits. Energy companies and trade bodies have urged Whitehall to maintain consistent retrofit funding so suppliers can train installers and scale up domestic supply chains. (Guardian)

Condé Nast UK profits drop and doorstep roofing scams surge

Pre-tax profits at the British arm of Condé Nast fell 36% last year to nearly £18m, excluding exceptional items, as domestic revenue slipped 7% to £70.6m. Strong growth in international income, which rose 18% to £29.7m, kept total turnover at the publisher of Vogue, GQ and Tatler steady at roughly £100m. Restructuring costs more than doubled from £1.9m to £4.3m due to severance payouts, even as overall staffing edged down by only five roles to 461. The figures follow an exceptional 2024 bolstered by the £64m sale of Vogue House in Hanover Square, and arrive shortly after the billionaire Newhouse family ruled out selling the global publishing group. (Guardian)

For British households, a more immediate financial hazard has appeared on the doorstep. Citizens Advice recorded more than 2,200 complaints about suspected roofing frauds in England and Wales in the year to August, a 10% rise that made bogus roof repairs the charity’s most commonly reported consumer scam. Three-quarters of cases begin with cold callers claiming to have spotted a loose tile before inventing costly gutter or timber defects and demanding immediate bank transfers for work that is never carried out. (Guardian)

Technology

The World Bank backs small AI as researchers test self-replicating worms

Speaking at the annual meetings of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund in Bangkok, World Bank chief knowledge officer Paschal Donohoe urged developing nations to build specialised, compact artificial intelligence models capable of running on mobile phones in local languages with minimal internet connectivity. Rather than chasing sprawling consumer chatbots, Donohoe pointed to tools such as the bank’s AgriConnect scheme in India, which gives smallholders localized soil advice where agricultural specialists are scarce. IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva warned the same gathering that while basic electricity and digital infrastructure could democratise AI adoption, roughly 40% of jobs worldwide face augmentation or elimination, threatening the routine entry-level roles that young workers traditionally use to start their careers. (Guardian)

At the other end of the computing spectrum, researchers at Anthropic have demonstrated a prototype self-replicating AI worm capable of finding software flaws and spreading autonomously across connected devices. Because everyday internet-connected appliances from smart fridges to routers rarely receive timely security patches, security analysts warn that adaptive malware could eventually exploit unpatched networks much faster than traditional computer viruses. Other security researchers countered that current prototypes move slowly and remain easy to block with strong passwords and routine patching. (Guardian, Guardian)

Cities push back on robotaxis and a police login leaks plate data

With federal autonomous-vehicle legislation stalled in Congress, American municipal governments are using street-management and zoning rules to curb driverless car fleets. Minneapolis is weighing an ordinance requiring human safety monitors inside autonomous vehicles, San Diego has moved to restrict Waymo pickups at its airport, and Austin firefighters have demanded rapid towing protocols and direct communication lines when driverless cars block emergency scenes. California bills would let cities cap fleet sizes or operating hours, while Santa Monica and Culver City have used zoning and noise rules to curb charging depots. Facing a local regulatory patchwork, operators such as Waymo and Uber are prioritising US states that prohibit municipal bans while preparing expansions in London, Manchester, Tokyo and Munich. (The Verge)

Municipal oversight of civic technology also came under scrutiny in Savannah, Georgia, where police commanders dismissed officer Amber Harpe after discovering she had shared her login for the city’s Flock automated licence-plate reader network with her husband, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent. Although Savannah police policy bars sharing Flock data with federal immigration authorities, Tyler Harpe used the account to run 983 searches across 97 vehicle plates, overwhelmingly registered to Hispanic drivers. Senior commanders overruled a recommended eight-hour suspension and fired Harpe alongside five other department employees caught misusing the surveillance system. (The Verge)

In consumer hardware, supply-chain reports indicate that Apple could unveil a redesigned MacBook Pro featuring an OLED display and touchscreen support as early as 6 November, alongside a next-generation HomeView smart display mounted on a motorised robotic arm slated for next year. Meanwhile, in Washington, Representative Ritchie Torres introduced the Power To The Players Act, directing the Federal Trade Commission to require offline play modes before publishers shut down servers for purchased video games, while Silent Hill 2 remake studio Bloober Team pledged to keep releasing physical discs and publisher Alliance Arts cancelled a public Steam demo for Drunken Goddess Reflux to prevent AI-generated clones. (9to5Mac, 9to5Mac, The Verge, IGN, IGN)

Shakespeare and Marlowe shared credit on Edward III, study finds

Computerised linguistic analysis has concluded beyond reasonable doubt that the Elizabethan history play Edward III, published anonymously in 1596 and omitted from the 1623 First Folio, was written primarily by William Shakespeare in collaboration with Christopher Marlowe. Researchers Rory Loughnane at the University of Kent and Brett Greatley-Hirsch at the University of Leeds compared the text against works by 10 dramatists from the late 1580s and early 1590s, examining word-frequency patterns and grammatical markers across individual scenes. Their tests attributed 23 segments of the play to Shakespeare and nine segments, including the closing martial speech, to Marlowe. (Guardian)

Because Marlowe was killed in a Deptford lodging-house brawl in May 1593 at the age of 29, the findings date the collaboration to around 1592, when both playwrights were in their late twenties. Following earlier scholarship linking Marlowe to the Henry VI trilogy, the study portrays the two dramatists as regular working partners rather than distant theatrical rivals. Separately, an exhibition opening at the Fitzwilliam Museum in Cambridge on 23 October restores Morris & Co designer Kate Faulkner to prominence, displaying her 6.3-metre silvered-gesso altarpiece, tiles, wallpapers and Red House embroidery. (Guardian, Guardian)

In Bristol, the Old Vic is countering tight school arts budgets by taking Muneera Pilgrim’s play Protests, Hymns and Cries of Triumph directly into 19 secondary schools, reaching roughly 4,000 pupils for free. (Guardian)

Sports

Madueke breaks the deadlock as Arsenal grind past Forest

Noni Madueke came off the bench at half-time to score an 80th-minute winner as Arsenal beat Nottingham Forest 1–0 at the City Ground. In a tight, low-tempo contest where Arsenal failed to register a first-half shot on target for the seventh time in 10 matches this season, Mikel Arteta replaced Eberechi Eze with Madueke at the break before introducing Jurri&ebreve;n Timber, Mikel Merino and Viktor Gyökeres in a 66th-minute triple change. Ten minutes from time, Declan Rice intercepted a loose clearance and fed Madueke, who cut inside and saw his strike deflect off Forest defender Jair Cunha past goalkeeper Matz Sels for Arsenal’s only shot on target of the afternoon. (Guardian, BBC)

The victory keeps Arsenal within reach of leaders Manchester City and extends the club’s remarkable reliance on its bench: Arsenal substitutes have contributed 26 Premier League goals and assists since the start of last season, more than any other side in the division. With summer signing Christos Tzolis sidelined by a hamstring injury, Madueke has seized his chance across both wings, following an impressive display against Leeds and a Champions League assist against Lille with Sunday’s decisive goal. Oliver Glasner’s Forest side, led energetically up front by Liam Delap, have still yet to score a home league goal in five attempts under their new manager. (Guardian, BBC)

Brighton hit five past Palace while United draw again

Brighton matched their record 5–0 derby victory over Crystal Palace, racing into a three-goal lead inside the opening 10 minutes at the Amex Stadium. After Palace defender Jaydee Canvot headed a Pascal Gross free-kick into his own net, Diego Gómez lobbed goalkeeper Walter Benítez from 51 metres, the longest-range Premier League goal since Wayne Rooney scored from 58 metres in 2017. Yasin Ayari added a deflected third before the interval, and second-half goals from Charalampos Kostoulas and substitute Jack Hinshelwood left Palace manager Pierre Sage apologising to supporters in shame after his side’s heavy defeat. (Guardian)

At Elland Road, Manchester United drew 1–1 with Leeds as Dominic Calvert-Lewin’s second-half strike cancelled out Bryan Mbeumo’s opener, leaving Michael Carrick’s side with seven points and a single victory from seven league matches. Bournemouth earned their first league win under Marco Rose by beating 10-man Sunderland 2–0 at the Vitality Stadium, where Brazilian striker Evanilson set up Marcus Tavernier’s opener, drew the 17th-minute foul that saw Kevin Danso sent off, and rounded Robin Roefs for the second. In the Women’s Super League, Lauren James and Ellie Carpenter each scored twice as Chelsea beat Tottenham 6–2, while Manchester City defeated Brighton 3–2 to stay two points clear. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

The Fold

A daily briefing for Londoners who want the full picture in one place.
