item.title: The Fold — 2026-10-18
item.description: The Fold morning briefing for 18 October 2026: The West Bank harvest attack, Brazil’s runoff, Scotland’s independence push, economic pressures, AI access and the weekend’s football.
item.content:encoded:
Sunday 18 October 2026 · London

The Fold

Your morning briefing from the UK & the world

In this edition

  • European diplomats and a French mayor are attacked during the West Bank olive harvest.
  • Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro prepare for their first shared presidential debate.
  • John Swinney renews Scotland’s independence campaign.
  • The IMF warns that conflict and debt are testing economic resilience.
  • Websites restrict AI agents as Meta revises its crawling terms.
  • Manchester City win a seventh straight league game and Arsenal Women draw again.

News

Diplomats attacked during West Bank olive harvest

Masked Israeli settlers attacked European diplomats, Palestinian civilians and a French mayor near Taybeh on Saturday, bringing international condemnation and fresh demands for action against settler violence. Belgium’s consul general, French and Polish diplomats and Catholic representatives were among those targeted in the predominantly Christian Palestinian village. Bernard Baudoux, mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France, described being knocked to the ground while taking part in the olive harvest alongside local residents. (Sky News)

A Belgian vehicle was damaged. Belgium’s foreign minister, Maxime Prévot, said his diplomatic team was safe and pledged to keep pressing for European Union sanctions against violent settlers. Poland also condemned the targeting of the diplomatic convoy. Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, denounced the violence and confirmed a police investigation, while criticising the lack of advance coordination with the Israeli military. The attack followed Friday’s assault on Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine, who was hospitalised after covering Palestinians gathering olives. (Sky News)

Israel’s military confirmed the assault and said no soldiers had been at the scene. Police promised to pursue those responsible. Benjamin Netanyahu’s office subsequently warned against drawing premature conclusions and raised the prospect of a campaign to discredit Israel. The violence comes shortly before an Israeli election in which security and the government’s treatment of Palestinians are under scrutiny. Opposition politician Gadi Eisenkot sharply criticised the attackers and the damage they were doing to Israel’s standing. (AP)

The harvest has become a particularly dangerous period for Palestinian communities. At least four people have been killed and more than 100 injured since it began earlier this month, according to the Palestinian health ministry. The West Bank has been under Israeli occupation since 1967; the UN and much of the international community regard the settlements as illegal. Saturday’s assault put visiting diplomats alongside the farmers, activists and journalists already exposed to attacks, with European governments now demanding protection and accountability. (AP)

Brazil’s runoff becomes a test of turnout

Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro are entering the final week of Brazil’s presidential campaign with a shared problem: getting supporters back to polling stations where the local election is already over. Only six states will hold a second round for governor. São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Rio de Janeiro, the country’s three largest electorates, settled their gubernatorial contests on 4 October, and all three gave Flávio an advantage in the presidential first round. Both campaigns are leaning on local allies to sustain the effort until the national runoff on 25 October. (Folha)

Flávio’s team is calling on governors and other elected politicians to mobilise their bases, while Lula’s campaign has set local targets for allies, including candidates who lost their own races. In the north-east, where Lula is strongest, only Rio Grande do Norte has a gubernatorial runoff. That makes maintaining campaign activity and access to the polls especially important. The candidates also have a direct opportunity to reach undecided voters tonight: both have confirmed their participation in the Band debate in São Paulo. (Folha, Folha)

The debate is scheduled to begin at 8pm in São Paulo, midnight in London, with about two hours of broadcasting across television, radio and digital channels. Eduardo Oinegue and Adriana Araújo will moderate. Its opening block includes 30 minutes in which the candidates can confront each other directly, followed by further questions and exchanges. Neither took part in a first-round debate, so this will be their first shared presidential encounter of the campaign. A final debate is planned for TV Globo on 23 October; Flávio’s participation there was still under evaluation in the account setting out tonight’s rules. (Folha)

New Datafolha findings help explain what each campaign is trying to activate. Among Flávio’s supporters, 41% cited change and alternation in power as a reason for their choice, followed by rejection of Lula and the Workers’ party at 31%. Among Lula’s supporters, social protection was the leading motive, at 48%, with his record and legacy cited by 22%. Respondents could give more than one reason. The survey interviewed 2,520 people in 153 municipalities on 13 and 14 October and has a two-point margin of error. It put valid voting intentions at 51% for Flávio and 49% for Lula, a narrow gap that leaves the final days consequential. The findings describe different priorities within the two camps; they do not establish how many supporters will actually turn out next Sunday. (Folha)

Brazil’s electoral court orders equal treatment by Meta

Brazil’s electoral court has unanimously upheld an order requiring Meta to give Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro equal treatment across its platforms until the runoff ends. The ruling bars artificial restrictions on the distribution of campaign content and requires human review when automated systems restrict candidate accounts or paid promotion. Where an automated restriction is applied, Meta must review it within two hours and tell the court what happened, why it happened and the outcome. (Folha)

The order also covers equal criteria for the company’s image-generation tool and restricts election advertising that has not been commissioned by a candidate, their national party or coalition, including advertising paid for from abroad. Non-compliance can bring a daily fine of R$500,000. Lula’s campaign brought the case after alleging repeated problems with distribution and promotion. Meta has disputed allegations of partisan interference and attributed problems to technical failures. The ruling puts the handling of those systems under close scrutiny for the campaign’s remaining days. (Folha)

Swinney renews the independence campaign

John Swinney launched a renewed push to persuade Scotland to leave the UK at the SNP conference in Aberdeen. The Choose Scotland campaign has a six-figure budget. The first minister is trying to turn his party’s fifth consecutive Holyrood election victory into momentum for another referendum, although the SNP fell short of the overall majority he had set as his target. Nationalist first ministers in Wales and Northern Ireland have added to his argument that the UK’s constitutional relationship is changing. (Guardian, PA / Scotland Press)

The immediate route to a vote remains uncertain. Westminster would have to agree to a referendum, and Swinney’s address also stressed delivery through the powers Scotland already has. He confirmed that the £2 bus fare cap would extend to the north-east from April, following its introduction in the Highlands and west central Scotland. He wants the cap available across Scotland by the end of the parliamentary term and the bus network brought under public control through regulation and franchising. (BBC)

Swinney also promised action to make misogyny a specific criminal offence and funding for community groups tackling racism. His speech became personal when he linked his commitment to independence to the future of his 15-year-old son. Andy Burnham had used his visit to Motherwell a day earlier to offer cooperation on deeper devolution to local communities. The two leaders remain open to working together on that agenda, even as they seek very different constitutional futures. (BBC, PA / Scotland Press)

Yemen’s war threatens airports and shipping

The UAE is set to resume funding Yemeni government forces, with Saudi air cover, as the two Gulf states respond to Houthi advances. The Iran-backed movement has repeatedly struck Saudi Arabia’s main international airport and gained territory near an important shipping chokepoint. Saudi Arabia’s superior weaponry has struggled to prevent the attacks. The Houthis’ ability to disperse fighters and equipment across mountainous territory helps them survive air campaigns while retaining the capacity to threaten energy facilities and trade routes. (Guardian, AP)

Economy

Economic resilience has a growing bill

The world economy is continuing to withstand war and disruption, but the room for governments to absorb further shocks is narrowing. At Saturday’s IMF meetings in Bangkok, the fund’s leadership warned about the combined pressure from conflict, high debt, inflation and climate risks. Disruption to shipping routes threatens food and energy security, with poorer countries and fragile states especially exposed. Governments face the difficult task of rebuilding their finances while protecting vulnerable people and preserving investment that can support future growth. (IMF)

Artificial intelligence is helping sustain investment and optimism, while also creating a concentration risk. IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva warned that relying heavily on one engine of growth leaves the economy vulnerable. The fund sees scope for productivity gains, alongside the possibility that the benefits will be distributed unevenly across countries and workers. Its message to governments was to strengthen institutions and cooperate with technology companies on safeguards while there is still time to shape how the technology spreads. (IMF)

The debate over household support shows why those choices are becoming harder. IMF research published earlier this month found that broad consumer subsidies can require three to six times as much public money as targeted transfers to provide the same protection to poorer households. Producer subsidies can be more expensive still. During Europe’s 2022–23 energy crisis, less than 20 cents of every euro spent holding down electricity, gas and petrol prices reached the poorest fifth of households. Wealthier households also benefited from those schemes because they consumed the subsidised goods. (IMF)

Temporary payments directed through social protection systems can therefore stretch limited budgets further. The fund recognises that governments may need wider measures during acute food insecurity or when they cannot deliver targeted help quickly. Clear expiry dates and careful design then matter. Food and energy shocks take a disproportionate share of poorer families’ income, and wages can remain depressed long after the first price surge has passed. That makes the way support is delivered a central part of managing the crisis. (IMF)

Apprenticeship policy shifts towards younger recruits

Ministers are considering higher employer contributions for older apprentices in England, creating a stronger incentive to recruit younger workers. The proposal comes as the existing funding system is already being redirected towards people aged 16 to 24. Under rules introduced this summer, government covers eligible training and assessment costs up to the funding limit for that age group at employers outside the levy system. It also covers them where a levy-paying employer has exhausted its available funds. (Guardian, Department for Work and Pensions)

A £2,000 hiring payment is available from October to eligible employers outside the levy when they recruit apprentices aged 16 to 24. Other changes have shortened the period in which employers can use newly credited levy funds from two years to one, and removed the automatic 10% top-up. Employers still have to cover costs above a course’s funding band. These details matter for the next stage of reform: hiring support, the amount available for training and the employer’s own contribution each affect the decision to offer a place. The new proposal concerns England; the other UK nations run separate apprenticeship arrangements. (Department for Work and Pensions)

Technology

The web puts limits on AI’s new assistants

AI assistants built to shop, book travel and handle everyday administration are meeting resistance from the websites they need to use. Yelp limits agents to participants in its paid data-licensing programme, Delta is blocking them from booking flights, and JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab have cited security concerns in restricting account access. Some failures also come from ordinary anti-bot systems, which can struggle to distinguish a customer’s chosen assistant from unwanted automated traffic. (The Verge)

The dispute raises a practical question for anyone delegating a task: an assistant’s capabilities depend on the services willing to let it act. Retail partnerships offer one route around the barriers, while the legal fight between Amazon and Perplexity continues. Even where commercial agreements exist, checkout and identity checks can still interrupt the process. Companies building agents want websites to treat them as acting for customers; website operators retain concerns about security, control over transactions and the commercial value of the visit. (The Verge)

Meta has meanwhile removed wording from its commercial terms that appeared to allow the use of material from linked websites to train AI. Legal and publishing observers had read the language as potentially overriding a site owner’s instructions against crawling. Meta disputed that interpretation and then deleted the passage. The company says the consolidated crawling terms concern advertising and business products, and that content owners can continue to indicate their preferences through robots.txt. (The Verge)

The change draws attention to two separate permissions: allowing a bot to visit a website and allowing material from that visit to be used for training. Meta says the revision gives it no new rights to disregard website owners’ preferences. For publishers, clear terms are consequential because a link shared through a commercial service can point to a much larger body of work. The removal settles the disputed wording, while wider disagreements over access and the use of online content remain. (The Verge)

Apple tightens rules on sexual deepfake apps

Apple has strengthened its App Store rules to address non-consensual sexual imagery, including material produced with AI. Its user-generated content requirements now explicitly cover this abuse, with developers facing removal if they fail to prevent it. The changes make responsibility for what an app enables more explicit as image-generation tools become easier to distribute. Apple already prohibits pornography in the store; the updated language addresses ways newer tools can be used to create abusive material. (MacMagazine, Apple)

A separate revision targets developers who wait until an app passes review before activating prohibited features. Those developers can lose their apps and membership of the developer programme. Apple has also clarified that apps facilitating human trafficking or child exploitation will be removed and barred from alternative distribution. These are changes to the rules and the sanctions available to enforce them. Their practical effect will depend on identifying violations and responding when developers change an app after approval. (Apple, MacMagazine)

EE sets out the cost of sharing a number across iPhones

EE will include Apple’s iPhone Handoff feature in its Full Works Plus plan and offer it for £5 a month on other plans. The service allows a customer to move between two iPhones while keeping the same mobile number, with calls and messages following the device in use. It requires the network’s support, so its availability and cost are part of the mobile contract as well as the phone’s feature list. (9to5Mac)

The UK service is still listed as coming soon, with Apple having indicated availability by the end of the year. EE is the first UK carrier to announce its pricing. In the US, T-Mobile has set a $5 monthly charge and Verizon a $10 charge. Those differences mean the convenience of using a lighter or spare phone can carry a recurring cost. Customers considering the feature will need to check their plan’s eligibility and the network’s launch date before relying on it. (9to5Mac, 9to5Mac)

A new macOS upgrade exposes old software dependencies

Organisations managing Macs are facing a transition problem around Rosetta, Apple’s compatibility layer for Intel software on Apple silicon. Installing macOS 27 removes Rosetta, although it can still be reinstalled; support is due to end with macOS 28. Some conventional apps prompt users to restore the component when needed. Testing has also found menu-bar utilities that fail without a useful prompt, leaving the person using the Mac with little explanation of what has stopped working. (9to5Mac)

That makes an inventory of older software important before a broad rollout. Reinstalling Rosetta through device-management tools can provide a temporary bridge, while administrators check that vendors have native Apple-silicon versions and test replacements where necessary. Background utilities deserve particular attention because a failure can be easy to miss during a quick application check. The immediate upgrade still allows a workaround. The following macOS release is the deadline that gives the audit its urgency, especially for workplaces where one small utility supports a larger daily task. (9to5Mac)

Sports

City make it seven, Liverpool recover at Brentford

Manchester City beat Ipswich 3–2 to move six points clear at the top of the Premier League. Erling Haaland scored twice and Phil Foden also found the net as Enzo Maresca became the first manager to win his opening seven matches in the competition. City have taken every available point, making the transition from Pep Guardiola exceptionally productive on the pitch. The home crowd’s support was vocal on a day when fans also protested against the Premier League following the club’s financial-rules verdict. (BBC, BBC)

Liverpool came from behind to win 2–1 at Brentford, who finished with nine players. Florian Wirtz created nine chances from open play and supplied the pass for the start of Liverpool’s recovery. Alexander Isak returned from injury to complete the comeback. The result restored momentum after the defeat to City and took Andoni Iraola’s side to fifth, with three victories from his first seven league games in charge. (BBC, BBC)

The win came with fresh injury concerns involving Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong. Liverpool face Villarreal in the Champions League on Tuesday during a stretch of four matches in ten days. Wirtz’s creativity gave them a route through Brentford, but the balance of a side playing two wingers and a number ten remains a concern. Liverpool created 21 attempts, including 14 after the interval, and still had to protect a narrow lead in the closing stages. (BBC)

Arsenal held again at the Emirates

Arsenal drew 1–1 with Birmingham City in the Women’s Super League, with Olivia Smith’s equaliser cancelling out Océane Hurtré’s opener. Arsenal had controlled much of the ball and Alessia Russo struck the post with a first-half header, but Birmingham went ahead after the break when Hurtré ran through to finish. Smith levelled in the 66th minute with a shot from outside the area. A second Arsenal goal never arrived. (Arseblog)

The match statistics underline the frustration: Arsenal had 76% possession and 27 shots to Birmingham’s five, yet put only four attempts on target. Sophie Baggaley made important saves and late Arsenal chances went begging. The result leaves Renée Slegers’s team with one victory in six league matches. With so much possession producing a single goal, finishing and the quality of the final action remain immediate problems to solve. Birmingham left with a point earned through disciplined defending, their goalkeeper’s interventions and the counterattack that put them ahead. (Arseblog, Sky Sports)

The Fold

A daily briefing for Londoners who want the full picture in one place.

item.title: The Fold — 2026-10-17
item.description: The Fold morning briefing for 17 October 2026: Amazon clearance reaches a record low before Brazil votes, London debates robotaxis, Britain weighs its place in European carmaking, and Australia tries to give users control of their feeds.
item.content:encoded:
Saturday 17 October 2026 · London

The Fold

Your morning briefing from the UK & the world

In this edition

  • Brazil’s Amazon clearance falls to its lowest level since records began in 1988, nine days before the presidential runoff.
  • London’s assembly wants the power to limit robotaxis as Uber and Wayve trials grow.
  • British food and drink exports to the EU are down by more than a third.
  • Apple tightens App Store review, and its first folding iPhone sells out into next year.
  • Manchester City will appeal after being found guilty on every charge.

News

Amazon clearance falls to its lowest level in 38 years

Brazil has recorded the smallest annual loss of Amazon rainforest since its government began measuring clearance in 1988. The Prodes satellite system found that 3,335 sq km was cut in the latest year, a fall of 41.8% from the year before. That total is 1,236 sq km below the previous record low, saving an area roughly the size of Rio de Janeiro in a single year. Since Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva returned to office in 2022, the rate has fallen by 71.2%, helped by stronger enforcement and renewed investment in environmental agencies. The numbers give Brazil something unusually concrete to take into the final days of a bitter presidential campaign: public policy has changed what is happening on the ground. (Guardian)

The improvement reaches beyond the rainforest. Clearance in the Cerrado, the vast savanna beside the Amazon, dropped to 5,516 sq km, its lowest level since 2001 and 48.4% below the rate four years ago. The Cerrado has often absorbed the pressure displaced by tighter rules in the forest because soy and beef producers may legally clear more land there. Within the Amazon, Pará, Mato Grosso and Amazonas still accounted for three quarters of all loss, though every one recorded a decline of more than 45%. Roraima, a stronghold of the Bolsonaro family, was the only state where the figure rose, by 0.4%. Progress remains uneven, but the direction is now visible across two ecosystems, extending beyond a single protected boundary. (Guardian)

The result lands nine days before Lula faces Flávio Bolsonaro in a runoff on 25 October. Lula treats the forest as a sovereign asset, a home for Indigenous peoples and a central part of the global climate response. Bolsonaro has courted landowners and extractive interests, followed his father’s pro-development politics and left the climate crisis out of his manifesto. Jair Bolsonaro’s term brought a 59.5% rise in Amazon deforestation as protection agencies lost staff and illegal miners, loggers and land grabbers encountered weaker enforcement. His son has promised to free him from prison and allow him a role in government. A narrow election will therefore decide whether the machinery behind this year’s record is strengthened, dismantled or redirected. (Guardian)

London wants the power to put limits on robotaxis

More than 100,000 people have joined Uber’s London waiting list for an autonomous ride since its first services with Wayve began in September. For now, only a handful of cars operate and each carries a human safety driver. The trial has already expanded to Manchester, while Uber plans to put 100,000 Nvidia robotaxis into service around the world from next year. That pace has sharpened the question of who controls the rollout. Transport for London can license a passenger service, yet the Department for Transport decides whether an autonomous vehicle may operate. Under the framework for future driverless services, TfL could grant or refuse consent without gaining the detailed power to set numbers, conditions or suspensions on London’s streets. (Guardian)

The London assembly’s transport committee wants that authority devolved. Its concerns include congestion, pressure on public transport, safeguarding, accessibility for disabled passengers and the livelihoods of more than 100,000 licensed drivers. The App Drivers and Couriers Union is due to protest outside Wayve’s London base this weekend. San Francisco offers an early glimpse of the scale that could follow: Waymo now supplies more than a quarter of rides there. London brings narrower roads, less predictable pedestrian movement and one of Europe’s largest private-hire markets. The immediate service may be small, but the rules written during this trial will determine how quickly it can grow and whether the city can intervene when the effects extend beyond the people inside the car. (Guardian)

Australia tries to give everyone an off-switch for the feed

Australia’s Digital Duty of Care bill would require social platforms to offer a persistent switch from recommendations to a feed made only from accounts a user follows. The option would have to be obvious, retain the ordinary functions of the app and stay selected after the user leaves. That last detail matters. Following-only feeds already exist in parts of Europe, but some platforms hide them behind menus, remove access to features or quietly return to algorithmic ranking at the next visit. A Dutch court forced Meta to preserve the choice after finding that design breached the EU’s Digital Services Act. Australia is attempting to put that standard directly into national law. (BBC)

The wider duty would cover social media, gaming services and chatbots. Children would have to be protected from material and design choices that encourage eating disorders, misogyny or exposure to pornography; adults would receive a narrower protection against illegal and seriously harmful content. Breaches could bring fines of A$100m, about £52m. The government’s existing ban on social media for children has struggled in practice, and surveys suggest most young users who were online before it remain there. The new approach shifts attention from proving a user’s age to changing the machinery presented to everyone. Nearly half of Australians say they would turn recommendations off, although two-thirds of Gen Z respondents would keep them. Choice alone will not repair every harm. It can still make endless optimisation for attention something a person actively accepts. (BBC)

Economy

Britain’s food exporters have lost more than a third of their EU trade

British food and drink exports to the European Union have fallen by more than a third since 2019, according to National Farmers’ Union analysis of HMRC data. Sugar exports were down 70% in the first seven months of this year against the same period before Brexit; poultry fell 53% and egg products 65%. Across the full years from 2019 to 2025, egg and egg-product sales dropped 74%, while horticultural exports declined by more than half. The EU still bought 68% of Britain’s agricultural food exports last year, so the collapse reaches far beyond a marginal market. Producers have lost volume where distance is short, tastes are familiar and supply chains once ran with comparatively little friction. (Guardian)

Customs codes and health certificates now follow every variation of a product across the border. A carton and its eggs need separate proof; fresh, dried, steamed and sweetened egg products each bring different paperwork. Scottish seed-potato exports to the EU, previously about 20,000 tonnes a year, remain banned because negotiators did not secure recognition of equivalent standards. Scottish salmon, Britain’s largest food export, faces document checks on every consignment, with the friction estimated to cost about £100m in lost sales. Fresh British burgers cannot be sold into the EU, and Welsh shellfish remains barred. The UK and EU largely agreed in May to reduce sanitary and phytosanitary checks from next summer, though important details and transition rules are unfinished. That deal could remove costs and delays for current exporters. Rebuilding customers and specialist supply chains that moved away during six years of barriers will take longer. (Guardian)

Britain’s route into ‘Made in Europe’ runs through Chinese cars

France has dropped its opposition to Britain joining the EU’s coming Made in Europe programme, opening a route back into industrial supply chains that matter deeply to UK carmakers. The proposed price is alignment with European trade defences against Chinese electric vehicles. Downing Street has left tariffs under review while insisting that the terms are still being negotiated; Beijing has warned against discriminatory restrictions. The calculation is difficult because about 80% of British-built cars are exported, more than half to the EU and 6% to China. Exclusion from preferential European procurement could cost billions of pounds in trade. Tariffs might protect domestic factories from subsidised imports, then raise prices for drivers and invite retaliation against the vehicles Britain sells abroad. (Guardian)

Chinese brands are becoming harder to treat as a distant concern. BYD’s UK sales rose 78% year on year in September, Chery’s rose 660% and Changan’s by more than 3,000%. The Franco-German proposal would let countries that were inside the single market on 1 January 2020 opt into the Industrial Accelerator Act if they accept dynamic alignment on investment conditions and relevant trade measures. European lawmakers have tabled 5,100 amendments, and final rules are expected near the end of this year or early 2027. Quotas could be introduced within months under World Trade Organization safeguards; formal anti-subsidy tariffs would require a longer investigation. Britain therefore has time to bargain, but the basic choice is already visible: preserve a permissive market for cheaper imports or secure a more protected place inside Europe’s manufacturing system. (Guardian)

Technology

Apple tightens the gate after harmful apps learned how to slip through

Apple has rewritten parts of its App Review Guidelines after a year of investigations found AI tools for creating non-consensual intimate images, disguised gambling services and other harmful features inside approved apps. The rules for user-generated content now name non-consensual intimate imagery directly and place developers who ignore safeguards or fail to correct known violations in breach of the Developer Code of Conduct. Another new section bars hidden, dormant or undocumented functions, including features concealed through code obfuscation, and makes removal from the store and termination of the developer account explicit penalties. Apps that facilitate child exploitation or human trafficking will also be blocked from alternative distribution as well as removed from the App Store. (9to5Mac, The Verge)

The change follows repeated evidence that review could be fooled by geography or timing. Dozens of gambling apps presented themselves as harmless games and utilities when opened outside Brazil, then exposed betting platforms to Brazilian users, including children. Separate inquiries found that App Store search suggestions and advertising directed people toward AI “undressing” services; San Francisco officials ordered eight of those apps removed in July. The sharper wording gives reviewers a clearer basis for enforcement, but it also underlines the gap between a rulebook and a live store containing millions of changing products. Apple controls the review process, payments and distribution for most iPhone software. Its next test is whether harmful functions are found before users and regulators document them. (9to5Mac)

Apple’s first folding phone sells out into next year

The iPhone Duo became backordered within minutes of pre-orders opening on Friday. By 8.30am on the US east coast, every colour and storage configuration showed an estimated delivery date in late January; customers in Brazil were seeing early February. Apple called demand extraordinary and kept orders open, while launch-day units are due on 23 October. The company’s first folding phone starts at $1,999 with 256GB of storage and rises to $3,199 for 2TB. It has a 5.4-inch display when closed, a 7.6-inch inner screen, an A20 Pro processor, two 48-megapixel rear cameras and Touch ID in place of Face ID. (9to5Mac)

The sellout is an imperfect measure of total demand. Production reports had already pointed to constrained hinge supplies and an initial run of roughly six to ten million devices for the rest of 2026, far below the volumes of Apple’s conventional flagship phones. Some early buyers immediately offered reservations online for thousands of dollars above retail. Even so, selling through a $2,000 experimental model within half an hour gives Apple the clearest possible signal that a folding iPhone can reach beyond a small demonstration market. The question now moves from product design to manufacturing: every delivery date pushed into 2027 is a customer Apple persuaded and cannot yet supply. (9to5Mac)

Ocarina of Time returns, while Remedy finds its fastest seller

Nintendo’s remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time arrives on Switch 2 on 5 November, and its first extended preview suggests a careful modernisation of the 1998 original. Link can sprint and jump manually, the camera rotates freely, items sit in a scrolling bar and aiming can use motion controls. The rebuilt Forest Temple keeps its interlocking rooms, central chamber and deliberately sparse clues, so the old spatial design carries the experience without a trail of instructions taking over. Two Japanese television spots released on Friday also gave the first brief look at Dark Link in the Water Temple, along with Ganondorf, the Master Sword and late-game scenes. New players are being offered a piece of game history with fewer layers of old hardware between them and the ideas that shaped later combat, dungeon and world design. (IGN, IGN)

Remedy, meanwhile, has reached one million sales of Control Resonant in three weeks, the fastest start in the Finnish studio’s history. Alan Wake 2, the previous record holder, needed two months to reach the same point. The result came despite the digital release being cracked and pirated shortly after launch; physical editions have only just gone on sale, leaving room for the total to grow. Remedy’s games have often earned critical admiration while selling more slowly than their budgets would prefer. A million copies this early gives the studio a stronger commercial base for its connected world of Control and Alan Wake, and shows that distinctive single-player games can still expand their audience without sanding away the strangeness that made people notice them. (IGN)

Sports

Manchester City’s appeal has a high legal bar to clear

Manchester City will appeal after being found guilty of every charge concerning breaches of Premier League financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18, including the use of sham contracts to inflate sponsorship revenue by £830m. The club maintains that the money came from the United Arab Emirates government as a shareholder in sponsors and that City’s owners did not provide it. It also argues that the commission made material errors of law, fact and principle. An appeal is a narrower legal exercise than a new hearing. City must identify a decisive legal or factual mistake, or serious procedural unfairness that changed the result. The commission had already examined extensive witness testimony and documents before concluding that sponsorship arrangements disguised owner funding. (BBC)

City’s lawyers are expected to challenge how leaked emails were interpreted and may introduce government records, bank statements or evidence from Etihad Airways. Fresh documents could establish a clearer trail for the disputed payments; material already considered by the commission will be harder to use as the foundation for reversal. Etihad says it was not given an opportunity to participate or correct the evidence, though the sponsor was not itself the respondent and had no automatic right to appear. League rules call for the appeal within 12 weeks, which points to Christmas Eve, but the scale of the case may stretch the timetable. The decision will shape City’s future and the authority of the financial system the rest of the league has been required to follow. (BBC)

Arsenal’s title has not spared the club from job cuts

Arsenal are considering up to 60 redundancies after a structural review begun by Boston Consulting Group before the end of last season. Catering and travel are among the departments affected, while the men’s and women’s first-team coaching and performance staff, academy, community operation, foundation and site security are exempt. The club hopes to redeploy some employees and reduce the final number of departures. Scrutiny has intensified because the review follows Arsenal’s Premier League title, a rise in annual operating costs from £148m to £201m and Mikel Arteta’s new contract worth more than £20m a year. Arteta described the process as part of improving the organisation, then left the detail to executives. Success has given Arsenal more income and ambition; it has also made the distinction between investment on the pitch and savings behind it much harder for the club to explain. (Guardian)

item.title: The Fold — 2026-10-16
item.description: The Fold morning briefing for 16 October 2026: new Reform footage reaches Nigel Farage, severe drought spreads across southern England, Britain prepares a bank tax, and AI moves deeper into browsers and desktop computers.
item.content:encoded:
LONDON · FRIDAY · 16 OCTOBER 2026 · MORNING EDITION

The Fold

Your Morning Briefing from the UK & the World

16/10/26 · 05:30 BST · London

News

The questions around Reform’s candidates now reach Farage himself

The latest footage from ITV’s year-long undercover investigation of Reform UK has moved the argument about the party’s vetting from its local candidates to Nigel Farage’s own decisions. Chris Parry, a retired rear admiral selected for the Hampshire and Solent mayoral election, had said that David Lammy should return to the Caribbean and questioned the primary loyalty of several politicians from minority backgrounds. Ed Sumner, Reform’s head of communications, was recorded calling Parry clearly racist and saying he should be removed. Three weeks after the dispute began, Parry was still the candidate and Farage publicly said an apology could settle the matter. In a private conversation recorded by the reporter, Farage instructed staff to secure that apology; Sumner answered that the leader was protecting him. (Guardian)

Parry was eventually suspended in March after further remarks emerged, including his description of members of a Jewish neighbourhood watch group as cosplayers. The delayed action is harder to explain as a screening failure. Senior staff had identified the problem, advised the leader and watched the candidate remain in place. Labour has asked Farage to explain why he stood by Parry, while the full documentary, Undercover: A Year in Reform, is due on Sunday. It follows footage released a day earlier in which councillors and candidates made racist and misogynistic comments and discussed extreme violence. Several have since left the party or been suspended, leaving some able to continue as independent councillors. (Guardian)

A second recording also exposed the party’s internal culture from another direction. Sarah Pochin, then Reform’s only female MP, described male officials as chauvinistic and said women were excluded, while acknowledging that she presented a friendlier picture in public. Reform has attacked ITV and Hardcash Productions for using false credentials and gaining access to headquarters, computer systems and security information. It says there is no room for racism in the party and that live investigations require due process. Those objections may shape the debate about how the programme was made. The central political question is already plain: when senior colleagues asked Farage to remove a candidate over racist statements, he chose an apology first and suspension only after more evidence became public. (Guardian)

NHS England redraws the rules for wards and changing rooms

Trans women will no longer be placed on female-only wards under new NHS England guidance covering inpatient accommodation, toilets and changing rooms. Single-sex facilities are to be used according to biological sex, with trusts expected to preserve the privacy, dignity and safety of trans patients as well as everyone sharing their accommodation. Clinical need remains the priority when it conflicts with the same-sex rule. Hospitals can provide single rooms or mixed-sex facilities made up of individually lockable rooms, and organisations have been told to audit what they offer. The change replaces guidance that allowed patients and staff to use facilities in line with their gender identity. (Guardian, BBC)

The policy follows the Supreme Court’s 2025 judgment that the Equality Act’s references to women and sex mean biological women and biological sex, including where a trans woman has a gender recognition certificate. A Darlington employment tribunal has since ruled that nurses forced to share a changing room with a trans colleague faced a degrading environment. Sex Matters welcomed the clearer basis for single-sex spaces but asked how trusts would enforce it. TransActual and the Trans+ Solidarity Alliance warned that hospitals short of space and staff will struggle to provide safe alternatives and that some trans people may avoid care. The practical test begins at ward level, where managers must translate a national legal rule into decisions about frightened, ill and vulnerable people while suitable private rooms remain scarce. (Guardian)

Southern England enters severe drought with reservoirs near empty

Parts of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex have been placed in severe drought after the hottest summer on record and the driest April-to-September period in the south-east and south-west for more than a century. Ardingly reservoir in West Sussex is at 19.4% of capacity and Wimbleball on Exmoor at 14.9%; the Environment Agency would normally expect reservoir storage to be around 75% at this point in the year. Wimbleball supplies roughly 300,000 properties across Devon, Somerset and Dorset, while Ardingly serves about 280,000 customers in Sussex. Other major reservoirs in Devon and Cornwall are between roughly a fifth and a little over a third full. (BBC)

The declaration increases daily monitoring, water-quality checks and enforcement of permits used by businesses that draw from rivers and groundwater. Drought orders already allow South East Water and South West Water to reduce by millions of litres the water they release from reservoirs into rivers, preserving supplies through winter while adding pressure to wildlife and downstream users. Southern Water has applied for restrictions in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. Ministers say household taps should keep running, but recovery depends on sustained rain and lower demand. An English winter can refill reservoirs quickly; after six exceptionally dry months, water companies cannot plan on ordinary weather arriving on schedule. (BBC)

Brazil’s two-point election becomes a contest over daily life

Flávio Bolsonaro leads Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva by 51% to 49% among valid votes in the latest Datafolha poll, a statistical tie inside the survey’s two-point margin of error with ten days left before the presidential runoff. Rejection levels are equally tight: 46% say they would not vote for Lula and 44% reject Flávio. The government enters the final stretch with a 41% negative rating and 35% positive, while violence and health are the problems voters mention most often. Both campaigns therefore need a small group of persuadable people at a stage when most supporters have settled their choice. Interviews on national television and a Sunday debate now carry unusual weight because neither candidate has a safe lead to defend. (Folha, Meio)

Lula is trying to turn congressional victories into a direct household offer. A day after the Senate approved the end of the six-day working week, he promised a constitutional amendment guaranteeing free public transport at weekends. That would move the campaign from broad economic confidence to hours at work, the price of a journey and access to a polling station. Abroad, the result is attracting a different kind of attention. Donald Trump’s administration replied to US lawmakers who asked about Washington’s intentions toward Brazil without saying whether it would respect the election result. The omission will deepen concern about outside pressure and election legitimacy. Inside Brazil, the decisive arguments remain immediate: safety, public services, work and whether either candidate can convert a narrow coalition into a governable majority after 25 October. (Folha, Folha)

Economy

A small growth surprise meets a large hole in the Budget

Britain’s economy grew by 0.1% in August, confounding forecasts of a small contraction and giving John Healey one useful number before his first Budget on 28 October. Production rose 0.8%, supported by manufacturing and energy, while construction fell 0.2% and the consumer-facing part of the services economy shrank 0.3%. Food, drink, sport and recreation were among the weak spots as higher petrol, diesel and household energy costs restrained spending. Across the three months to August, GDP expanded 0.7%; output was 2.1% higher than a year earlier, the strongest annual rate since August 2022. Business investment in computing equipment linked to AI infrastructure has helped, though economists expect expensive energy and higher interest rates to slow the final months of the year. (Guardian)

Healey is preparing to ask banks for more money as the Middle East war raises inflation, government borrowing costs and the price of supporting households. The leading option would reverse Jeremy Hunt’s cut to the surcharge on bank profits, taking it from 3% towards its previous 8% and raising more than £2bn a year. HSBC, NatWest, Barclays and Lloyds together generated about £200bn in pre-tax profit over the past five years as higher interest rates widened earnings. Bank executives have lobbied against another rise and warn that a heavier tax burden could move jobs and investment overseas. Smaller lenders want the profit threshold at which the surcharge begins raised from £100m to £500m, an adjustment that could protect new competitors while the largest institutions carry the increase. (Guardian, BBC)

The arithmetic leaves little room for a comfortable compromise. Rising bond yields may have cut as much as half from the £24bn margin previously available under Labour’s fiscal rules. Healey wants to give households and businesses breathing space from energy prices, reassure lenders that debt will be controlled and avoid squeezing departments whose settlements already imply difficult choices. The IMF has upgraded its UK growth forecast and praised progress toward balancing the books, yet it also expects energy costs to bring slower growth in 2027. August’s expansion helps the story he can tell. It contributes only a fraction of the money he needs, which is why the Budget is turning toward a profitable and politically visible sector. (Guardian, Guardian)

Britain pays windfarms to stop while gas plants start

Balancing Great Britain’s electricity network cost £47.9m on Wednesday as the system operator paid windfarms and hydro plants to switch off in areas with excess generation, then paid gas and biomass stations to start where supply was tight. One half-hour period alone cost £1.6m. About nine gigawatts of renewable capacity was curtailed, enough to power more than eight million typical homes, while electricity was also imported through subsea cables. These payments are passed on through energy bills. September’s balancing bill reached a record £505m, and the annual total is expected to climb to £3.2bn. (Guardian)

The country has generating capacity; the difficulty is moving power from windy parts of Scotland to demand further south. The £150bn upgrade of transmission networks is failing to keep pace with renewable projects connecting to the grid. The National Energy System Operator recently asked France for emergency assistance on two days, although it says supplies remained secure and describes the requests as established tools, with no wider failure indicated. New lines could halve balancing costs by the end of the decade if they arrive on time. Until then, households are paying three times for the same bottleneck: to build renewable generation, to leave some of it idle and to run fossil-fuel stations closer to demand. (Guardian)

Technology

ChatGPT steps through the browser door

ChatGPT can now inspect the tabs already open in Google Chrome when its extension is installed and a user tags Chrome from the web or desktop app. OpenAI’s examples include comparing products across several pages, summarising research and bringing information from different tabs into one answer. A redesigned sidebar keeps the full conversation history available beside the current page. In ChatGPT Work, the connection goes further: the assistant can control tabs to send messages, complete forms, download files and group or organise the pages on screen. The change brings much of the abandoned Atlas browser’s ambition into the browser people already use. (The Verge)

Browser context makes the assistant more useful because the user no longer has to copy every relevant detail into a prompt. It also gathers sensitive material into a powerful new permission: personal accounts, draft messages, work documents and shopping decisions often sit open together. The value will depend on how clearly the extension shows what it can see, when control is active and which action is about to be taken. Sending a message or submitting a form carries a different cost from summarising a sofa listing. Moving the model into the sidebar removes friction from ordinary work; careful boundaries now have to become equally ordinary. (The Verge)

An 800-billion-parameter model fits on two desks

Meta has released the weights for Muse Spark Open, a multimodal mixture-of-experts model with more than 800bn parameters and 40bn active for each token. Apple and Meta worked together to optimise it for the M5 Ultra Mac Studio and MLX, Apple’s open-source machine-learning framework. Even compressed to four bits, the model needs 493GB of memory, so the practical setup uses at least two machines and divides the workload between them through RDMA over Thunderbolt 5. Apple’s tests found that linking systems can reduce the delay before a first token by as much as 1.8 times for very long contexts. (MacStories, The Verge, 9to5Mac)

This remains an enterprise experiment. Apple’s 512GB Mac Studio is due at the end of the year, while the current 256GB model with 2TB of storage already costs more than $11,000 and two machines are the minimum. The achievement is architectural: a frontier-scale open model can run locally on computers that sit on a desk and draw power from ordinary wall sockets. Organisations can keep private data on their own hardware, examine the model weights and avoid sending every query to a remote service. Today’s cost confines that freedom to well-funded researchers and companies. The direction is still important. Local AI is moving from small, specialised models toward systems that can challenge the capability of large cloud services. (MacStories, The Verge)

Culture

Croydon turns an awkward plot into Britain’s best building

Lion Green Road in Coulsdon has won the RIBA Stirling prize, making it only the second council-led housing project to be named Britain’s best new building. Croydon council originally asked Mary Duggan Architects and Ruff Architects for 80 homes on a steep, wooded site. The final scheme fits 157 flats into five star-shaped brick towers while retaining mature trees, bluebell woodland and a public path to the old railway embankment. Each home has light and ventilation from two sides, an inset balcony and views arranged by rotating the otherwise repeated tower plan. Three blocks provide affordable homes rented at local housing allowance rates; two are for private rent. Every entrance and lobby receives the same treatment, with no lesser route for lower-cost tenures. (Guardian, BBC)

The scheme survived 257 objections and only 18 letters of support when planning began in 2017, largely over parking. Its construction cost of about £2,500 a square metre made it the cheapest project on the Stirling shortlist. The award is also a postscript to Brick by Brick, Croydon’s council-owned developer, which was halted when the authority went bankrupt in 2020 after weak financial controls, difficult sites, Brexit and the pandemic damaged its plans. The company still completed 751 homes, more than half affordable. Lion Green Road shows what survived that failure: dense housing with shared gardens, play areas, allotments and privacy, delivered on public land without reducing every decision to the highest short-term return. As the government prepares £39bn for housing, the winner offers a model worth copying and a warning about the governance needed to carry it through. (Guardian)

AI speed overwhelms a community built on patient reverse engineering

Decomp.dev, a central index for video-game decompilation projects, is closing its main directory and will stop accepting new projects after a wave of AI-assisted ports disrupted the community it served. Decompilation is the painstaking work of reconstructing source code from a finished game, often line by line, so enthusiasts can understand how it works, preserve it and build careful ports. New models can accelerate parts of that process dramatically. The site’s administrator says opportunists have taken years of existing volunteer work, used AI to rush the final stretch and released unstable ports before the original teams were ready. Projects differ over legal risk, the ethics of AI and the quality of outside contributions, yet the same pattern has repeatedly denied their maintainers a meaningful choice. (IGN)

The website will remain online so existing projects can still be tracked. Its retreat will do little to slow the broader trend: Halo: Combat Evolved and Grand Theft Auto V have already appeared briefly as browser games before their publishers intervened, while stranger remixes circulate as demonstrations of what current models can assemble. The loss is social as much as technical. Traditional projects trained programmers, documented old systems and distributed credit through years of visible collaboration. A fast fork can produce a playable result while stripping away that apprenticeship and the trust that kept the work organised. AI has lowered the cost of finishing a port; decomp.dev’s closure shows that communities can pay the difference. (IGN)

the full picture in one place.

item.title: The Fold — 2026-10-15
item.description: The Fold morning briefing for 15 October 2026: Reform faces a crisis over racist and violent comments, Ukraine loses vital Starlink capacity, Brazil approves a shorter working week, and eight US states sue OpenAI.
item.content:encoded:
LONDON · THURSDAY · 15 OCTOBER 2026 · MORNING EDITION

The Fold

Your Morning Briefing from the UK & the World

15/10/26 · 05:30 BST · London

News

Reform’s vetting promise collides with a year of undercover footage

Reform UK is trying to contain its most serious test of candidate vetting after an ITV investigation recorded councillors and election candidates using racist and misogynistic language and discussing extreme violence. Three councillors have left the party, while Reform says everyone shown in the programme has resigned, been suspended or is under investigation. Alan Feeney, a Solihull councillor and the borough’s deputy mayor, was filmed describing Asian homeowners as parasites and arguing that the non-white share of Britain’s population should be limited to 1%. He has left Reform and remains an independent councillor. Chris Whelan, who appeared in footage from the same campaign, resigned earlier this week; another councillor shown making offensive comments is still in office. (Guardian, BBC)

The recordings were gathered across England and Wales during a year in which undercover reporters joined local campaigns, four byelections and activity around the party’s headquarters. Another councillor was filmed calling for the king to be killed and speaking violently about migrants crossing the Channel. Reform has accused ITV and the production company Hardcash of deception, pointing to the false credentials used to gain access to its office and computer systems. The broadcaster’s methods will be argued over. The immediate political problem is simpler: Nigel Farage has repeatedly promised to remove extremists and bigots, and the party says every prospective candidate undergoes checks. The investigation found people who passed through those checks, won public office and received ceremonial responsibilities. (Guardian, BBC)

Farage has postponed a planned announcement in Essex as further footage is expected, including material recorded inside Reform’s London headquarters. The crisis arrives while the party is stalling in opinion polls and facing separate scrutiny over officials’ discussion of foreign donations and Farage’s declaration of a £5m gift. Reform’s defence is that a small number of unsuitable people can evade even improved procedures. Its opponents will press a wider question about the culture that attracted them and allowed them to advance. The answer will matter far beyond a television broadcast: these are elected representatives exercising local power, and several can continue doing so after leaving the party whose name put them on the ballot. (Guardian)

Ukraine’s Starlink slowdown reaches the drones defending its cities

Ukraine says an unexpected Starlink speed limit is disrupting battlefield missions and the drone interceptors that protect civilians from Russian attack. Connections were cut on Tuesday night for aircraft travelling faster than 100mph, with some crews finding that communication failed at roughly half that speed. Mykhailo Fedorov, Ukraine’s former defence minister, said service had partly returned by Wednesday evening but urged the removal of the restriction. Elon Musk replied that the military Starshield system is owned and controlled by the US government, so its limits are decided by the US military and ultimately the president. Washington has not explained whether it ordered the change. (BBC, Guardian)

The timing has made a technical explanation difficult for Kyiv to accept. Russia launched one of its largest recent attacks as the limit appeared, hitting power and communications facilities and leaving at least 600,000 people without electricity. Ukraine also says western partners failed for a second night to provide warning of incoming ballistic missiles, though Donald Trump and Nato secretary general Mark Rutte deny that intelligence-sharing has been paused. Starlink guides many mid-range drones behind Russian lines and connects fast interceptor drones to the system that brings down jet-powered Shaheds. It is already disabled inside Russia’s recognised borders, so throttling it has little effect on the long-range strikes against oil refineries that have angered Trump. The heavier cost falls on air defence and operations in occupied Ukrainian territory. (BBC, Guardian)

Volodymyr Zelensky used a visit to London to ask for the connection to be restored and described feeling betrayed by the US decision to buy 300,000 tonnes of Russian diesel. Prime minister Andy Burnham promised continued British support and accelerated deliveries of lightweight missiles used against Russian drones. That help addresses one part of the defensive gap. The episode also demonstrates how a commercial satellite network, a military contract and presidential diplomacy can converge inside a single drone flight. Ukrainian commanders are already replanning missions around other technologies, which can cost many times more. Every day of uncertainty reduces the margin available to intercept the faster weapons now reaching homes, hospitals and power plants. (BBC, Guardian)

Brazil approves a two-day weekend as its election tightens

Brazil’s Senate has approved a constitutional amendment ending the standard six-days-on, one-day-off working pattern, handing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva a major legislative victory 11 days before the presidential runoff. The measure passed both rounds by 75 votes to one after senators adopted a special timetable. It reduces the normal week from 44 hours to 40, requires two weekly rest days, including Sunday where possible, and protects existing pay. The change will be phased in and still needs formal promulgation. Specific rules for platform workers, aviation and other sectors with unusual schedules will follow, leaving employers and unions to negotiate how the shorter week works in practice. (Folha, Meio)

The vote became a rehearsal for the final stretch of the campaign. Lula’s allies presented the amendment as a durable gain for workers and hope to hold the promulgation while he is in Minas Gerais. Flávio Bolsonaro voted in favour after previously calling the proposal opportunistic and supporting an hourly-pay alternative. His PL party freed its senators to vote as they wished, while opposition figures argued that a future government would need payroll-tax relief to protect jobs. Public support made resistance costly: a Datafolha survey in March found 71% backing an end to the six-day schedule. Both campaigns now claim ownership of a change that Lula’s coalition brought through Congress and Bolsonaro joined once approval became unavoidable. (Folha, Meio)

A new Quaest poll shows why neither side could afford to stand apart. Flávio has 46% of total voting intentions and Lula 44%, a statistical tie within the survey’s two-point margin of error; 9% plan to cast a blank or invalid ballot and 1% remain undecided. Among decided voters, 91% say their choice is final. Flávio led the first round by 47.03% to 45.15%, while rejection is almost identical for the two candidates. Lula performs better among people who abstained or rejected all candidates in the first round, giving him a possible route to recover the small deficit. The shorter working week now moves from Congress into campaign advertising, where implementation, business costs and political credit will be tested before voters on 25 October. (Folha)

Britain puts Eritrea’s visas behind its demand for migrant returns

The government has threatened to suspend entry for all Eritrean nationals unless Asmara accepts more citizens who have no right to remain in Britain. From today, Eritrean diplomats will need permission to travel more than 60km outside London, and fast-track visas for VIPs have been withdrawn. The Home Office says Eritrea abruptly ended cooperation on returns earlier this year. Eritreans formed the largest national group among people arriving in small boats in the 12 months to June, accounting for 18% of the total, which makes the dispute central to ministers’ wider effort to increase removals. (BBC)

Visa pressure has worked elsewhere: Angola and Namibia agreed changes before threatened restrictions took effect, and measures against the Democratic Republic of the Congo were later lifted after cooperation improved. More than 20,400 people have crossed the Channel in small boats so far this year, 40% fewer than at the same point in 2025. Returns and deportations rose 8% to more than 40,600 in the year to June, with fewer than 6,000 involving someone convicted of a criminal offence. Those figures leave the policy spanning two distinct groups that political language often merges: foreign offenders and people whose immigration claims have failed. The test is whether blanket pressure on ordinary visa applicants changes a government’s behaviour without adding another obstacle for families already separated across borders. (BBC)

Economy

Hospitality offers a first rung to 100,000 young people

Pubs, restaurants and hotels will offer up to 100,000 jobs to young people outside work or education over the next three years under a programme backed by the Department for Work and Pensions. Wagamama, Nando’s, Burger King, Premier Inn, Fuller’s and Mitchells & Butlers are among the employers providing placements of up to four weeks for people aged 18 to 24, followed by a route into permanent work. The programme follows a similar retail partnership with Marks & Spencer, Asda, Pets at Home and John Lewis. It arrives before Alan Milburn’s review of youth unemployment, which warns that the number of young people classed as Neet could reach 1.25 million within five years without intervention. (Guardian)

The placement is short, so the measure will be judged by how many participants gain stable hours, training and progression after it ends. Education secretary Lucy Powell is also reviewing school exclusions after research linked persistent absence to a nearly fourfold increase in the risk of leaving education without a job. Milburn has signalled that his recommendations will combine benefit reform with stronger job support, apprenticeships and a national readiness programme. That broader approach recognises a long path into unemployment that often begins before someone reaches a Jobcentre. Hospitality can supply the first rung quickly; schools, employers and public services still have to make sure the ladder continues. (Guardian)

American inflation rises to 3.7% as fuel carries the shock

US consumer-price inflation accelerated from 3.4% to 3.7% in September, exceeding forecasts in the final release before next month’s midterm elections. Vehicle fuel prices jumped 9.1% in a single month and 34.2% over the year, accounting for more than half of the latest increase. Fuel oil used for heating is 74.2% dearer than a year ago, while broader energy prices are up 20.4%. Disrupted Middle Eastern production and transport during the US-Israel war with Iran have pushed crude above $100 a barrel, turning a foreign-policy crisis into a visible number on filling-station signs and household bills. (BBC)

Underlying inflation is steadier: food prices were flat during September and 2.5% higher over the year, while the core measure excluding food and energy stood at 2.6%. The Federal Reserve must now decide how far the energy shock will travel into transport, manufacturing and services. Tariffs add a separate pressure. Research by the New York Fed found that overseas exporters absorbed little of the new levies and US businesses carried close to 90% of the cost; each percentage-point rise in average tariffs lifted consumer-goods prices by almost 0.25% after a year. Social Security benefits will rise 3.6% in 2027, giving about 72 million recipients an average extra $75 a month. That adjustment protects some purchasing power after prices have risen, while doing little to settle an election dominated by the cost of living. (BBC)

OpenAI’s rewards and risks grow in public together

OpenAI’s 110 London employees received an average of £2.3m each in salary and equity during 2025, according to accounts for its Westminster-based British company. Together they shared £87m in pay and £168m in shares, more than doubling the previous year’s average package. The distribution is uneven, with the largest awards aimed at frontier-model researchers during an intense recruitment contest with Meta and other rivals. London has become OpenAI’s biggest research centre outside the US, drawing on machine-learning talent from British universities and competing directly with Google DeepMind. Its UK turnover more than tripled to £293m and produced a £20.3m profit. (Guardian)

On the same day, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho and Montana filed separate lawsuits accusing the company of putting profit ahead of child safety and misleading customers about ChatGPT’s risks. The complaints cite cases brought by families who allege the chatbot contributed to deaths, and say vulnerable users can encounter dangerous medical advice, reinforcement of paranoia and unhealthy emotional dependence. The states also accuse OpenAI of collecting data from minors and failing to keep under-age users away. They seek civil penalties, changes to the company’s public claims and, in some cases, deletion of data gathered unlawfully. (The Verge)

OpenAI says it has built age-specific protections, including parental controls, break reminders and models tuned for younger users, while acknowledging that no system is perfect. The litigation will examine whether those safeguards match the way the product was marketed and used. The accounts and lawsuits describe the same expansion from different directions: enormous rewards for the people pushing model capability forward, alongside a growing legal bill for harms that state authorities say were foreseeable. A planned move to King’s Cross and a possible $1tn stock-market valuation will keep the financial scale visible. The harder measure is whether safety systems mature as quickly as the product and the compensation attached to it. (Guardian, The Verge)

Culture

Sally Rooney’s books stop moving through Britain’s supply chain

Faber will no longer supply Sally Rooney’s books in the UK because it cannot pass British earnings to the author without risking an offence under terrorism law. Rooney said last year that she intended to use income from her work to support Palestine Action, which was proscribed in Britain in July 2025 but remains legal in the Republic of Ireland. Section 15 of the Terrorism Act can punish someone who provides money knowing or suspecting it may be used for terrorism, with a maximum sentence of 14 years. Rooney and Faber agreed that continuing to fulfil British publishing contracts could create that exposure. Ebook editions have already been removed; shops can sell physical copies they hold, but they cannot order more through the publisher. (Guardian, BBC)

The practical effect is unusually wide. Rooney has sold 2.3 million books in Britain and more than six million worldwide; Normal People, Conversations With Friends, Beautiful World, Where Are You and Intermezzo will all disappear from ordinary replenishment. She previously cancelled a British visit because she feared arrest, and payments connected to BBC adaptations have also become legally sensitive. More than 3,700 people are believed to have been arrested over alleged support for Palestine Action, with about 2,500 charged; trials await a Supreme Court challenge to the ban next month. The withdrawal turns that pending judgment into a question readers can see on shelves. It also gives publishers, broadcasters and other intermediaries a preview of the decisions they may face whenever an artist’s declared use of earnings meets a proscribed organisation. (Guardian, BBC)

Ocarina of Time rebuilds its old lessons for modern hands

Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time changes far more than its resolution. Link can sprint, jump on command, turn a free camera and aim with motion controls; the game runs at 60 frames a second with an orchestrated score and newly detailed environments. Those abilities reshape rooms that once taught players how to handle one of gaming’s first great 3D adventures. A boulder maze built around recentering the Nintendo 64 camera now teaches jumping. A Forest Temple fight replaces an awkward bottomless hole with acid, preserving the constraint on Link while giving the skeleton enemies a reason to cross it. Familiar puzzles, dialogue and cutscenes have been revised throughout. (IGN, Guardian)

The remake keeps loading screens between Kokiri Forest, Hyrule Field and Castle Town and leaves the compact geography intact. Its visual language makes those limits feel deliberate, using pools of light, fog and more theatrical combat to present Hyrule as a series of stage sets. That approach suits a game whose original lock-on fighting system was inspired by Japanese period drama and whose story treats Link as a child stepping into an old legend. His glossy, doll-like new face has divided early viewers, and the open field that felt enormous in 1998 now looks small beside Breath of the Wild. The hands-on previews suggest Nintendo understands that tension. It is rebuilding the logic around a classic instead of enlarging it until its identity disappears. The remake arrives on 5 November. (IGN, Guardian)

Sports

PSG absorb City’s rebellion while Liverpool find their new finisher

Paris Saint-Germain beat Manchester City 4-2 at the Etihad after producing a first half that showed why a third consecutive European title has entered the conversation. Désiré Doué cut inside to score from distance, then crossed for Ousmane Dembélé 75 seconds later. Vitinha added a third before the interval as PSG’s movement repeatedly opened City’s defence. Maghnes Akliouche made it 4-1 after the break with a shot Gianluigi Donnarumma appeared to save before the ball dropped behind him and crossed the line. The cushion proved essential. Erling Haaland scored twice, City hit the woodwork and forced a goal-line clearance, and their 27 shots produced a second half fierce enough to make an improbable comeback briefly feel available. (Guardian, BBC)

Liverpool’s 6-3 win at Lask supplied a different kind of release. Bradley Barcola scored the first goals of his Liverpool career and completed his first professional hat-trick after six appearances without a goal or assist. Ronald Araújo, Jeremie Frimpong and Lewis Koumas added the others, with Koumas replacing Steven Gerrard as Liverpool’s youngest player to score and assist in a Champions League game. Florian Wirtz also supplied an assist during a performance that gave two expensive summer signings room to settle. Lask scored three after the contest had moved beyond them, a reminder that Liverpool’s defensive control did not match the ease of their attacking work. (Guardian, BBC)

Elsewhere, José Mourinho’s Real Madrid came back from 3-1 down to win 4-3 on his return to Roma, scoring three times late in the match. Aston Villa recorded the biggest European victory in their history, beating Fenerbahce 6-0 with two goals each from Nicolas Jackson and Ross Barkley. The evening’s scale was set by attacks: PSG’s established champions cut through City, Liverpool’s new forwards found their timing, and Madrid turned a defeat into seven-goal theatre. City’s response still offered Enzo Maresca something useful. His half-time changes created chances against Europe’s most accomplished side, even if the damage accumulated before them was too deep to repair. (Guardian, Guardian)

The Fold

A daily newsletter for Londoners who want
the full picture in one place.
