item.title: The Fold — 2026-10-10
item.description: The Fold morning briefing for 10 October 2026: Labour holds Holborn, Brazil’s runoff narrows, international law faces a defining test, Europe strikes a car deal with China, and Manchester City await their appeal.
item.content:encoded:
LONDON · SATURDAY · 10 OCTOBER 2026 · MORNING EDITION

The Fold

Your Morning Briefing from the UK & the World

10/10/26 · 05:31 BST · London

News

Labour holds Holborn and gains a little room to breathe

Labour has kept Holborn and St Pancras, the north London seat vacated by Keir Starmer, with a result that gives Andy Burnham’s leadership its first clear electoral lift. Sagal Abdi-Wali won 45% of the vote, ahead of Green leader Zack Polanski on 33%, after a campaign that had briefly looked capable of delivering a second extraordinary Green capture from Labour. Turnout was 38.7%. The margin broadly matched late expectations, yet the ease of the final victory matters in a diverse inner-city constituency of exactly the kind the Greens have been building towards. Labour can now argue that some voters who left during the final Starmer period are prepared to reconsider the party under new management. (Guardian, BBC)

Abdi-Wali arrived in Britain as a child refugee from Somalia in the 1990s and used her victory speech to answer doubts about who belongs in public life. Reform UK’s Zia Yusuf had questioned her Britishness early in the contest; voters have now sent her to the Commons for one of the capital’s most recognisable seats. Labour deputy leader Lucy Powell presented the result as evidence that the party has listened to progressive voters and can bring them together again. That claim will need more than a single favourable night. Burnham still has to turn a change in mood into wider enthusiasm, and the low turnout suggests many people in a safe Labour area remain detached from the offer. (Guardian)

The Greens leave with their second-best byelection result and an immediate argument over Polanski’s judgment. Their 33% confirms that they can organise a serious campaign in Labour territory. It also arrives days after the party conference adopted a motion equating Zionism with racism and supporting a single Palestinian state. Polanski missed the vote while campaigning in Holborn and later said he would have opposed the motion after two amendments he favoured were defeated. The chair of Jewish Greens called for him to resign, while other members of the group challenged her view; Caroline Lucas said he should have attended and voted. Polanski intends to stay. The party has no formal mechanism for removing its leader between its two-year elections, so the dispute will be settled through authority, membership pressure and future results. (BBC, Guardian)

The broader lesson is still unsettled. Labour was facing a Green party polling above it earlier this year, when the upset in Gorton and Denton weakened Starmer and helped accelerate the pressure on his leadership. The Greens are now around 11% nationally, while Labour has opened a lead of more than 15 points over them. Holborn suggests Burnham has interrupted that movement on the left and made Labour legible again to some former supporters. It does not show how the party will fare against Reform, or whether people who stayed home will return. For one Saturday, however, Labour has a new MP, a repaired defensive wall in London and time to make its case before the next test arrives. (Guardian)

Brazil’s runoff begins inside the margin of error

Flávio Bolsonaro has opened the second round with 52% of valid votes against Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s 48%, according to Datafolha. The four-point lead sits at the edge of the survey’s margin of error, and the spontaneous question produces an even tighter 46% to 44%. Bolsonaro is strongest among evangelical voters, residents of the south and south-east, and households earning between two and five minimum wages. Lula leads among Catholics, north-eastern voters and the lowest-income group. Those familiar divisions explain much of the contest. The decisive movement may come from people who avoided a firm camp in the first round and now have sixteen days to decide whether either candidate can speak to their daily concerns. (Meio, Folha)

Rejection remains high on both sides. Forty-six per cent say they will not vote for Lula under any circumstances, while 43% say the same about Bolsonaro; 3% reject them both. The remaining 8% has no fixed barrier to either name. Among voters who describe themselves as neither petista nor bolsonarista, 23% currently choose a blank or invalid ballot or do not know how they will vote. That group is large enough to reverse the lead. It is also unlikely to respond to the kind of language that excites the committed base, making the next debates unusually important: 78% of voters regard the candidates’ participation as very important. (Folha, Folha)

Lula’s campaign is concentrating on pensions, Bolsa Família and the risk that social programmes would face cuts under Bolsonaro. The difficulty is that dissatisfaction has weakened the president even among some people who depend on those programmes. Bolsonaro begins with wider regional support and has inherited more voters from defeated candidates, although he must keep a coalition that includes people attracted by change without deep loyalty to his family. Each campaign is asking voters to imagine the other presidency as a danger. The race may turn when one of them gives the unaligned electorate a practical reason to vote for his own programme. (Meio, Folha)

A peace prize and US sanctions put international law under the same spotlight

South African jurist Navi Pillay has received the Nobel peace prize for a career built around the idea that law can restrain violence. The 85-year-old defended anti-apartheid activists, served on the tribunal for Rwanda, became UN high commissioner for human rights and now sits at the International Court of Justice. Her work on the Rwanda tribunal helped establish rape and sexual violence as instruments of genocide. More recently, she chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel had committed genocidal acts in Gaza with an intent to destroy Palestinians there. Israel rejected that finding and reacted furiously to the award. The Nobel committee placed Pillay’s independence and the institutions of international law at the centre of its decision. (Guardian)

Hours later, the Trump administration sanctioned the International Criminal Court as an institution. American businesses will be barred from providing services to the court, including banking and software, after a six-month wind-down period. Seventeen judges and officials had already faced individual measures. Washington says the ICC threatens US sovereignty through the possibility of prosecuting Americans and through its arrest warrants for Israeli officials, including Benjamin Netanyahu. The ICC has no current case against a US national and describes itself as a court of last resort for cases that domestic systems cannot or will not handle. The United States, Israel, Russia, China and India are among the countries outside its 125-state membership. (BBC, Guardian)

The measures could reach beyond judges and prosecutors. If payment systems, technology and suppliers become unavailable, trials and appeals may become impossible to conduct fairly. Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte and other defendants accused of grave crimes are already in The Hague; licences will temporarily allow detention facilities to keep operating, but a court without a functioning administration could eventually have to release people awaiting judgment. The UK, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Denmark and the Netherlands have rejected the sanctions and reaffirmed support for the court. Pillay’s prize celebrates legal institutions as a peaceful route to accountability. The sanctions test whether allied governments are willing to provide the practical protection those institutions now require. (BBC, Guardian)

A newborn vaccine trial advances despite an ethical revolt

A trial in Guinea-Bissau will enrol 14,000 infants and delay the hepatitis B vaccine for six weeks in half of them, after ethics bodies in Denmark and Guinea-Bissau allowed the study to proceed. Mothers will be tested before birth, and babies whose mothers test positive will receive the vaccine and remain outside the trial. The other newborns will enter a randomised study of vaccination, mortality and several broader health outcomes. Four members of the Danish committee have resigned in protest. Their concern is simple and serious: the vaccine already prevents a known infection that can produce chronic liver disease and cancer, while the hoped-for wider effects under investigation are speculative. (Guardian)

Guinea-Bissau has one of the world’s highest rates of hepatitis B, with about 18% of adults carrying the virus. Infection can pass from relatives and carers as well as during birth, the maternal test can produce false negatives, and children infected during their first year face a particularly high risk of lasting harm. The World Health Organization recommends vaccination at birth. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has set aside $1.6m for the work, matched by private foundations, and health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr has praised the Danish researchers while trying to remove the routine birth dose from US recommendations. The trial places the scientific question inside a population whose exposure is high and whose universal newborn programme has been delayed until 2028. That combination is why critics see consent and local approval as insufficient answers to the central ethical problem. (Guardian)

A plant selfie reveals a giant waterlily already close to extinction

A photograph of a swimmer among waterlilies in Colombia’s Inírida River has led botanists to identify a species so large that its leaves can be seen in satellite images. Kew Gardens specialist Carlos Magdalena noticed the picture on Instagram three years ago and realised the plant sat beyond the known range of Victoria amazonica. He traced the location, studied images from space and joined Colombian botanists and Indigenous communities on a five-day expedition through flooded forest. With ten hours left before their flight home, a local driver guided the team overnight to a small lake. The material collected there has now been formally described as Victoria colombiana. (Guardian)

Only three other giant waterlily species are known. Their leaves can reach three metres across and carry the weight of a small child, and their lineage predates the separation of the continents. Researchers estimate that just 30 to 50 plants of the new species remain in the wild, which would make it critically endangered almost as soon as science has named it. Work is under way to secure a Red List assessment, collect seeds and perhaps establish a more accessible population within Indigenous territory before attempting cultivation in Bogotá or at Kew. A casual picture supplied the clue; years of local knowledge, permits, taxonomy and patient fieldwork turned it into a discovery with a chance of survival. (Guardian)

Economy

Europe and China try a negotiated brake on car imports

China has agreed to moderate hybrid-car exports to the European Union in a deal Brussels believes could cut shipments by more than half over four years. That would keep several million plug-in and battery-assisted hybrids out of the European market as carmakers confront intense price competition and governments worry about factory jobs. The agreement emerged from talks that began in June and forms part of a 16-point programme covering cars, rare-earth export licences and European food and drink access to China. It is an unusual attempt to manage a trade surge before tariffs and retaliation harden into a longer conflict. (Guardian)

The practical mechanism may involve minimum prices for Chinese hybrids sold in Europe, with company undertakings used to slow volumes while remaining within World Trade Organization rules. Europe’s trade deficit with China is running at about €1.18bn a day, and the political concern reaches chemicals and textiles as well as vehicles. Chinese manufacturers have gained share through scale, lower costs and a faster transition to electrified cars; European producers are trying to protect employment while making that same transition without pushing affordable models beyond consumers’ reach. Brussels calls the car arrangement a first step and will brief diplomats before next week’s leaders’ summit. Its durability will depend on measurable export restraint, credible enforcement and enough domestic investment to give Europe’s industry something useful to do with the time it has bought. (Guardian)

Technology

Microsoft gives Windows another AI centre of gravity

Microsoft is extending Windows 11 around agents that can move between local models and cloud services, with a new class of Nvidia-powered computers aimed first at developers and creators. The Surface Laptop Ultra starts at $2,599 and uses the RTX Spark platform to run models with more than 120bn parameters on the device; competing machines from Asus, Dell, HP, Lenovo and MSI will follow, with the most expensive configurations reaching $6,999. Local processing can reduce cloud fees and keep some sensitive work on the computer. It also gives Microsoft a direct answer to developers who currently reach for a MacBook Pro when they need a powerful portable workstation. (Verge)

The broader idea, called hybrid intelligence, would let Copilot and third-party agents choose where work runs and act across the operating system. GitHub Copilot demonstrated local coding, Microsoft listed a growing range of compatible models, and Windows Search received a faster interface that behaves more like a launcher. The difficult part is still the ordinary use case. Copilot Plus PCs arrived two years ago with similar promises for neural processors, then delivered a small collection of creative tools and a troubled Recall feature whose privacy concerns delayed its launch. The new machines have a clearer audience because model builders can calculate the saving from local work. Windows users will judge the agentic system by simpler measures: whether it solves a repeated task, protects private files, shows what it changed and remains easy to stop. (Verge)

Apple prepares to bring its intelligence system into the home

Apple has scheduled a “Welcome home” launch for 13 October, with a smart display expected to lead its first coordinated home-product push in years. The device, commonly called HomePad before launch, is described as a six-inch square screen on a rounded base, with wall-mounted and countertop versions. It is expected to recognise different household members and adjust its display to the person speaking or approaching, combining Siri and Apple Intelligence with interface elements borrowed from the iPad, Apple Watch and the iPhone’s StandBy mode. An in-person press event in New York will sit alongside an online presentation. (9to5Mac, MacMagazine)

A new Apple TV 4K and the first substantial HomePod mini update are also expected. Faster chips would give both devices access to Siri’s newer AI functions, while software references point to an Apple TV surround system using four full-size HomePods. Apple has also worked with LG on locks, cameras, a thermostat and a doorbell that may appear later as jointly developed HomeKit accessories. Together, the pieces suggest a home platform organised around people and rooms, with the separate boxes working as one system. The launch will show whether Apple can make that arrangement feel coherent, and whether its delayed AI work is dependable enough for a device shared by an entire household. (9to5Mac, MacMagazine)

Gears of War turns strong attention into a difficult sales question

Gears of War: E-Day reached an estimated 1.7 million players through Game Pass while selling about 230,000 copies across Xbox and PC in its first week, according to unofficial data from Alinea Analytics. Steam accounted for 168,000 sales and the Xbox ecosystem for 62,000. At the same time, about 722,000 Game Pass members paid $30 for a Premium upgrade that unlocked five days of early access. The figures suggest a large and engaged audience for the well-reviewed prequel, alongside a steep decline in the role of the traditional $70 sale on Microsoft’s own platform. Microsoft has not confirmed the estimates, and new or retained subscriptions are missing from the calculation. (IGN)

The distinction matters because Microsoft needs revenue as well as reach from its renewed emphasis on exclusive games. Estimated earnings were $27m inside the Xbox ecosystem and about $37m in total, before accounting for any subscriptions attracted or retained by the release. Internal documents disclosed during the Activision Blizzard deal had already acknowledged that putting a game into the service reduces base-game sales during its first year. Game Pass can give a blockbuster an immediate audience and lower the cost of trying it. E-Day shows how that success can leave the value of each player harder to read, especially when the most committed customers pay for early access to a game they still do not own. (IGN)

Sports

Manchester City’s guilty verdict moves into football’s long appeal

Manchester City have been found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules across the nine seasons from 2009-10 to 2017-18, bringing an independent commission’s long inquiry to a verdict and sending the case immediately into appeal. City continue to deny wrongdoing. A serious punishment is expected if the decision survives, but the appeal may keep the outcome unresolved into the new year. That leaves the current league leaders returning to play at Anfield on Sunday while clubs and supporters try to separate the competition in front of them from a judgment that reaches back through the most successful period in City’s history. (Guardian, BBC)

The consequences cannot be recreated through a revised table alone. Michael Carrick was in the Manchester United side that lost the 2011-12 title on goal difference after Sergio Agüero’s stoppage-time winner, and later worked on the staff of another United team that finished second to City. A medal awarded years later would leave the emotion of those afternoons exactly where it was. Liverpool finished behind City in 2013-14, 2018-19 and 2021-22; their supporters will give Sunday’s meeting an anger that exceeds an ordinary match between rivals. Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta, formerly Pep Guardiola’s assistant, says his conscience is clear but will wait for the appeal before addressing the findings in detail. Former City captain Vincent Kompany continues to take pride in what the players achieved on the pitch. (Guardian, BBC)

Rui Pinto, the Football Leaks founder whose disclosures helped trigger the investigation, will meanwhile remain in Portugal’s witness-protection programme. Authorities suspended a decision that would have removed him on Saturday after finding that he had not been properly notified or given an opportunity to challenge the risk assessment. Pinto, who shared City emails and financial records with Der Spiegel in 2018, received a suspended sentence in Portugal for offences including unlawful access to data and attempted extortion; he was later acquitted on 241 other counts. His complicated record does not lessen the importance of the documents. The Premier League must now finish the process with enough speed to preserve the present competition and enough care to produce a result that can carry the weight of the seasons under examination. (BBC, Guardian)

The Fold

item.title: The Fold — 2026-10-08
item.description: The Fold morning briefing for 8 October 2026: Brazil’s decisive runoff voters, Badenoch’s Conservative conference, the long aftermath of 7 October, Britain’s living-standards warning, and a new generation of adaptive software.
item.content:encoded:
LONDON · THURSDAY · 8 OCTOBER 2026 · MORNING EDITION

The Fold

Your Morning Briefing from the UK & the World

08/10/26 · 05:37 BST · London

News

Brazil’s runoff will be decided beyond the loyal camps

Brazil’s presidential runoff is settling around an electorate that has resisted belonging to either side. Flávio Bolsonaro led Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva by 1.87 percentage points in the first round, a narrow advantage inside a result that also left millions of votes available. In the north-east alone, the campaigns are pursuing about nine million people who chose defeated candidates and eight million who did not vote. Many of the voters now receiving daily appeals have changed their preference during the campaign and feel little obligation to a party or government. Their decision on 25 October is likely to turn on a more practical question: which candidate understands how ordinary life feels now. (Meio, Folha)

Bolsonaro’s coalition continued to grow on Wednesday. Republicanos formally endorsed him, joining the União Brasil–PP federation, Podemos and Ronaldo Caiado in a rapidly consolidating bloc; most state branches of the MDB are also moving towards support, while ACM Neto promised to mobilise allies in Bahia. The candidate is tying that electoral machine to the right’s new strength in Congress. He has spoken of using majorities in the Chamber and Senate to rewrite the constitution, reform criminal law and the judiciary, and “redemocratise” the country, while leaving the scope of those changes unclear. The Centrão’s increased willingness to discuss impeaching a supreme court justice gives that language immediate institutional weight. (Folha, Meio, Folha)

Lula has begun to answer a weaker first round with visible changes in style. He told allies that the campaign had been his least organised presidential effort since 1989, an assessment accidentally broadcast on the PT’s YouTube channel. Later he published a direct-to-camera video asking supporters to take the campaign into the streets. Younger PT deputies have pressed him to spend less time on his biography and make a sharper offer for the future, while his communications team faces criticism over a digital operation that allowed Bolsonaro to set the pace. The new format matters because Lula needs to reach people who know him chiefly as a permanent figure in the system, rather than through the trade-union story that shaped his first campaigns. (Folha, Folha, Folha)

The contrast is becoming clearer. Bolsonaro can point to endorsements, a strengthened PL and a legislature already leaning towards his programme. Lula has incumbency, social programmes and a long political record, but must translate all three into a credible promise about income, work and security for the next four years. The movable voter sits outside the emotional core of both campaigns and may distrust their largest claims. Winning that voter requires detail and presence: what will become cheaper, what will improve locally, which constitutional changes are intended, and who would share the benefits. A close first round has made Brazil’s least partisan citizens the most powerful people in the campaign. (Meio, Folha)

Badenoch leaves Birmingham in command of a smaller Conservative party

Kemi Badenoch ended the Conservative conference with authority inside her party and a difficult route beyond it. Her programme in Birmingham included exempting homes from inheritance tax, extending free childcare to households earning more than £100,000, opposition to net zero policy and a large reduction in human-rights protections. The inheritance-tax proposal is most relevant to homes worth more than £500,000, concentrating its benefit in London and the south-east. Some Conservatives see a way to recover prosperous voters lost to the Liberal Democrats; others worry that a collection of expensive promises for wealthier households leaves the cost of living in the background. (Guardian, BBC)

The party remains near 20% in national polling, yet Badenoch’s own position looks more secure than it did a year ago. Departures to Reform UK have removed several internal opponents, and a much smaller parliamentary party has fewer organised factions. YouGov research cited at the conference found that 90% of voters recognise Badenoch; only 22% recognise her new shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith. That gap has produced a disciplined, highly personal opposition in which policy carries the leader’s stamp and colleagues struggle for attention. Birmingham gave the Conservatives unity and a recognisable voice. The next test is whether those assets can reconnect the party with voters who still place it behind Labour and Reform. (Guardian, Guardian)

Three years after 7 October, remembrance meets a stalled future

Israel marked the third anniversary of the Hamas-led attacks with memorial ceremonies for about 1,200 people killed on 7 October 2023, most of them civilians. Families and communities gathered while the country continued to live with the political and human consequences of the day that began the war. In Gaza, the subsequent Israeli offensive has killed about 73,000 Palestinians, most of them civilians, and wounded many more. The scale of those losses can make the anniversary feel numerical from a distance. On both sides it remains intimate: a missing relative, an empty room, a place where a familiar routine stopped. (BBC, Guardian)

A ceasefire has been in place for a year, although Gaza’s death toll has risen by about 1,400 during that period and airstrikes continue. Most residents remain inside a landscape of damaged homes and weak services. Water, nutritious food and medical care are scarce; infectious disease spreads in crowded displacement sites; reconstruction has barely begun. Hamas controls the part of Gaza outside the Israeli military’s zone and provides fragments of administration, while the plan for disarmament, Israeli withdrawal and rebuilding has stalled. People preserve pieces of their former lives through objects and routines: a schoolbag, a house key, battered plastic chairs, a haircut prepared for a wedding in a tent. Those details carry the shape of a normality that diplomacy has yet to restore. (Guardian)

Gene therapy gives ten blind patients a measure of sight

A small clinical trial has shown that optogenetic gene therapy can safely restore limited visual function for people with advanced retinitis pigmentosa. All ten participants received a single injection into their worse eye. A harmless synthetic virus carried instructions that made a ring of surviving retinal ganglion cells responsive to light. Special goggles then captured the scene ahead and converted it into pulses of a single wavelength, allowing the treated cells to send a monochrome impression to the brain. The method works around the many different genetic faults that can cause the disease because it targets cells that usually survive after the retina’s natural light receptors deteriorate. (Guardian)

Six participants achieved a clinically meaningful improvement in light sensitivity. With training, some could find and touch a notebook, locate a door or follow a line on the floor, and the benefit remained stable for four or five years. They still could not recognise faces, and the researchers describe high-resolution sight as a goal for the next five to ten years. One serious eye-related side effect resolved within minutes, with no treatment-related effects elsewhere in the body. The advance is deliberately modest: reliable shapes, obstacles and light where there had been almost none. For someone navigating a room, those gains can change the boundaries of an ordinary day. (Guardian)

Economy

Britain’s living-standards squeeze could become a record decline

The Joseph Rowntree Foundation estimates that average household income after housing costs will be £440 to £770 lower in real terms in 2029–30 than when Labour entered government in 2024. Even the smaller fall would be the largest recorded over a parliament since the modern series began in 1961. The forecast combines weak income growth with energy and housing costs that have moved towards the Bank of England’s adverse scenario. Five-year fixed mortgage rates reached an average of 6% this week, while some projections put a typical annual dual-fuel bill near £2,000 in the first quarter of next year. More than seven million families already go without essentials such as food or basic toiletries. (Guardian)

The budget on 28 October will show how much immediate relief the government is prepared to provide. Chancellor John Healey is considering an extra £100 for households receiving the £150 warm home discount, funded through taxation, as part of an energy package worth more than £1 billion. The foundation wants cheaper baseline units of gas and electricity for every household, with additional support for people in greater need, and it has also proposed reconnecting housing allowance to rents and raising universal credit. First secretary Louise Haigh is leading two cross-government workstreams, one on near-term housing and energy help and another on structural measures such as public control. Their recommendations are intended to feed a ten-year plan later this autumn, making the October budget an opening instalment rather than a complete answer. Each measure reaches a different part of the squeeze. A discount can soften the winter bill; housing and benefit reform would decide whether the same households begin the next winter with any more room to breathe. (Guardian)

Boots returns to the Weston family’s British high street

Canada’s Weston family has agreed to buy Boots for $8.9 billion, or about £6.74 billion, bringing one of Britain’s best-known retailers under the same holding company as Loblaws supermarkets and Shoppers Drug Mart. Wittington Investments will acquire Boots’ 1,800 UK and Irish stores, its opticians, the No7 beauty brand and its Thai franchise business, with backing from Fairfax. The Nottingham-based group employs about 50,000 people. Regulatory approval is still required, and the deal is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027. It also ends two decades in which Stefano Pessina remained involved through a succession of private and public owners. (Guardian)

The promise is stable ownership and fresh investment after years of uncertainty over a sale or stock-market flotation. Boots has closed more than 300 outlets in recent years, and many remaining shops need modernisation while online competitors and discount chains take a larger share of health and beauty spending. The estate still offers something hard to reproduce on a website: trusted pharmacists, convenient town-centre locations and a large loyalty scheme that connects routine purchases to health services. The Westons sold Selfridges in 2022 and are returning to the UK high street with a business whose social role is broader than ordinary retail. What they invest in stores, staff and pharmacy capacity will matter more than the familiarity of the new owner’s name. (Guardian)

Technology

ChatGPT starts building an interface around each answer

OpenAI has begun rolling out GPT-6 with an “Intelligent UI” that can answer with graphics, forms, charts, buttons and interactive tools alongside ordinary text. The system chooses a format from the question: a comparison can become a side-by-side view, a technical explanation can produce a diagram, and a practical request can create a working bill splitter, savings calculator or small game in the conversation. A library of native components keeps the designs familiar, while a compiler assembles and streams the interface as the model produces it. The answer can appear in stages, giving a reader useful material while the model continues to reason or search. (OpenAI, Verge, MacMagazine)

The launch begins with Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise accounts, followed by Free and Go accounts from today; workplace availability also depends on administrator settings. OpenAI says an internal test found GPT-6 Instant begins answering web-search questions 44% sooner on average than GPT-5.6 Instant. The more consequential change is the move away from a fixed chat box as the only shape of AI software. A generated control can make a model’s reasoning easier to inspect by letting someone change an input and watch the output respond. It also increases the importance of design judgment: the model must know when interaction clarifies an answer and when a plain paragraph remains the most useful interface. (OpenAI, 9to5Mac)

Microsoft builds a Surface for local AI, then gives Copilot more reach

Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra will go on sale on 16 October as a high-end Windows machine built around Nvidia’s Arm-based RTX Spark platform. The range starts at $2,599 with 24GB of memory and 512GB of storage and rises sharply for larger configurations. A 15-inch mini-LED touchscreen sits above a practical selection of USB-C, USB-A, HDMI, SD-card and headphone ports. Charging now uses a magnetic USB-C connector, preserving the easy breakaway behaviour of the old Surface plug while adopting a standard cable. Microsoft is pitching the machine at developers and creators who want generative models and video tools to run locally, including people who might otherwise choose a MacBook Pro. (Verge, MacMagazine)

The hardware arrived with a broader idea Microsoft calls Hybrid Intelligence. New Windows features will let Copilot combine cloud models with local processing, search files on the PC and take actions across the operating system. A demonstration showed an agent collecting documents requested by an accountant for a tax return. That kind of access can remove tedious transfers between email, folders and applications, while also putting more private material and consequential actions inside an automated workflow. The value will depend on clear permissions, a reliable record of what the agent changed and an easy way to stop or reverse it. A powerful local processor can keep more work on the device; the software still has to make its boundaries visible. (Verge)

Two successful games expose the insecurity behind their launches

Bit Reactor has begun bringing back employees who were furloughed shortly before Star Wars Zero Company launched in August. About 80% of the studio was reportedly placed on unpaid leave despite strong reviews for the tactical game. Chief executive Greg Foertsch described the recalls as a step towards continued support, and staffing has now recovered to more than half its pre-furlough level. A substantial group remains without pay. The sequence is unusually stark: years of specialist work, a well-received release and an employment crisis arrived together, leaving the people who made the game waiting to learn whether its success would secure their jobs. (IGN)

At Microsoft’s The Coalition, the release of Gears of War: E-Day has produced similar anxiety. Xbox has cut nearly 2,000 jobs this financial year, closed or reorganised studios, and laid off the game’s story director a week before early access. Staff have reportedly postponed any sense of celebration until several months after launch, expecting another round of cuts. Studio head Mike Crump offered no guarantee, though he said the new game provides a foundation that should make the next Gears faster to produce. Shared technology can shorten development. It does not answer the immediate question facing both teams: whether acclaimed work still creates durable employment in an industry reorganising faster than its games can be made. (IGN)

Sports

Arsenal secure the manager who ended their title wait

Mikel Arteta has signed a four-year contract worth more than £20 million a season, making him the Premier League’s best-paid manager and tying him to Arsenal until June 2030. The agreement rewards a season in which Arsenal ended a 22-year wait for the league title after three consecutive second-place finishes, then reached the Champions League final before losing to Paris Saint-Germain on penalties. Arteta took charge in December 2019 and is now the division’s longest-serving manager following Pep Guardiola’s departure from Manchester City. His coaching staff have extended their deals too, keeping the structure that rebuilt the side around a consistent style and a young core. (Guardian)

Declan Rice is also close to agreeing a new long-term contract, continuing the club’s effort to settle key futures before negotiations become distractions. Arsenal have shelved a major expansion of the Emirates Stadium after concern about the disruption of a temporary move, so the immediate investment remains concentrated on the team. Saturday’s home match against Leeds offers a quick return to ordinary competitive pressure: the champions need to respond to a 3–0 defeat at Brighton that ended their perfect league start. The new contracts express confidence over years. Their first demand is simpler, restoring rhythm after one poor afternoon. (BBC, Guardian)

The women’s Club World Cup collides with the domestic season

Arsenal and Chelsea could disappear from the Women’s Super League for as long as a month next season if the inaugural women’s Club World Cup goes ahead in the United States from 5 to 30 January 2028. Arsenal are guaranteed a place as the 2025 Champions League winners. Chelsea are likely to qualify through the European coefficient, although Manchester City would take England’s second slot if they win this season’s Champions League. A run deep into the tournament could force the English clubs to miss four WSL weekends and the fourth round of the FA Cup, leaving a lopsided table and a backlog just as the European knockout stage begins. (Guardian)

Moving the WSL winter break offers little relief because transatlantic travel and recovery would consume most of January. The calendar tightens again in August, when the Los Angeles Olympics will feature an expanded 16-team women’s tournament with senior internationals eligible to play, shortly before European domestic seasons resume. European Leagues has added the women’s competition to its complaint to the European Commission over Fifa’s use of power in setting the calendar. A global club tournament can give women’s football a valuable stage and new revenue. Its credibility also depends on allowing the best players to arrive healthy and return to domestic teams without turning spring into an exhausting sequence of make-up fixtures. (Guardian)

item.title: The Fold — 2026-10-07
item.description: The Fold morning briefing for 7 October 2026: Brazil’s runoff coalitions take shape, French school protests spread, Britain prepares energy-bill support, and AI’s infrastructure strains the grid and the land.
item.content:encoded:
LONDON · WEDNESDAY · 7 OCTOBER 2026 · MORNING EDITION

The Fold

Your Morning Briefing from the UK & the World

07/10/26 · 05:41 BST · London

News

Brazil’s runoff becomes a contest of coalitions

Brazil’s presidential runoff entered its first full day with the advantage moving from arithmetic to organisation. Flávio Bolsonaro began converting a 1.87-point first-round lead into a wider political front, collecting the formal support of the União Brasil–PP federation and Podemos while opening talks with Republicanos. Ronaldo Caiado, the defeated PSD candidate and re-elected governor of Goiás, also appeared with Bolsonaro and endorsed him. Eduardo Leite, the PSD governor of Rio Grande do Sul, is leaning towards neutrality, denying Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva an ally in a state where the president needs to recover ground. The final ballot is on 25 October. With 56.1 million votes already behind him and much of the organised right falling into place, Bolsonaro’s task is to keep his coalition disciplined for another two and a half weeks. (Folha, Folha)

Lula is rebuilding his campaign around the voters who did not feel spoken to in the first round. A record 21.07% of the electorate abstained, and the president finished with 45.16% of valid votes after losing 3.4 million votes from his 2022 first-round total. His team plans to warn that a Bolsonaro government could weaken social programmes, while trade-union leaders are preparing an effort aimed at workers who chose another candidate. Guilherme Boulos will travel through cities in the South and South-east, the regions where Lula’s deficit is most urgent. The deeper difficulty is economic and emotional. Lower-middle-income families have endured high food and household costs and often see a government describing its legacy rather than their present pressure. Lula needs to restore that connection without making the people who stayed home the villains of the result. (Meio, Folha, Folha)

The congressional result gives the presidential contest an unusually concrete second track. Bolsonaro has presented the new conservative majority as a mandate for constitutional change and for making it easier to impeach supreme court justices. The PL grew to 121 seats in the Chamber of Deputies, although União Brasil, PP and Republicanos still hold enough votes to decide whether ambitious reforms pass. Those parties lost ground to the ideological right and gained leverage at the same time: either president would need their cooperation from January. For Bolsonaro, their support connects his campaign to the machinery of government. For Lula, it makes the warning about institutions more immediate, while also showing the constraints he would face if re-elected. The runoff will choose a president whose room to govern has already been defined by a legislature further to the right. (Folha, Folha)

Voters should finally see the two candidates confront each other directly. Bolsonaro has committed to the second-round debates after skipping the first-round encounters, and Lula has also indicated that he will attend. Their closeness leaves little space for a cautious campaign. Bolsonaro must explain how a programme built around constitutional change, security and the family name would work in office. Lula must make a fourth-term proposition sound like an answer to 2026 rather than a defence of earlier achievements. The first round showed a country divided by less than two points and a Congress with a clearer direction than the presidency. The debates can now expose whether either candidate has a plan for governing across that divide. (Folha, Meio)

France’s school revolt becomes a national crisis

More than 250,000 pupils, teachers and parents marched across France on Tuesday, turning a protest over daily school conditions into the government’s largest domestic crisis in months. The movement began in the northern suburbs of Paris more than a fortnight ago and has spread through Marseille, Lyon, Rennes and scores of other cities. Students are demanding reliable cover for absent teachers, repairs to ageing buildings and relief from days that can run from 8am until 6pm. About 1,800 of France’s 3,700 high schools were blockaded or closed. Riot police used teargas, water cannon and baton charges as some protesters burned bins and threw projectiles; nearly 500 people were arrested during the day. (Guardian, BBC)

The toll accumulated before Tuesday was already severe. Government figures counted 215 injured teenagers, 85 injured school staff and 715 injured police officers, while individual cases include a pupil who lost a hand, one who lost the use of an eye and another whose jaw was badly injured. Prime minister Sébastien Lecornu has ordered ministers to address the practical complaints, and the interior ministry has opened investigations into allegations of police brutality. The dispute arrives seven months before a presidential election and during an argument over debt, weak growth and public spending. France’s schools have supplied the language of the protest—missing adults, crumbling rooms, unequal chances—and the state’s response will help decide whether the movement returns to classrooms or expands beyond them. (Guardian)

Ebola reaches Kenya as the outbreak accelerates

Kenya has recorded its first Ebola case and death as an outbreak centred in the Democratic Republic of the Congo pushes across borders. The patient, a Kenyan man who had lived in the DRC for seven years, became ill there, travelled overland to Kampala and flew to Nairobi on 3 October. He was isolated on arrival at hospital, tested positive and died on Monday night. Officials have identified 28 contacts among relatives and health workers and are looking for another 23 passengers and four crew members from his flight. No second infection has yet been confirmed. Uganda contained imported cases earlier in the year and was declared Ebola-free in August, showing both the reach of regional travel and the value of rapid tracing. (Guardian)

The larger emergency remains in the DRC, where 4,082 people had died among 8,463 confirmed cases by 2 October. It is the country’s seventeenth Ebola outbreak and involves the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is no approved vaccine or specific treatment. The virus has spread from Ituri to seven provinces; North Kivu now accounts for 40% of new cases and has only four treatment centres for a health zone of about two million people. Armed conflict, attacks on health workers, public mistrust and cuts to international aid all slow the response. Kenya can concentrate resources around a single chain of transmission. The DRC is trying to contain several chains at once across insecure territory, and every missed case creates another route towards a crowded city or a national border. (Guardian)

A photographer is beaten during the West Bank olive harvest

Armed Israeli settlers beat and robbed Agence France-Presse photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh while he covered an attack near the village of Aqraba in the occupied West Bank. Ashtiyeh, 58, was wearing press identification and trying to enter a marked car when two men struck him repeatedly with rifle butts. He suffered injuries to his head and torso and remains under observation in hospital in Nablus. A second photographer was threatened at gunpoint, and a Palestinian olive picker was shot in the foot. About a dozen Israeli soldiers were visible roughly 500 metres away and did not intervene, according to witnesses. AFP and the Foreign Press Association have demanded an investigation; the Israeli military had not responded by publication. (Guardian)

The assault sits inside a recurrent struggle over the olive harvest, a crucial source of income and a cultural anchor for Palestinian communities. Settler attacks, theft and vandalism have intensified in recent months, and accountability is rare. Roughly 500,000 Israeli settlers live among three million Palestinians in the West Bank, territory captured by Israel in 1967; the settlements are illegal under international law. Media groups also describe increasing obstruction and intimidation of journalists. Nineteen have been detained in the West Bank during the three years since the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023. The violence near Aqraba harmed the people harvesting, the person documenting it and the public record that his camera was there to preserve. (Guardian)

Economy

Britain prepares another layer of winter energy support

Chancellor John Healey is preparing to spend more than £1 billion on energy support in this month’s budget as forecasts point to another sharp rise in January. The leading option would add about £100 to the £150 warm home discount received by households on certain benefits, with taxpayers funding the increase. The intervention follows estimates that the Iran war could lift the energy price cap by as much as £442, wiping out the benefit of the electricity VAT cut announced by prime minister Andy Burnham. Healey is also trying to find £4.7 billion for defence and rebuild a fiscal buffer diminished by higher borrowing costs. A targeted discount is cheaper than removing levies from every bill, though it leaves many households exposed to most of the increase. (Guardian)

Officials are developing longer-term changes that would alter the price itself. A social tariff could charge lower unit rates to poorer households, but it would require tax, Treasury and supplier data to work together. A rising-block tariff would price a protected amount of essential energy cheaply and increase the rate above that level. Energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh has proposed moving all green and efficiency levies into general taxation, cutting average bills by up to £120 at a cost of as much as £3.2 billion. Each choice distributes the burden differently: through progressive taxation, a targeted benefit or charges linked to use. The immediate budget measure can cushion January. A durable system needs to respond before every international shock becomes a fresh emergency package. (Guardian)

Paramount and Warner Bros become one $111bn media empire

Paramount has completed its $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery after a bidding war with Netflix and months of litigation. The combined business is called Skydance and puts Paramount and Warner Bros studios, HBO Max, CBS News and CNN under the same parent. David Ellison will lead it with former Mattel chief Ynon Kreiz as co-executive. Two of Hollywood’s five surviving legacy studios have now become one, concentrating a huge library of films and television alongside streaming, broadcast networks and two global newsrooms. For audiences, the first changes are likely to emerge through release schedules, bundled subscriptions and the decisions about which overlapping services and production teams the company keeps. (Guardian, BBC)

California, New York and ten other states challenged the merger on competition grounds before reaching a settlement last month. Skydance must release at least 30 films and more than 180 television programmes a year, and CBS News and CNN must retain independent editorial boards under the supervision of a trustee. Those conditions acknowledge the two risks created by scale: fewer stories reaching screens and one owner gaining influence over a larger share of the news. CNN chief Mark Thompson will remain in place, while Ellison has already reshaped CBS News since acquiring Paramount last year. The agreement has preserved output targets and formal newsroom protections. Their force will depend on enforcement after the attention surrounding the deal fades and the difficult work of integrating two businesses begins. (Guardian)

Technology

Google’s computing expansion meets two kinds of limit

Finland has ordered Google to suspend work at two planned data centres after the company cleared land before completing the required environmental assessments. At Muhos, a Google representative felled 330 hectares of forest; nearly 200 hectares were logged at Kajaani. The sites form part of a €13 billion programme across northern Finland. Regulators say tree removal, stripped topsoil and new access roads changed the environment before the assessment process could measure those effects. Google has accepted that it fell short of its standards and says it will follow the authority’s direction, including biodiversity and planting work. The halt captures the physical speed of the AI build-out: demand for computing capacity can move faster than small municipalities, environmental review and the landscapes asked to host it. (Guardian)

In the United States, the same expansion is being measured in electricity. Google has signed a 20-year agreement with nuclear operator Constellation to upgrade six existing power stations. Constellation expects more than $4.3 billion of investment to add a combined 890 megawatts over five years, enough capacity to serve roughly 800,000 homes. The arrangement supplies predictable revenue for equipment improvements and gives Google a route to more constant low-carbon power for data centres that run around the clock. Together, the Finnish stop order and the American energy contract reveal the size of the bargain behind cloud services and generative AI. New capacity demands land, transmission, cooling and generation long before a user types a prompt. The industry’s growth will be judged as much by those local systems as by the performance of the models they support. (Verge, Guardian)

Apple’s home strategy starts with hardware made by LG

Apple is working with LG on a family of smart-home products that could include a video doorbell, smart lock, thermostat, indoor and outdoor cameras and a floodlight camera. The devices are expected to carry LG’s brand and connect tightly to Apple’s long-rumoured home hub, which may appear at an event on 13 October. Support for Thread and Matter would give several of them a common language with products outside the Apple ecosystem. The collaboration gives Apple a faster route to a complete range without designing every appliance itself, while LG gains access to customers who already use iPhones, Apple TVs and HomePods as the centre of their homes. (Verge, 9to5Mac, MacMagazine)

The reported range suggests a reset larger than another HomePod. Locks, cameras and heating controls require long support lives, clear privacy rules and reliability when the internet or a subscription fails. Matter can simplify setup across brands, though a shared standard does not decide where video is stored, how household access is granted or which features remain free. Apple’s advantage is an installed network of phones, watches and speakers that can identify people and deliver alerts. Its challenge is trust at the front door and inside private rooms. A partnership can fill the hardware catalogue quickly; the experience will still be judged by how calmly all those devices behave after the launch event is over. (Verge, 9to5Mac)

The people who make Dungeons & Dragons organise around AI

Workers on Dungeons & Dragons, Magic: The Gathering and Duel Masters are joining the Communications Workers of America unit formed by the Magic Arena team earlier this year. The expanded Wizards of the Coast union has asked Hasbro to recognise it voluntarily by 13 October. Its demands cover job security, fair pay, remote work and creative ownership, with a particularly direct call for an enforceable policy on generative AI. Employees argue that management has pushed large language models into their work without agreement from the teams responsible for building the games. The dispute places AI policy inside collective bargaining, where questions about efficiency become terms of employment and the people producing the material have a formal voice. (IGN)

The union is also challenging a company rule that can claim ownership over intellectual property employees create in their own time, even when it is unrelated to Wizards’ worlds. That concern connects naturally to generative AI: both disputes ask who controls creative work, who benefits from it and what consent means when a large company supplies the tools and contracts. The Arena group won its union election after Wizards declined voluntary recognition, so the larger unit may again need a vote supervised by the US labour board. Hasbro owns some of gaming’s most valuable shared universes. The people expanding those universes are using collective action to define the conditions under which human work remains theirs, on the job and after hours. (IGN)

Culture

Eva Marie Saint leaves a career built on quiet force

Eva Marie Saint has died at her Los Angeles home aged 102, closing one of the last careers still connected to Hollywood’s postwar golden age. Her film debut came opposite Marlon Brando in Elia Kazan’s On the Waterfront, and it brought her the 1955 Academy Award for supporting actress. Four years later she played Eve Kendall in Alfred Hitchcock’s North by Northwest, combining composure, wit and danger in a role that could easily have been overwhelmed by the machinery of the thriller around it. Saint arrived from radio and live television, where she had learned to make small gestures register. That restraint became her signature on the cinema screen and allowed her characters to carry strength without announcing it. (Guardian)

Her six-decade film career included A Hatful of Rain, Exodus, Grand Prix and Raintree County, alongside repeated returns to television. Later audiences knew her as Martha Kent in Superman Returns, released in 2006, and she continued to appear on screen into her nineties. Longevity can flatten an actor’s work into a list of famous titles, but Saint’s importance lies in the precision within them: Edie Doyle’s moral clarity in On the Waterfront, Eve Kendall’s divided loyalties and the ability to suggest a life continuing beyond the edge of the scene. She outlived most of her collaborators and never became a relic of their era. The performances stayed alert, modern and entirely her own. (Guardian)

item.title: The Fold — 2026-10-06
item.description: The Fold morning briefing for 6 October 2026: Flávio Bolsonaro takes the advantage into Brazil's runoff, Spain calls a snap election, mortgage rates reach 6%, and Europe gets invisible AI watermarks.
item.content:encoded:
LONDON · TUESDAY · 6 OCTOBER 2026 · MORNING EDITION

The Fold

Your Morning Briefing from the UK & the World

06/10/26 · 05:35 BST · London

News

Brazil's right takes the lead, and the runoff begins on new ground

Flávio Bolsonaro enters Brazil's presidential runoff as the favourite after finishing ahead of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in a first round that moved the country's politics sharply to the right. Bolsonaro won 56.1 million votes, or 47.03%, against 53.8 million and 45.16% for the incumbent. The deciding ballot comes on 25 October. The gap is only 2.2 million votes in an electorate of continental scale, yet history weighs on it: since democracy returned in 1985, no second-place candidate has overturned the first-round order. Lula now has three weeks to do something Brazil has never seen in the modern era. (Guardian, Meio, Folha)

The presidential numbers tell only part of the story. Jair Bolsonaro's Liberal party will hold 28 of the Senate's 81 seats, and the broader hard right has 43, enough for a majority. The PL also expanded from 98 to 121 deputies in the lower house. Michelle and Carlos Bolsonaro won Senate seats; Jair Renan Bolsonaro and the former president's brother Renato entered the Chamber of Deputies. Tarcísio de Freitas kept the governorship of São Paulo and Sérgio Moro won in Paraná. Jair Bolsonaro remains under house arrest while serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after the 2022 election, but his family and movement have secured the institutional strength to pursue an amnesty and pressure the supreme court. The next presidency will begin with a Congress transformed around that possibility. (Guardian, Folha)

Lula's first task is to understand the voters who stayed home. A record 33 million people abstained, while the president lost 3.4 million votes compared with his 2022 first-round total. His campaign must persuade disaffected supporters that a second ballot matters and find a route into Minas Gerais and Rio Grande do Sul, two states central to Bolsonaro's advantage. Votes cast for three other rightwing candidates add up to more than 5.5 million and are more naturally available to Bolsonaro; Romeu Zema has already declared his support, as have former president Michel Temer and influential figures across the centre-right. Lula can point to a close national margin. The map beneath it is more difficult. (Guardian, Folha)

Flávio Bolsonaro has held elected office for more than two decades, though his candidacy has been sold as renewal. At 45, he offers a generational handover without asking the movement to loosen its connection to his father. Lula, now 80, is relying on his record in government and warning that the Bolsonaro family would entrench itself in power. The campaign will also draw international attention. Donald Trump celebrated the first-round result, and Benjamin Netanyahu signalled support for Bolsonaro, while Brazil's position on climate, trade and democratic institutions gives the outcome consequences far beyond the family drama. For the next 19 days, the question is whether Lula can turn abstention and fear of a restored Bolsonaro project into a coalition broad enough to defy the country's electoral precedent. (Guardian, Meio)

A Green conference vote opens a European rupture

The Green party of England and Wales is facing a serious break with its European allies after members adopted a binding policy declaring Zionism a form of racism. The motion, passed at the Brighton conference on Sunday, supports a single democratic Palestinian state across historic Palestine and says Zionism should be treated in the same way as other forms of racism. Four of the party's five MPs voted against it. The European Green party, an alliance of 47 parties, backs a two-state solution and has demanded clarity from the British leadership about Israeli and Jewish self-determination and the protection of Jewish members. Germany's Green co-leader called the new policy incompatible with the positions of both his party and the European group. (Guardian)

The vote has also exposed a problem created by the Greens' rapid growth. A little more than 1,000 members backed the motion, amounting to about 0.4% of total membership. Policy is made directly at two annual conferences, a model intended to keep power with activists. It can now produce binding positions for a national party through participation by a very small and self-selecting group. Former co-leader Ellie Chowns wants the process modernised; other senior figures argue that direct democracy is fundamental to the party's identity. One longstanding member has resigned and accused the party of failing to confront antisemitism. Zack Polanski says antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state must remain distinct, while defending pressure on the government over Gaza. His immediate challenge is organisational as well as moral: the party needs a credible way to reconcile member control, parliamentary responsibility and alliances it may depend on as its electoral reach expands. (Guardian)

Spain turns a housing defeat into a general election

Spain will vote in a snap general election on 29 November after Pedro Sánchez's emergency housing laws were defeated in Congress. The measures included a ban on evictions until 2030 and tighter rules for temporary and room-by-room tenancies. The conservative People's party, the far-right Vox party and the Catalan party Junts combined to reject them on Friday. Housing anger has intensified since an 87-year-old Madrid resident was evicted from the flat where she had lived for 70 years after an investment fund demanded a 230% rent rise. Tens of thousands marched at the weekend, and a tent camp has grown in Puerta del Sol. Sánchez is betting that voters will connect the defeated laws to the daily cost and insecurity of renting. (Guardian)

The prime minister is also trying to reset a government that has been unable to pass a budget since 2023 and depends on a difficult coalition with Sumar and Catalan independence parties. Corruption cases involving his brother and wife, both of whom have denied wrongdoing, have damaged his position. The handling of a mass crossing into Ceuta during the summer added another source of pressure. The People's party leads the polls but may need Vox to govern, giving Sánchez a clear argument about the direction of the country even as his own record faces scrutiny. An election due by next summer has become a seven-week campaign shaped by rent, migration and the limits of minority rule. (Guardian)

Yemen's government retakes ground beside a vital shipping lane

Saudi-backed forces in Yemen have recaptured Dhubab and two other towns near the Bab al-Mandab strait as the internationally recognised government begins an offensive across Houthi-held territory. The Saudi-led coalition says 100 fighter jets are supporting the campaign and providing air protection over the narrow route between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. The advance follows a rapid Houthi push along the coast and towards Taiz, where the group cut a main supply road to Aden and tightened its encirclement of the city. More than 70 fighters on both sides were reported killed around Taiz and neighbouring Lahj in a single day. Each movement of a few miles now changes access to a city, a port or one of global trade's most sensitive chokepoints. (Guardian)

The war is again crossing Yemen's borders. The Houthis say they attacked Saudi Aramco sites in Riyadh and Khurais with missiles and drones after dozens of coalition strikes, while Saudi oil exports are already constrained by Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. Washington has defended Riyadh's right to respond but has not disclosed the extent of coordination. The government has declared an ambition to recover the whole country, a goal it failed to achieve through years of war after the Houthis seized Sanaa in 2014. The early territorial gains may protect Bab al-Mandab. They also deepen an escalation in which Yemeni civilians, energy facilities and merchant shipping share the same widening field of risk. (Guardian, BBC)

Economy

The average five-year mortgage reaches 6%

The average five-year fixed mortgage in Britain has reached 6.00% for the first time since September 2023. The average two-year fix is close behind at 5.98%, its highest level since December that year. The Bank of England has kept its base rate unchanged since last December, but fixed mortgages are priced from market expectations as well as today's official rate. Turbulence in global bond markets has lifted swap rates and made lenders' funding more expensive, prompting banks and building societies to reprice. The speed of the move is visible in the choices left to borrowers: only nine fixed deals below 5% remain, down from 1,494 at the start of September. (Guardian)

Households reaching the end of an existing fix face the most immediate shock. A £250,000 mortgage fixed for five years at 6% costs about £158 more each month than the same loan at 4.94%, the market average at the start of February. Buyers may have to reduce budgets or leave the market, while owners considering a move have another reason to stay put. Nationwide has already found that annual house-price growth halved in September. The figures also narrow the government's room on housing: building more homes will not restore affordability if financing them moves out of reach. For borrowers, the practical priority is to begin comparing options well before a current deal expires and to judge fees alongside headline rates. For policymakers, the return to 6% is a reminder that confidence in inflation and public finances arrives in monthly household payments. (Guardian)

Sainsbury's and Morrisons explored a supermarket merger

Sainsbury's and Morrisons held exploratory talks this year over a deal that would have created Britain's second-largest supermarket group with 23.6% of the grocery market. The discussions are no longer active, but they show how quickly the industry's structure could change. Tesco holds 27.8%; Sainsbury's has 15.2%, while Morrisons has fallen behind Lidl since its 2021 purchase by the American private equity firm Clayton, Dubilier & Rice. That takeover placed more than £7 billion of debt on Morrisons' balance sheet. Its owner remains open to a combination with another large grocer, and Asda could also be drawn into future discussions. (Guardian)

Any agreement would face a long competition review. Regulators blocked Sainsbury's £7 billion attempt to merge with Asda in 2019 because fewer rivals could mean higher prices, and the same concern is more politically sensitive after years of food inflation. Store disposals might answer local competition problems, though the national effect would remain large. Sainsbury's has recently sold Argos for £120 million, a decade after paying more than £1 billion, to concentrate on food. Lidl, meanwhile, has lifted annual British revenue by 10% to more than £13 billion and pre-tax profit by 30%. Traditional chains are looking for scale while discounters keep gaining it through growth. A dormant conversation between two grocers therefore says something active about the market: consolidation pressure is building even before a deal reaches the table. (Guardian)

Technology

AI writing gets an invisible mark in Europe

OpenAI is adding an invisible, machine-readable watermark to text produced by eligible ChatGPT and Codex users in the European Union. The system, called textGrain, will roll out across all plans over the coming weeks as providers adapt to the EU AI Act. API customers worldwide can opt in for selected models, while approved researchers and specialist organisations may apply for access to a detector. The detector will answer a limited question—whether it finds an OpenAI watermark—without identifying a user or revealing prompts and conversations. Google DeepMind and Anthropic have developed related approaches. The common purpose is provenance: giving platforms, institutions and investigators another signal when they need to understand how a piece of text was made. (Verge, 9to5Mac)

The limits matter as much as the mark. OpenAI says detection is fallible and can produce misses or false positives, which is why the tool will not be public at launch. A watermark cannot show whether the text is accurate, who owns it, how much a person contributed or whether an unmarked passage was written by a human. It may also be weakened when text is heavily edited, translated or passed through another model. Performance tests indicate that adding the signal does not materially reduce output quality, but OpenAI is keeping the first general rollout regional while it learns from use. Schools, publishers and regulators should treat the result as one piece of evidence that requires context, never a verdict. Europe is receiving a new trace in the text; the harder work is deciding what that trace can fairly prove. (Verge)

Utah lets an AI begin prescribing acne treatment

Adults in Utah with mild or moderate acne can now scan their faces in an app and receive a prescription selected by an AI system. Nolla Health's pilot costs $4.99 a month and can prescribe eight skin treatments. Two doctors will approve every recommendation for the first 100 patients. During the next phase, covering as many as 500 patients, doctors will review prescriptions after they have been issued; after that, at least 10% will be checked each month, together with every escalation or reported side effect. The company says uncertain cases will be directed to a physician. Utah had already allowed AI systems to renew some medicines, and this programme takes the further step of issuing an initial prescription. (Verge)

Acne is a deliberately narrow place to test autonomous prescribing: it is common, visible in images and often treated through standard pathways. That makes the pilot easier to evaluate, while the staged reduction in supervision creates a clear measure of how much confidence regulators and clinicians are willing to place in the system. Important questions remain around skin-tone performance, image privacy, contraindications, pregnancy risk, follow-up and the point at which a changing condition needs a physical examination. Low-cost routine care could reach people who struggle to see a dermatologist and leave specialists more time for complex cases. The benefit depends on a safety system that notices when an ordinary-looking problem stops being ordinary, then hands the decision to a person quickly. Utah is now testing that boundary with real prescriptions and real patients. (Verge)

Culture

Two games stories show what disappears when platforms move on

NBA 2K25 will be removed from digital stores on 30 October, just over two years after its release, and its servers will close on 1 January 2027. Owners will retain offline modes including Play Now, MyNBA, The W and MyWNBA. MyCareer, however, is a single-player story tied to online progression and virtual currency, so it will become unplayable along with multiplayer and MyTeam. Players who built a character, advanced through seasons and spent money inside the mode are approaching an expiry date imposed by infrastructure. Their copies remain otherwise functional. Annual sports games have always encouraged migration to the latest edition. Server-dependent design turns that commercial rhythm into permanent loss. (IGN)

At Ninja Theory, the loss is happening before unfinished work reaches players. Staff at the Cambridge studio behind Hellblade have begun announcing departures after Microsoft said it intended to close the company when two rescue deals failed. Programmers, audio specialists and performance-capture staff describe projects they will not finish and production systems built over years. Microsoft unveiled Senua, a third Hellblade game, in June, and the trailer is widely understood to have been intended to attract a buyer. The closure sits inside a larger Xbox reorganisation that has also brought layoffs at Halo Studios and moved several development teams under Activision or Bethesda. One story removes a game people paid for; the other disperses the people and knowledge needed to make the next one. Together they sharpen an old preservation question: ownership in digital culture can be temporary, and the archive is often controlled by the company with the next release to sell. (IGN, IGN)

Jeffrey Archer dies on the eve of his final novel

Jeffrey Archer has died aged 86, one day before the publication of what he had described as his final novel. His publisher said he died suddenly and peacefully at home between writing sessions. Archer sold about 300 million books in 119 countries and 49 languages; Kane and Abel alone sold more than 30 million copies. The writing career began after bankruptcy forced him to leave Parliament in 1974. His first novel, Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less, restored his finances and opened five decades of novels, short stories, plays and children's books. On Sunday he was still signing books and speaking to a sold-out audience in Leicester Square. (Guardian, BBC)

His public life repeatedly rose and collapsed. Archer entered the Commons at 29, returned to Conservative prominence as deputy chair under Margaret Thatcher and became the party's candidate for London mayor. That campaign ended when evidence showed he had lied during a successful 1987 libel case over allegations involving a sex worker. He was convicted of perjury and perverting the course of justice in 2001, sentenced to four years and served half. He later returned to writing and remained in the House of Lords until retiring in 2024, without taking an active role. The scale of his readership and the gravity of his conviction resist a tidy closing judgment. His last book, Adam and Eve, arrives today with the author absent and with that contradiction intact: a disciplined popular storyteller whose appetite for reinvention could never erase the court record that ended his politics. (Guardian)
